decisions.title: Native compile-time host reads keep the two-part Impure gate
decisions.situation: Jet can read a file or other host input while compiling, but only when the code is wrapped in a marked block and the build command also grants permission. The old compiler honored both parts. The new compiler refuses every such read, even when both are present, while its error message still tells you to add them. We recommend restoring the documented two-part gate exactly, recording every input it reads, and keeping the old compiler until this port is proven.
decisions.gist: Should the native compiler honor the marked block plus build permission for compile-time host reads?
decisions.lesson: Compile-time code normally cannot touch the outside world. A marked block plus a build-command grant lets it read host input on purpose. A restores that two-part gate and records each input. B removes the ability and rewrites the promise.
decisions.explainer: Each half has a job. The marked block, with a reason string, shows reviewers where the build reads the host. The build grant lets CI see and refuse builds that read the host. Recording each input read lets caches and audits notice when that input changes. Without the grant, the code gets a clear error naming the missing half. Pinned inputs such as embedded files and hashed downloads need neither half and stay unchanged.
decisions.story: Priya bakes a configuration file into her program at build time. She writes the marked block with a reason and passes the grant in CI. She needs the build to work as the manual says, or to fail with advice that actually works.
decisions.inWild:
# Rust build scripts read the host freely and must declare what they read
# so Cargo knows when to rerun them.
# https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/build-scripts.html#rerun-if-changed
println!("cargo:rerun-if-changed=config.txt");
# Bazel forbids undeclared host reads unless a rule opts out explicitly.
# https://bazel.build/docs/sandboxing
decisions.detail:
Revised 2026-10-10 because the owner did not ratify the posted A. The posted A recommended restoring the gate. Its one recorded loss was porting work, which never ranks an option and is not a cost to users. This version keeps that recommendation and closes the two real gaps it left open. First, the native compiler records every input an allowed read observes, as the spec requires. Second, the old compiler path stays until this port passes its tests, so no user loses the feature in between.

The ratified contract. Docs/spec/reference/metaprogramming.md:83-129 defines three compile-time tiers. Tier 2 (ambient file, environment, process, clock, random or unpinned network access) needs #Impure("reason") in source and --gate impure=allow on the build command. A runtime statement inside #Impure needs no grant. The spec also says to keep declarations, grants and resulting inputs in the package and lock records.

Snapshots: tests/ui/impure_tier2_no_gate.stderr expects E3410 without the block. tests/ui/impure_no_flag.stderr expects E3411 with the block but without the grant. tests/ui/impure_net_stub expects E3412: even with both halves, only the pinned fetch is a compile-time network operation. Shipped examples teach the gate: Examples/features/comptime/comptime_tiers.jet and Examples/features/effects/audited_gate_ladder.jet.

Native state (FixLeadSema evidence). The Rust evaluator checked impure depth, then Policy::resolve_invocation(Impure, gates) (crates/jet-comptime/src/Comptime/Methods/dispatch/eval_method.rs:846-871). The native pieces exist but are not connected. MIR has MIRScopeKind.Impure (JetFoundation/Source/MIR/MIR.jet:112), lowering keeps the scope (JetCodegen Statements.jet:2396), and JetEval records active scopes (Evaluator.jet:9973-9989).

The missing links. Driver/Identity.jet:240 carries request.gate_set, but the evaluator configuration (EvalValues.jet:561-575) has no GateSet, and the CLI never assigns --gate into the request. The canonical MIR evaluator refuses every effectful Core call with E3410 regardless of scope (crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/MIREval.rs:22441-22472 in Rust; same rule natively). D-NATIVE-ANALYSIS-GAPS1 lists the same missing authorization state under its E3412 row.

What A does. Assign --gate into the request, pass the GateSet into the evaluator, and keep the inherited Impure scope when comptime bodies are synthesized. Without the block, E3410. With the block but no grant, E3411. With both, the read runs and its path and content hash join the lock and build receipt. Stronger policy forbids still win, and network stays limited to pinned fetch (E3412). The old compiler path is not deleted until this row's tests pass natively, which is the staging rule in D-NATIVE-ANALYSIS-GAPS1.

Precedent. Cargo build scripts read the host freely but must declare rerun-if-changed inputs. Missing declarations are a known source of stale builds. Bazel sandboxes actions so undeclared reads fail. Zig and Rust const evaluation forbid I/O entirely and push it to build scripts, which split one feature into two languages. Jet's gate keeps one language, makes the read visible in source and in CI, and records the input like Cargo and Bazel.

Why not B. B removes a ratified, documented capability because one evaluator is unfinished. It also needs a contract rewrite, new E3410 advice and new snapshots. Users would move host reads into build entries, which is a second mechanism for the same job.

options.name: Restore the two-part gate and record every input it reads
options.detail: A compile-time host read works only inside the marked block and with the build grant. A missing half gets its own clear error. Each allowed read is recorded with its content hash, so caches rebuild and audits see it. The old compiler path stays until this port passes its tests.
options.technical: Thread --gate into request.gate_set and the evaluator's GateSet; keep inherited Impure scope in synthesized comptime bodies. E3410 bare, E3411 gated but not allowed, execute when allowed; append path and hash to the lock and receipt. Policy forbids win; E3412 still limits network to pinned fetch.

options.name: Refuse all compile-time host reads
options.detail: Compile-time code may never read the host, even with the block and the grant. The contract, the E3410 advice and the snapshots are rewritten. Host reads move to build entries or runtime.
options.technical: Keep the MIR refusal; delete the advice that names #Impure plus --gate; reviewed snapshots expect E3410 or an earlier purity error. BuildContext services stay separately governed.

comparisons.note: Host reads are allowed but must be declared so the build reruns when they change.
Sandboxed actions fail on undeclared host reads; opting out is explicit.

recommendation.why: A keeps a ratified, documented feature working exactly as the manual says. Every host read is visible in source, granted in CI, and recorded for caches and audits. Keeping the old path until the port is proven means no user loses it in between.
gains: The documented block-plus-grant combination works natively.
Each missing half gets an error whose advice works.
Every host read is recorded, so builds stay auditable and caches stay correct.

whyNot.reason: B deletes a ratified capability because one evaluator is unfinished, and pushes host reads into a second mechanism.

recommendation.tradeoff: None for users: the feature, its errors and its audit trail match the ratified contract.

decisions.checkInstructions: Run native tests/ui/impure_tier2_no_gate.jet (E3410), tests/ui/impure_no_flag.jet (E3411) and tests/ui/impure_net_stub.jet (E3412). Add an allowed block-plus-grant read that runs and records its path and hash in the lock and receipt. Add nested helper calls, inherited comptime context, branches that do not run, policy-forbid precedence, and a runtime-only #Impure block needing no grant. Check the old compiler path is not deleted before these pass.

surface.gist: Should the native compiler honor the marked block plus build permission for compile-time host reads?
surface.lesson: Compile-time code cannot touch the host unless a marked block and a build grant both allow it. A restores that. B forbids it.

current.note: Refused even with the block and the grant; the advice cannot work.

wild.note: Host reads are allowed but declared, so builds rerun when inputs change.

options.name: Restore the two-part gate
options.gist: Block plus grant allows the read; each read is recorded.
gains: The manual is true again.
Errors give working advice.
Every host read is auditable.

proposed.code:
jet build --gate impure=allow
# read runs; path and hash recorded

options.name: Forbid host reads
options.gist: Refuse even with block and grant; rewrite the manual.
gains: No compile-time host reads at all.
losses: A documented feature is removed.

proposed.code:
jet build --gate impure=allow
# still refused

recommendation.why: A keeps the documented feature, with each host read visible, granted and recorded.
gains: Working feature and working advice.
Auditable builds.

whyNot.reason: It deletes a ratified feature because one evaluator is unfinished.

recommendation.tradeoff: None for users.

decisions.title: Keep the release password-salt rule by making the salted helper private to Core
decisions.situation: Jet's safe password hashing picks a random salt for you, using a helper that also accepts a caller-chosen salt. A fixed salt makes every user's hash predictable, so the old compiler refused direct calls to that helper. The new compiler does not, because the helper is now ordinary library code that the safe function itself calls. We recommend making the helper private to the core library, so no user code can reach it and the existing refusal keeps working unchanged.
decisions.gist: How should the native compiler keep user code from choosing a fixed password salt?
decisions.lesson: A salt is random bytes mixed into a password hash so equal passwords hash differently. A hides the fixed-salt helper inside Core. B keeps it public and teaches the compiler which callers may use it. C keeps it public with no rule.
decisions.explainer: The safe function and the fixed-salt helper live in the same core library file. Making the helper private changes nothing for the safe function, because it calls the helper from inside. Any outside call is then a misuse by definition, so the compiler can report the existing salt error without tracing who called what. Fixed test vectors keep their audited route: the expert Argon2id function inside an unsafe block, which the error message already recommends.
decisions.story: Priya writes a login service and calls the safe password function, which must pick a fresh salt every time. Her teammate tries the fixed-salt helper to make a test print the same hash twice. Jet should point the teammate to the audited expert route instead of letting a fixed salt reach production.
decisions.inWild:
RustCrypto Argon2 separates random-salt password hashing from the explicit-salt key-derivation primitive. https://docs.rs/argon2/latest/argon2/
Argon2::default().hash_password(password)?; // documented random salt
Argon2::default().hash_password_into(password, salt, &mut output)?; // explicit salt
decisions.detail:
Revised 2026-10-10 because the owner did not ratify the posted A. The posted A kept the helper public and asked the native checker to tell vetted Core callers from user callers by tracing source origin. Its recorded loss was implementation machinery, which never ranks an option. The real flaw was a public function whose every outside call is an error. The new A removes that contradiction, so the tracing is not needed.

Current code (dev). Core/crypto/crypto.jet:771-775: pub fn password_hash draws random.bytes(16) and calls password_hash_with_salt. Lines 777-787: pub fn password_hash_with_salt(password: Secret, salt: [U8]) runs rawcrypto.argon2id inside #Unsafe. password_verify (789-813) calls rawcrypto.argon2id itself and never calls the helper. Core/crypto/expert.jet:515 is pub fn argon2id with explicit salt and cost, the audited expert route.

The ratified contract. D-CRYPTO-DIAG1=A gives focused E2702 crypto-misuse diagnostics. tests/ui/crypto_release_entropy_seam.stderr expects E2702 at the salt argument. Its fix text says to use crypto.password_hash so Jet generates the salt, or to move a fixed vector to expert.argon2id inside #Unsafe. D-PWHASH1=A ratified password_hash and password_verify as the password surface; the salted helper is not part of it.

Why the old guard fails natively. The Rust checker (crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerCoreLib/core_call.rs:681-695) matched the name core.crypto.password_hash_with_salt. It ran only on the fixed-signature path, which still typed the password as String (CorePlatformSignatures.jet:209). A Secret-typed call left that path and was admitted, so Examples/features/crypto/primitive_matrix.jet:154 compiled. The native compiler checks the real Jet source, so the old fixture now gets E0112 for String, and a Secret-typed call gets no E2702.

What A changes. Drop pub from the helper. Remove it from the core.crypto export rows (CoreCallRows.jet:1831, CoreSources.jet:28) and delete its stale String signature row. The native checker gets one misuse row keyed by the helper's declaration. A reference from outside Core reports E2702 with the existing why and fix, ahead of argument typing, so the golden stays byte-identical. Visibility already separates Core's own call from user calls, so no source tracing is needed.

Migration. primitive_matrix.jet prints its fixed vector with expert.argon2id inside the #Unsafe block it already has, and keeps the password_verify round trip through password_hash. tests/conformance/corpus/core/crypto/password_hash_with_salt.jet becomes a password_hash plus password_verify check. Jet is pre-1.0, so a clean break needs no deprecation.

Precedent: RustCrypto Argon2 and libsodium (crypto_pwhash_str) expose random-salt password hashing as the safe API. Explicit salt lives only on the lower-level key-derivation primitive.

options.name: Make the salted helper private to Core
options.detail: The helper stops being public. The safe password function keeps calling it from inside Core. Any reference from user code reports the existing salt error, which names the safe function and the audited expert route. Fixed test vectors use the expert Argon2id function inside an unsafe block.
options.technical: Drop pub; remove the export rows and stale signature row; add one native E2702 misuse row keyed by the declaration, checked before argument types. Migrate primitive_matrix.jet and the conformance case. The E2702 golden is unchanged.

options.name: Keep it public; trace which callers may use it
options.detail: The helper stays public. The checker reports E2702 for user calls but allows Core's own call, by tracing where each call comes from.
options.technical: Resolve declaration identity and source origin, validate arguments first, then publish CryptoMisuse with solved-effect diagnostics. Test aliases, imported names and Core-internal calls.
options.code:
crypto.password_hash_with_salt(pw, fixed)   // E2702 from user code
// same call inside Core: allowed by origin tracing

options.name: Keep it public with no salt rule
options.detail: Release code may hash passwords with a salt it chooses. The salt error is retired and the old fixture's snapshot becomes the plain type error.
options.technical: Revise the D-CRYPTO-DIAG1 entropy row and the E2702 golden; document that callers own salt policy.
options.code: crypto.password_hash_with_salt(pw, fixed)   // admitted

comparisons.note: The password API generates the salt; explicit salt exists only on the lower-level derivation call.

recommendation.why: A keeps the ratified salt rule and its exact error with no new compiler machinery, because privacy already separates Core's own call from user calls. It matches the ratified password surface, and fixed test vectors keep the audited expert route.
gains: User code can never choose a password salt by accident.
The existing error and fix text stay exactly the same.
The safe password function works unchanged.
No caller tracing in the compiler.

whyNot.reason: B keeps a public function that is always an error from outside, and needs caller tracing to excuse Core's own call.
C lets release code ship predictable password hashes and drops a ratified safety error.

recommendation.tradeoff: None: the helper was never part of the ratified password surface, and its one legitimate caller is inside Core.

decisions.checkInstructions: Run native tests/ui/crypto_release_entropy_seam.jet: E2702 at the salt span with the existing why and fix, before any type error. Also check a Secret-typed user call, an aliased module and an imported-name call; each gives E2702. Check password_hash and password_verify round-trip, and that Examples/features/crypto/primitive_matrix.jet and the conformance case pass after migration. Check password_hash_with_salt is absent from the core.crypto export rows.

surface.gist: How should the native compiler keep user code from choosing a fixed password salt?
surface.lesson: A salt makes equal passwords hash differently. A hides the fixed-salt helper inside Core. B traces callers. C drops the rule.

current.note: A typed call to the fixed-salt helper is no longer refused.
current.code: crypto.password_hash_with_salt(pw, fixed)   // admitted today

wild.note: Password hashing picks the salt; explicit salt sits on a lower-level call.

options.name: Private to Core
options.gist: Only Core's safe function can use the fixed-salt helper.
gains: Same error and fix as before.
No caller tracing needed.

proposed.code:
crypto.password_hash(pw)                    // random salt
crypto.password_hash_with_salt(pw, fixed)   // E2702

options.name: Public, trace callers
options.gist: The checker tells Core's call from user calls.
gains: The helper stays public.
losses: A public function that is always an error outside.

proposed.code: crypto.password_hash_with_salt(pw, fixed)   // E2702 from user code

options.name: Public, no rule
options.gist: Callers own salt choice.
gains: Fewer rules.
losses: Predictable password hashes can ship.

proposed.code: crypto.password_hash_with_salt(pw, fixed)   // admitted

recommendation.why: Privacy keeps the salt rule exact with no new compiler machinery. Test vectors keep the audited expert route.
gains: No accidental fixed salts.
Same error as before.

whyNot.reason: A public function that always errors outside Core.
Predictable password hashes could ship.

recommendation.tradeoff: None: the helper was never part of the public password surface.

decisions.title: Whether standard input reports if it is a terminal
decisions.situation: Core lets a program ask whether stdout or stderr is a terminal with is_tty. Standard input has no such question. Jetpack asks it in 13 places before prompting: trust gates, download confirmation, environment export and the dashboard. Without it, Jetpack cannot tell a person at a keyboard from a pipe. You choose whether stdin gets the same method. We recommend adding is_tty to StdinHandle, mirroring Stdout and Stderr exactly.
decisions.gist: Should term.stdin() answer is_tty like stdout and stderr?
decisions.lesson: A program prompts only when a person can answer. Stdout and stderr already report is_tty. A adds the same method to stdin, B adds one module function, and C keeps prompts on an explicit flag.
decisions.explainer: Prompting into a pipe hangs or reads garbage. Today Jetpack's prompt checks cannot compile. Adding one read-only query changes no existing behavior.
decisions.story: Ravi pipes a script into jetpack env export. Today the trust gate cannot ask whether stdin is a terminal, so it cannot safely skip the prompt.
decisions.inWild:
# Python asks the same question on every standard stream.
# https://docs.python.org/3/library/io.html#io.IOBase.isatty
sys.stdin.isatty()
# Rust exposes IsTerminal on stdin, stdout and stderr alike.
# https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.IsTerminal.html
std::io::stdin().is_terminal()
decisions.detail: Core/term/term.jet: Stdout.is_tty and Stderr.is_tty call core.term.__stdout_terminal and __stderr_terminal. StdinHandle has only read_line. Callers: Jetpack Foundation/Terminal (3), Trust/TrustGate (3), CLI DownloadConfirm, EnvExport, ToolCommand, Dashboard (2), Nix FallbackPolicy, Foundation test.

options.name: Add is_tty to StdinHandle
options.detail: Add fn is_tty(&self) -[IO]> Bool to StdinHandle. It returns true only when standard input is a terminal. It reads no input and never fails.
options.technical: New raw leaf core.term.__stdin_terminal beside the stdout/stderr leaves; one runtime symbol for every tier (I9).

options.name: Add a module function
options.detail: Add fn stdin_is_tty() -[IO]> Bool to core.term. Handles keep their current methods.
options.technical: Same raw leaf, exposed as a module function.

options.name: No query; prompts need an explicit flag
options.detail: Core adds nothing. Jetpack prompts only when the user passes an interactive flag.
options.technical: Rewrite the 13 Jetpack call sites to read a flag.
options.code: jetpack env export --interactive

recommendation.why: A mirrors the existing Stdout and Stderr method, so every stream answers the same question the same way.
gains: Jetpack prompt checks compile with one rename.

losses.loss: Core gains one public method and one runtime leaf.
losses.mitigation: It mirrors two existing methods and their leaves.

whyNot.reason: B spells the same question differently for one stream.
C makes every interactive command require a flag.

recommendation.tradeoff: One small public method in exchange for uniform terminal checks.

decisions.checkInstructions: Check stdin().is_tty() is false under a pipe and true under a PTY on every tier, and that the 13 Jetpack callers use it.

decisions.title: Which compiler layers Jetpack may call
decisions.situation: Jetpack builds as one unit with a slice of the compiler: foundation, lexer and parser files. Four Jetpack paths call deeper compiler layers. The Rust bridge checks inline assembly with sema. Module evaluation calls the CLI's comptime evaluator. Cache publication reuses the static linker's error. Project jobs call the compile driver. Those layers are outside the slice, so the unit cannot check. You choose the boundary. We recommend moving the four shared pieces down into Foundation.
decisions.gist: May Jetpack call sema, the CLI evaluator, the linker and the driver?
decisions.lesson: Jetpack compiles with only part of the compiler. Four calls reach past that part. A moves the shared pieces down, B lists the deeper layers in Jetpack, and C removes the calls.
decisions.explainer: Each layer Jetpack calls must build with Jetpack. Listing whole layers grows the unit past its memory budget. Moving small shared pieces keeps the unit small and the layering one-way.
decisions.story: Ana checks the Jetpack unit after a sema change. Today the check fails on names Jetpack borrowed from sema and the driver, not on her change.
decisions.inWild:
# Cargo depends on cargo-util and crates-io helpers, not on rustc internals.
# https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/tree/master/crates
cargo build -p cargo-util
# Go's cmd/go reuses go/build and go/parser, never the compiler backend.
# https://pkg.go.dev/go/build
go list -deps cmd/go
decisions.detail: The edges come from Jetpack/Bootstrap/compiler-slice.mjs. RustBridge/Externs calls JetSema InlineAssembly. EnvModel WorkspaceFile and ModuleEval call JetCli ConfigEval comptime_evaluate and JetSema sema_e3402. Store/CachePublication calls JetBackend StaticLink link_error. CLI/Jobs/ProjectEntry calls JetDriver compile-mode and error helpers.

options.name: Move the shared pieces into Foundation
options.detail: Move the inline-assembly target table, the comptime evaluation entry, the link error type and the compile-mode check into JetFoundation. Jetpack and the compiler both call them there.
options.technical: Relocate four small APIs; the slice check then passes with no new layers.
options.code: foundation_inline_assembly_target_supported(target)

options.name: List the deeper layers in Jetpack
options.detail: Add JetSema, JetCli ConfigEval, JetBackend StaticLink and JetDriver files to Jetpack's compiler slice.
options.technical: Extend the Compiler front-end section; the slice closure pulls most of the compiler.
options.code:
# == Compiler front end ==
Compiler/JetDriver/Source/Driver/Pipeline.jet

options.name: Remove the four calls
options.detail: Jetpack stops validating inline assembly, evaluating modules through comptime, reusing link errors and compiling jobs in-process. It shells out to jet instead.
options.technical: Replace calls with jet subprocess invocations.
options.code: process.cmd(["jet", "check", entry])

recommendation.why: A keeps the Jetpack unit small and makes the shared pieces one-way dependencies.
gains: The slice check passes with no growth.

losses.loss: Four APIs move to Foundation.
losses.mitigation: Each has one or two callers; the move is mechanical.

whyNot.reason: B pulls most of the compiler into an already memory-bound unit.
C trades typed in-process results for subprocess output.

recommendation.tradeoff: Move four small APIs to keep the layering clean.

decisions.title: Port every missing native check before the Rust compiler is deleted
decisions.situation: Jet is replacing its Rust compiler with one written in Jet, which already builds itself. Seventeen checks and runtime safety reports still exist only in the Rust compiler, and shipped examples use most of them. Deleting Rust now would either refuse those programs or let them through unchecked. We recommend porting all seventeen first, in a fixed order, each proven by its existing test, and deleting the Rust compiler the day the last one passes.
decisions.gist: How should the cutover handle checks that only the Rust compiler performs today?
decisions.lesson: A compiler must check a feature or refuse it, never skip it. A ports every missing check before deleting Rust and keeps today's behavior meanwhile. B deletes Rust now and refuses those features until ported. C keeps the Rust compiler with no end date.
decisions.story: User wants Rust gone from the repository. Lee builds the shipped web example, and Ana counts on runaway recursion stopping with a clear error. Both need exactly the checks they have today on the day Rust is deleted.
decisions.detail:
Revised 2026-10-10 at Main's request because the drafted A refused features users rely on. Mapping: new A is the drafted B (finish every check first), staged and sized. New B is the drafted A. C is unchanged in substance but marked open-ended. No code, snapshot or Tower state was changed by this file.

Why the drafted A had a real loss. A text census of shipped examples (git grep on Examples/**/*.jet, 2026-10-10) found uses of most rows. Web targets appear in Examples/features/web (29 files) and Examples/embedded/browser_wasm. OS targets appear in Examples/features/lowlevel/os_target_gating.jet, io/os_process_control.jet and comptime/fact_plane.jet. Context blocks appear in effects/smart_context.jet and concurrency/deadline_context.jet. Contracts appear in contracts/pre_post.jet and carrier_binding.jet.

More uses: budgets in game/core_game_headless.jet and tooling/testing_helpers.jet. Layout blocks in ui/layout_basic.jet. Frame scheduling in game/resource_schedule/run.jet. Build actions in foundations/tooling/graph/graph.jet. No-OS targets in embedded/heap_free_core. Rust imports, which reach the foreign-breach boundary, in 9 files. Refusing those features would stop shipped examples from building.

Why waiting is the only loss-free schedule. Every earlier deletion either refuses programs that check today or accepts them unchecked. Philosophy: implementation difficulty is not a reason to lower the bar. Go followed the same rule in Go 1.5: the C compiler was deleted once the translated Go compiler produced the same results.

Meanwhile. The native compiler already self-hosts (stage1 == stage2), so nothing builds Jet with Rust. Everything in the cutover that deletes no needed check lands now: tooling, homes, seed and CI, peers, and the emit retirement. The Rust-backed lanes keep running only the gap rows' snapshots. The native compiler refuses each unported feature at its entry point, so a native run never skips a check.

decisions.title: How Jetpack gets compiler work done when the work is the compiler itself
decisions.situation: Jetpack, Jet's package manager, still borrows three pieces of the compiler that cannot move down into a shared base. Two of them need the whole compiler: working out computed values in environment files, and fully checking a project to list its jobs. The third generates a Rust wrapper for C functions a Jet library imports, under a name the compiler no longer produces. We recommend that Jetpack ask its sibling jet program for checked results, and that imported C functions be called directly.
decisions.gist: How should Jetpack get checking and evaluation from the compiler, and how are imported C functions named?
decisions.lesson: Jetpack is built with only a thin slice of the compiler. A asks the jet program that ships beside it and calls imported C functions by their own name. B plugs the compiler into Jetpack through interfaces and shares one naming function. C builds Jetpack with the whole compiler inside.
decisions.explainer: The earlier ruling moved small shared pieces below both programs. These three cannot follow it. Evaluating a computed config value means type-checking and running a small Jet program, and listing jobs means checking the whole project. Both are the compiler's job, and the language keeps exactly one compile-time evaluation path. Jet and Jetpack already ship as two programs that call each other with an exact version check. The C import wrapper exists only because the old Rust backend could not call C directly; the native backend can.
decisions.story: Ana adds a computed field to her environment file and runs a Jetpack command. Jetpack must get the same value and the same error message that jet would give, without carrying a second copy of the compiler.
decisions.inWild:
# Cargo never links rustc; it runs it and reads JSON records back.
# https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/external-tools.html#json-messages
cargo build --message-format=json
# rust-analyzer runs macros in a separate, version-matched server process.
# https://rust-analyzer.github.io/book/configuration.html (procMacro.server)
# Bazel keeps one long-lived worker per tool to avoid startup cost.
# https://bazel.build/remote/persistent
decisions.detail:
Follow-up to D-JETPACK-LAYERS1=A (ratified 2026-10-10), which moved shared pieces into JetFoundation. CutoverPrep landed edge 1 (inline-assembly register tables, dev 8c745981d). It reported that two edges cannot follow A because the callee is the compiler. Main added a third edge: the RustBridge guest-import wrapper name.

Edge 1, config values. Jetpack/EnvModel calls comptime_evaluate in Workspace/WorkspaceFile.jet:221,427 and ModuleEval/ComputedFields.jet:124. ComputedFields serves DevServiceEval, EnvFields, IntegrationImports and SecretSpecs. That function lives in Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/ConfigEval.jet. A plain literal returns at once. Every other value becomes a small self-contained Jet program, which jet_driver_compile checks and evaluates in Comptime mode. This is the I8 single comptime path; moving it into Foundation would drag the driver with it.

Edge 2, the job registry. Jetpack/CLI/Source/Jobs/ProjectEntry.jet:100-105 calls jet_driver_load_entry, jet_driver_check_bundle and jet_driver_has_errors to check the whole entry bundle before listing #Job functions. Its own header already says jetpack never links the compiler in-process for running (D-JPK-DISPATCH1); this check is the one exception.

Edge 3, guest C imports. Jetpack/PackageModel/Source/Foreign/RustBridge/Externs.jet:345-351 builds a Rust wrapper for each #Import(c) function, named by sema_guest_import_wrapper_name. The Rust compiler spelled that name as mangle_path("jet_ffi_guest.<owner>.<name>") in crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/Guest.rs:91-94.

Its codegen called the same function, so both sides agreed. The native compiler has no successor. Its Rust emitter names foreign rows with jet_rust_emit_generated_path(foreign.key), and D-RUST-EMIT1=A retired that emitter. The two sides can no longer agree on the name.

Why A removes edge 3 instead of renaming it. The native backend already lowers direct C imports by their declared symbol (Compiler/JetBackend/Source/Lower/CForeign.jet:211, lower_c_import_call). It supports C scalars and read-only text, which covers the guest scalar law in Docs/spec/architecture.md. An #Import(c) function becomes an ordinary C foreign row whose symbol is the string the user wrote, so no wrapper and no generated name exist. The Rust bridge keeps serving extern rust helpers (D-FFI-RUST1=A).

The existing boundary A reuses. D-JPK-DISPATCH1=B: jet runs the jetpack binary by name after an --engine-protocol handshake, and version skew is E1227. A runs the same lookup in reverse: the sibling jet next to the running jetpack first (cli_find_jet_binary already exists), then PATH, with the same exact-version handshake.

The session. One jet self session process per jetpack command, started on first need. Requests and replies are JSON lines on standard input and output. Each carries Foundation records both programs already share. A config request sends the program text and base directory and gets a CtValue or Diagnostic. A job request sends an entry path and gets the checked job registry or diagnostics. jet renders nothing; Jetpack renders the returned Diagnostic with the Foundation renderer it already has, so messages match jet's exactly.

Proven right ways: Cargo never links rustc and reads its JSON, and Go's cmd/go runs compile as a subprocess. rust-analyzer runs proc macros in a version-matched server. Bazel persistent workers keep one long-lived process to remove startup cost. Known wrong ways: tools that link a private copy of the compiler drift from the real one; rust-analyzer had to add its proc-macro server for exactly this reason. One process per request is also wrong when requests are many; Bazel workers exist to fix that.

Plain literal values never start jet. #Import(c) functions are called directly by the C symbol the user wrote, so the Rust wrapper and its generated name are retired.

Delete Jetpack's comptime_evaluate and jet_driver_* calls. decisions.title: A Copyable trait for copies inside generic code
decisions.situation: Some Jet values own a cleanup duty, like an open socket that must close exactly once, and Jet refuses to copy them. A generic function, written once for any type T, can still copy T, and Jet accepts that even when T is a socket. Four library functions also name a Clone trait that does not exist, and the random-pick one cannot be called at all. You asked whether a trait would help, and it does. We recommend a built-in Copyable trait that Jet gives every copyable type automatically, which a generic names when it copies T, with an error that writes it for you.
decisions.gist: Should copying a value inside generic code require a Copyable trait that Jet grants automatically?
decisions.lesson: A trait is a named ability a type has, such as Equatable for ==. A generic function works for any type T, and Jet already makes it write T: Equatable before using == on T. Copying is the one ability Jet never asks for, so a socket can be copied through a generic. Jet's checker already knows which types are copyable. This vote decides how generic code says it needs that.
decisions.explainer:
Your question: yes, a trait is the clearest fix. Copyable is a built-in trait like Equatable or Printable. It names exactly the values that have .copy(). Jet works it out from a type's fields, so nobody writes it on a type.

Beginner path: most people never type it. Calling pick([1, 2, 3]) just works. Writing a generic function that copies T gives one error whose fix adds T: Copyable, and jet fix applies it.

Expert path: write T: Copyable when a generic copies T. Leave it off when T only moves, so lists, options and helpers can still carry sockets. Write #!Copyable on a type that must never be duplicated, such as a one-time ticket, using the refusal mark Jet already has for derived traits.

What a caller sees: Socket isn't Copyable because it closes once. Move it with ^, or pass something copyable.
decisions.story: Priya writes pick(items) to return a random item for her game, and it copies the chosen item. Later Sam passes a list of open sockets to pick. Jet accepts it, so two owners of one socket could both try to close it.
decisions.detail:
Owner question, 2026-10-11 UTC, verbatim: "this is not at all clear to me, please rework. it seems like having a trait would be useful". This revision answers yes. It rebuilds the ballot around a Copyable trait and weighs it against inferring the need from function bodies, and against Swift's copyable-by-default model.

The hole, from FixLeadSema's five probes on the Rust-host jet built from 79f81529e. Concrete Resource.copy() is E0211. Generic duplicate<Resource>, pick<Resource>, a generic method pick<Resource>, and duplicate_list<Resource> are each accepted with status zero. Follow-up probes on the same binary on 2026-10-10 show a move-only identity<Resource> and a [Resource] list accepted, and they must stay accepted. Scripts and outputs live in the FixLeadSema probe results and the BallotRework probes folder.

A second concrete gap on the same binary. [Resource].copy() and Holder{inner: Resource}.copy() are accepted, although the spec says a type holding a resource by value has a cleanup duty. The native classifier in Ownership/Copy.jet already rejects both by walking fields. That walk is source evidence only; it was not executed.

Why unconstrained T passes. Native Ownership/Copy.jet:282-288 treats a type parameter as cloneable unless it is bounded by Close. The Rust host's Diagnostics.rs:731 also treats a type variable as cloneable. No check later rejects the concrete instantiation.

Library calls that fail. Core/math/random.jet:120, 125 and 142 declare pick, weighted_pick and sample with T: Clone, and Core/web/table.jet:314 declares update_row with T: Clone. No Clone trait is registered in either compiler's built-in list. A probe calling random.rng(7) then pick on a String list fails with E0905, String isn't Clone, plus cascading errors. update_row uses the same unregistered bound [INFERENCE: not probed]. The comment at random.jet:152 claims Clone excludes Close owners, which nothing enforces.

Jet's existing rule for other abilities. A probe confirms that a == b on an unconstrained T is E0312 and a > b is E0109. With T: Equatable and T: Comparable both pass. Copying is the only ability generic code may use without stating it. D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1=A says bounds are checked at the definition. D-INFER-LEVEL1=A says signatures stay written, with an error that writes them.

Derived traits already work this way. Under S55 and D-META-AUTO1=A, Printable, Equatable, Debug, Comparable, Encode and Decode are derived whenever every field qualifies. A type refuses one with #!Name. Copyable fits the same family and the same refusal mark. It generates no code; it only names a fact the copy classifier already computes.

How other languages do it. Rust requires T: Clone and checks it where the generic is written; Clone is opt-in per type.

Swift made every type Copyable by default and added ~Copyable in SE-0390. SE-0427 then had to let generic code opt out with T: ~Copyable, and standard types such as Optional needed updates to hold noncopyable values.

Mojo's library defines a Copyable trait that generic containers name. C++ templates show the cost of inference: a deleted copy constructor fails deep inside a template body, and C++20 added std::copyable concepts to move that error to the signature. Zig infers from the body at instantiation and reports errors inside the generic code.

Size of the change, by a heuristic census on 2026-10-10. Core, Examples and Jetpack have 314 generic function declarations. At most 60 contain .copy() in their body, and some of those copy a String key rather than T. Of those 60, only the 4 Clone declarations state any copy requirement today. The Rust codegen already emits where T: Clone for parameters it finds copied in a body, at Emit/Functions.jet:2178, which is the inference the front end lacks.

Edge cases under A. Shared<T> stays Copyable for every T, because copying it shares one handle. A generic struct Box<T> is Copyable when every stored field is, and a phantom parameter does not count, as for Equatable. A distinct type follows its base type; the classifier now marks every distinct type cloneable at Copy.jet:448, which A corrects.

More edge cases. Recursive types follow the classifier's existing cycle rule. Function values, trait values, Cell guards, tasks and foreign handles are not Copyable, with the reasons E0211 gives today. An implicit copy of T counts the same as a written one, including a read view that must become an owned copy.

options.name: Copyable trait, named where a generic copies
options.detail: Copyable is a built-in trait that Jet derives for every type whose parts can all be copied and that owns no cleanup duty. A generic writes T: Copyable to copy T. Without the bound, copying T is an error whose fix adds it. A caller passing a socket gets an error at its own line that says why. Generics that only move T need nothing, and #!Copyable lets a type refuse copying.
options.technical:
Register Copyable beside Close in the built-in trait lists: Rust Generics.rs:62-77 and native TypeRelations.jet:714-719. Satisfaction is the existing classifier result, cloneable and not a resource, from Ownership/Copy.jet. One walk answers both x.copy() and T: Copyable. No hand-written impl is accepted, because .copy() stays compiler-owned under D-COPY-WORD1=A. Copyable generates no code, so the package auto-derive switch does not apply to it; #!Copyable is its only refusal.

Change the type-parameter facts at Copy.jet:282-288 and Rust Diagnostics.rs:731. An unbounded T is not copyable, T: Copyable is copyable, and T: Close stays a resource. Copying an unbounded T reports E0211 with a Safe edit that adds the bound. The existing bound check at the call reports E0905, naming why the argument is not Copyable.

Migrate random.jet:120,125,142 and table.jet:314 from Clone to Copyable, fix the random.jet:152 comment, and update the embedded generic-method UI fixture. Run jet fix over every generic that copies T. Under the ratified unbuilt generic form the bound reads fn pick(prep T: Copyable, items: [T]), with the word set by the compile-time keyword vote.

options.name: Infer the need from the function body
options.detail: No bound is written. The checker records that a generic body copies T, carries that need through calls, and rejects a socket at the call. The trait name can appear in messages, but signatures never show it.
options.technical: Record copy requirements per type parameter, propagate them through forwarding and recursive generic calls to a fixed point, and validate each concrete substitution with the existing classifier. API snapshots must store the inferred requirement so a body edit is a visible semver change. Core RNG and table drop their Clone bounds.

options.name: Copyable by default, opt out to carry resources
options.detail: Every type parameter is assumed Copyable, as in Swift. A generic that must accept a socket writes an opt-out on T. Copying T then needs nothing, but every container, option and helper that may hold a resource needs the opt-out.
options.technical: Adds an implicit Copyable bound to every type parameter and a new relaxation spelling, such as T: ?Copyable, registered in Syntax.rs. List, Map, Option, Result, channels, tasks and every Core generic that may carry a resource add the opt-out. Today's legal move-only generics break until annotated.
options.code:
fn pick<T>(items: [T]) -> T? { Val(items[0].copy()) }   // T is Copyable unless told
fn keep<T: ?Copyable>(item: T) -> T { item }            // opt out to accept a socket
pick([socket])         // error: Socket isn't Copyable

comparisons.note: Copyable by default; generic code opts out to hold a value that cannot be copied.
comparisons.code: func keep<T: ~Copyable>(_ item: consuming T) -> T { item }

comparisons.note: C++20 concepts moved the copy requirement into the signature after years of errors deep in template bodies.
comparisons.code: template <std::copyable T> T pick(const std::vector<T>& items) { return items[0]; }

recommendation.why: Jet already makes generic code name Equatable before == and Comparable before >. Copyable completes that rule with the same trait family, the same refusal mark, and the classifier Jet already runs. The signature tells callers what they may pass. A caller's error points at their own line, and generics that only move a socket keep working.
gains: One rule for direct and generic copies, stated in the signature.
Callers see errors at their own call, with the reason the type cannot be copied.
Move-only generics, lists and options still carry resources with no annotation.

losses.loss: A generic function that copies T writes one more word in its signature.
losses.mitigation: The error's Safe fix writes T: Copyable, jet fix migrates the library, and at most one generic in five copies T.

whyNot.reason: The need hides in the body, so a body edit can silently break callers, and their error points into code they did not write.
Every container, option and helper that may hold a resource needs a new opt-out spelling, the migration Swift needed two proposals for.

recommendation.tradeoff: One written word on generics that copy, for a requirement every reader and caller can see.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Reworked by BallotRework on 2026-10-10 for the owner's question; validated offline with validate.mjs. No Tower write was made.

Passing a Close type to a T: Copyable parameter is E0905 naming the cleanup duty. Cover explicit and inferred type arguments, generic methods, imported aliases, nested containers, structs holding a resource, forwarding and recursive generics.

Keep move-only generics, [Resource] lists, options and Shared<Resource> copies accepted. Check that #!Copyable makes .copy() E0211 and that impl X.Copyable is refused. Migrate the four Clone bounds and every generic that copies T with jet fix, then re-run the random and web table tests. Do not execute a duplicated live resource; list changed goldens for owner review.

decisions.title: Which byte comparison proves Jet compiles itself: stage1 == stage2 or stage2 == stage3
decisions.situation: Jet proves it can build itself by compiling its own compiler in stages and comparing the files byte for byte. On 2026-10-11 the gate was stage1 equals stage2. Since then stage1 is built by an older Jet compiler, so its machine code comes from that older code generator and can never match. On 2026-10-16 the owner moved the gate to stage2 equals stage3, but that lives only in a card title. We recommend ratifying stage2 equals stage3 as the self-hosting gate, the same check GCC's bootstrap uses.
decisions.gist: Should the self-hosting gate compare stage2 with stage3, as the owner said on 2026-10-16, or stage1 with stage2, as ratified on 2026-10-11?
decisions.lesson: Stage1 is the new compiler source built by an older compiler. Stage2 is that source built by stage1. Stage3 is the source built by stage2. Stage1's bytes come from the older compiler's code generator, so they differ from stage2 whenever the new source changes code generation. Stage1 and stage2 run the same source, so a correct, deterministic compiler makes stage2 and stage3 identical.
decisions.story: Omar runs the gate after a commit that improves register allocation. Stage1 was built by last week's compiler, so its code uses the old allocator, while stage2 uses the new one. Under the old rule the gate fails on every such commit even when nothing is wrong. Under the new rule it fails only if stage1 and stage2 behave differently.
decisions.inWild:
# GCC's three-stage bootstrap compares stage2 and stage3 objects
make bootstrap      # stage1 by the system compiler, stage2 by stage1, stage3 by stage2
make compare        # stage2 and stage3 object files must be identical
decisions.detail:
Why stage2 == stage3 is the fixed point. Let S be the new compiler source and C0 the older seed compiler. Stage1 = C0(S): a program with S's meaning but C0's machine code. Stage2 = stage1(S) and stage3 = stage2(S): both are produced by S's own code generator.

Stage1 and stage2 implement the same source, so a deterministic, correct S gives stage2 == stage3 byte for byte. Stage1 == stage2 holds only if C0 generates the same code as S. That was true on 2026-10-11, when the seed was built from the same source. It is false whenever S changes code generation, runtime layout or the assembly preamble.

What stage2 == stage3 proves: if C0 miscompiled stage1 in a way that changes its output, stage2 differs from what stage2 itself produces, and the comparison fails. A miscompile that changes nothing observable cannot matter to later stages.

Records. #4956 log, 2026-10-11 10:20: owner ratified stage1 == stage2, with stage3 as a follow-up receipt. #5032 (2026-10-16): the native gate is stage2 == stage3; stage1 vs stage2 differences are recorded in comparisons.json and fixed after Rust removal. #5012 plans s2 == s3, then det1 (--threads 1) == s3. SPEED-500K.md also gates every milestone on stage2 == stage3.

Follow-ups under A: land-cutover.sh and native-smoke must read the self-rebuild receipt as the fixed point. D-SEED-DIST1's published seed becomes the stage2 binary of the stage2 == stage3 proof. Cost: one extra full self-compile per gate run.

options.name: stage2 == stage3, whole file, byte for byte
options.detail: The gate is stage3 built by stage2, compared byte for byte with stage2. Differences between stage1 and stage2 are recorded, not gating. Land tooling reads the self-rebuild receipt, and the published seed is the proven stage2 binary.
options.code:
s1 = old_jet build compiler      # older code generator
s2 = s1 build compiler            # new code generator
s3 = s2 build compiler            # new code generator
cmp s2/jet s3/jet                 # gate: identical bytes
# s1 vs s2: recorded in comparisons.json, not gating

s2 = s1 build compiler

options.name: stage2 == stage3, plus stage1 and stage2 must agree on examples
options.detail: Gate on stage2 == stage3, and also require stage1 and stage2 to produce identical output on the example corpus. It catches more seed problems, but today's recorded stage1 and stage2 differences would block self-hosting until all are fixed.
options.code:

rustc's stage0 is the previous release, so stage1 is never expected to match later stages byte for byte.

recommendation.why: With an older seed, stage2 == stage3 is the only byte comparison that a correct compiler always passes. It is the classic bootstrap fixed point, and the owner already chose it on 2026-10-16.
recommendation.tradeoff: Each gate run pays one extra full self-compile; stage1 and stage2 differences are tracked instead of blocking.

whyNot.reason: It fails on every commit that changes code generation, even when nothing is wrong.

losses.mitigation: The stage3 build already runs as the self-rebuild receipt and is the first speed measurement.

decisions.title: When the one-thread byte check runs again
decisions.gist: Should the compiler's one-thread versus many-thread byte check run on every chain now, or wait until the self-build is faster?
decisions.lesson: The compiler should produce identical bytes whatever the thread count. Checking that takes about 35 minutes per chain on one core, so the check can wait until the build is much faster.
decisions.story: Ruth runs the self-build chain each night. Under option A the one-thread check is skipped, and the nightly run takes minutes less, but the two-run check stays. Under option B the one-thread check adds about 35 minutes each night, and the team sees a thread bug sooner.
decisions.inWild:
Go: builds are reproducible with the same inputs, and the toolchain's own tests check build output across runs. Source: https://go.dev/doc/go1.21#go-command

Rust: rustc's test suite compares output across codegen settings to catch nondeterminism. Source: https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/tests/intro.html
decisions.detail:
Owner ruling, 2026-10-18 (card #5065): the det1 check compares stage 2 at --threads 1 with stage 3 at --threads 16 for byte-identical jet.o. It costs about 35 minutes of single-core time per chain. It is deferred and skipped with SKIP_DET1 in the chain script. Re-enable it when self-compile is under 5 seconds (target a0_007). Until then, two 16-thread runs must match.

Owner order, 2026-10-22 (card #5092): determinism is deferred until self-compile is about 10 seconds. When resumed, compiler and diagnostic bytes must match across --threads 1 and N on every phase. Speed lanes prove patches without single-thread builds.

No ratified decision found by keyword scan records this deferral. D-SELFHOST-GATE1 (2026-10-17) fixes which byte comparison proves self-hosting, not thread-count independence.

options.name: Defer one-thread check until self-compile is fast
options.detail: Skip the one-thread byte check now. Keep the two 16-thread runs. Resume the one-thread check at about 10 seconds of self-compile, under the card's rule.
options.technical: Set SKIP_DET1 in the chain script. Keep the stage2 == stage3 comparison. Record the resume condition in the chain notes.
options.code:
$ chain --threads 16 stage2
$ chain --threads 16 stage3   # bytes must match

options.name: Run the one-thread check on every chain
options.detail: Keep the det1 check on every chain, at about 35 minutes of single-core time each.
options.technical: Remove SKIP_DET1. Accept the added chain time.
options.code:
$ chain --threads 1 stage2
$ chain --threads 16 stage3   # bytes must match

comparisons.note: Build output is reproducible for the same inputs. Source: https://go.dev/doc/go1.21#go-command
rustc's test suite compares output across settings to catch nondeterminism. Source: https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/tests/intro.html

recommendation.why: The byte check is correct but costs about 35 minutes per chain. The owner deferred it until self-compile is fast enough.
gains: Each nightly chain is about 35 minutes shorter.
The two 16-thread runs still catch most drift.

losses.loss: A thread-count bug may reach the chain later than it would with the one-thread check.
losses.mitigation: Two 16-thread runs must still match on every chain.

whyNot.reason: B spends about 35 minutes per chain on a check the owner deferred.

recommendation.tradeoff: Shorter chains, with a later catch for thread-count drift.

decisions.title: Where a package states the effects it may use
decisions.situation: A package file lists the effects its code may use, such as network or file access, and the ones it must never use. Today that list sits two levels deep, inside authority and then holds, beside unrelated settings such as trust rules and dependency grants. You asked whether it could be a plain effects block with allow and deny. This vote decides where the list lives; we recommend a top-level effects block, which is also the shape Jet first ratified for it.
decisions.gist: Should a package state its allowed and denied effects in a top-level effects block instead of authority.holds?
decisions.lesson: An effect is something code does beyond computing, such as using the network or the file system. A package lists the effects it may use, and Jet refuses code that uses others. Today the list is authority: { holds: { allow, deny } }. The authority block also holds dependency grants, trust rules and provider limits, which this vote leaves where they are.
decisions.story: Sam starts a small web service and opens package.jet to let it use the network. The allow list is inside holds, which is inside authority, next to trust and provider rules he has never used. He has to read the whole block to find the one line he needs.
decisions.detail:
Owner request 2026-10-20: accepted and denied effects should not sit two levels deep under authority and holds; the owner asked for an effects block with allow and deny. Review status: no review pass, because the owner asked for no subagents in this round.

History. D-EFFBUDGET1=D ratified a top-level effects: { allow, deny } block with always-on effect reporting and opt-in enforcement. D-AUTHORITY-MANIFEST1=A later moved the package's own bound into authority: { holds: { allow, deny } } so that one block held every grant. Option A restores the first shape for the package's own list only.

Today in code. Jetpack/PackageModel/Source/Manifest/Blocks/Authority.jet parses authority with the fields holds, needs, grants, trust and providers; holds carries allow and deny. The Syntax rows MANIFEST_BLOCK_EFFECTS, EFFECTS_FIELD_ALLOW and EFFECTS_FIELD_DENY still exist in Compiler/JetFoundation/Data/Syntax/predicates.jet.

Census 2026-10-20 by git grep: 1,608 holds: { sites in 1,433 tracked files. Most are in tests/cases (717 files), Examples (291) and Tools/agent-eval (168). 158 files mention authority.holds, holds.allow or holds.deny in prose or diagnostics.

What changes under A. The package parser reads effects: { allow, deny } into the same AuthorityHolds value, so effect checking and budgets keep their meaning. authority.holds becomes an unknown field. jet init and jet fix templates, the lockfile and ledger printers, diagnostics text, the spec and every fixture are migrated in one cutover. The rewrite is mechanical.

Edge cases. A package with no effects block keeps today's default. A package that writes both effects and authority.holds gets the unknown-field error for holds, which names effects. Workspace policy keeps its own policy: { deny, grants } block, which this vote does not change.

Amends D-AUTHORITY-MANIFEST1=A for the package's own bound only, and restores the D-EFFBUDGET1=D key. Syntax rows: MANIFEST_BLOCK_EFFECTS, EFFECTS_FIELD_ALLOW and EFFECTS_FIELD_DENY are re-tied to this decision; AUTHORITY_FIELD_HOLDS, AUTHORITY_HOLDS_FIELD_ALLOW and AUTHORITY_HOLDS_FIELD_DENY are removed (I7).

options.name: Top-level effects block
options.detail: The package's own effect list moves to effects: { allow: [...], deny: [...] } at the top level of package.jet. authority keeps grants, needs, trust and providers. This restores the block D-EFFBUDGET1=D ratified, which D-AUTHORITY-MANIFEST1 later folded into authority.holds.
options.technical: Package parser in Jetpack/PackageModel/Source/Manifest/Blocks/Authority.jet: a top-level effects block parses allow and deny with today's effect-list rules. It fills the existing AuthorityHolds value, so effect checking, budgets and the lockfile's meaning do not change. authority.holds becomes an unknown authority field. Syntax rows MANIFEST_BLOCK_EFFECTS, EFFECTS_FIELD_ALLOW and EFFECTS_FIELD_DENY already exist; AUTHORITY_FIELD_HOLDS and the AUTHORITY_HOLDS_FIELD_ rows are removed. The lockfile and ledger print the effect list under effects.

options.name: One level, inside authority
options.detail: allow and deny move up one level and sit directly in authority, beside grants, needs, trust and providers. Every permission setting stays in one block, as D-AUTHORITY-MANIFEST1 wanted.
options.technical: Same parser change, but allow and deny become authority fields; holds is removed. The lockfile and ledger keep one authority section.

options.name: Keep authority.holds
options.detail: Nothing changes. The package's own effect list stays two levels deep under authority and holds.
options.technical: No change to D-AUTHORITY-MANIFEST1=A.

comparisons.note: Deno groups permissions in one flat map of allow lists per kind, with no wrapper object.
An app lists each permission it uses directly in its manifest, one line each.

recommendation.why: The effect list is the permission setting most packages need, so it gets its own short top-level block. The rarer grants and trust rules stay in authority.
gains: The common setting is one level deep and named for what it holds.
Matches the block Jet first ratified for effects.

losses.loss: Permission settings live in two blocks instead of one.
losses.mitigation: effects holds only this package's own list, and jet inspect rights already shows allowed, denied and granted effects together.

whyNot.reason: Still inside a block of rarely used settings, and allow beside grants reads as if it granted dependencies.
Keeps the common setting two levels deep, the problem you raised.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two permission blocks, for a one-line effect list where most packages need it.

decisions.title: Compile-time code runs the runtime's own IR
decisions.gist: Should compile-time evaluation run the runtime library's own compiled IR, or keep a hand-written copy of some routines?
decisions.lesson: The compile-time machine hand-routes 57 symbols, and the builder emits 219 more. Most of the library has Jet bodies, so a hand copy can drift from the real one.
decisions.story: Ivo writes a comptime call to a string helper. Under option A the helper runs the same IR as the program does, so the answer matches the run. Under option B the hand copy handles the call, and a small difference from the runtime version can appear only at compile time.
decisions.inWild:

Jai: compile-time code runs the same language, not a separate copy. Source: The Way to Jai, https://github.com/Ivo-Balbaert/The_Way_to_Jai
decisions.detail:
Owner ruling, 2026-10-22 about 20:30 (card #5101): comptime runs the runtime pack's own IR; no hand-written duplicate routes. This settles PLAN-A item G-A3.

State in the card: the IR machine hand-routes 57 symbols; the builder emits 219 more; 111 have Jet bodies in JetRuntime.

Ratified D-TIER-ONEIR1 (2026-09-03, option A) says every mode reads one lowering. It does not decide the hand-written routes, so this ballot records the 10-22 ruling.

options.technical: Delete the 57 hand routes once the runtime pack provides each symbol. Emit the 219 builder symbols from the pack. Prove each deletion with the comptime suite.
options.code: fn run() { const s = comptime text.upper("ok"); print(s) }   // same IR at comptime and run

options.name: Keep the hand routes
options.detail: Keep the 57 hand-written routes for compile-time use. Emit the rest from the pack.
options.technical: Keep the hand table in the IR machine. Add a test that compares each route with its runtime body.

comparisons.note: Compile-time code is run from the same typed definitions as runtime code. Source: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/#comptime
Compile-time code is written in the same language as the program. Source: https://github.com/Ivo-Balbaert/The_Way_to_Jai

recommendation.why: One runtime body per routine means compile-time and run-time answers cannot differ. The owner ruled this on 2026-10-22.

losses.mitigation: A comptime test per route proves each replacement.

whyNot.reason: B keeps a second copy of some routines, which the owner ruling removes.

recommendation.tradeoff: Some work first, for one body per routine.

decisions.title: How named tuples sort and compare
decisions.situation: A named tuple is a small value with labelled parts, such as a key and an index. When a list of them is sorted, Jet compares the parts in alphabetical order of their labels, not in the order they were written. So a list of key and index pairs comes back sorted by index, and a user reported sort as broken. The owner decides which rule sorting follows; we recommend keeping the alphabetical rule and documenting it with a tested example.
decisions.gist: When a list of named tuples is sorted, which member decides the order?
decisions.lesson: A named tuple is a small value with labelled parts, like (key: "a", index: 1). Jet treats (key, index) and (index, key) as the same type, so the written order is lost. Sorting and < compare the parts in alphabetical order of their labels. Users expect the first written part to win. Whichever option wins, sort_by still picks any order explicitly.
decisions.explainer: Sorting needs one fixed order for a type. Jet treats two named tuples with the same labels as the same type, whatever order the labels were written in. The written order is therefore not available when the program sorts. Each option either names that rule, forbids plain sorting, or warns about it.
decisions.story: Mia keeps (key, index) pairs and calls sort() to order them by key. The list comes back unchanged, because it was already in index order and index sorts first alphabetically. She thinks sort() is broken and files a bug.
decisions.inWild:
-- Elm: tuples sort by position; records (labelled) do not sort without a field
List.sort [ (2, "b"), (1, "a") ]
List.sortBy .key [ { key = "b" }, { key = "a" } ]
-- https://package.elm-lang.org/packages/elm/core/latest/List#sort
decisions.detail:
Found on card #5907 at dev 8d2082ea63. S73 (Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:1141) sorts a named tuple's fields by name for its identity. JetIR orders tuples member by member in that order (BuildTypes.jet:1898 ir_order_into over ir_tuple_members). The same law orders tuple Map and Set keys (BuildMaps.jet ir_ordered_type).

A census of all 236 sort() and sort_desc() calls in Compiler/ and Core/ found three on tuple lists. BuildMerge.jet:239 sorts (key, local) and gets key first by luck. BuildStatic.jet:460 and 467 sort (key, at) and got at first; that latent bug is fixed with sort_by under any ruling.

options.name: Alphabetical, written down
options.detail:
This is today's behaviour, made a rule. S73 (Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:1141) says a named tuple's identity sorts its fields by name. So (key: String, index: Int) and (index: Int, key: String) are one type. Their order must therefore depend only on that type.

The order compares members in label order (JetIR ir_order_into, BuildTypes.jet:1898). jet run, jet build, comptime constants, < and <=> all agree. This was checked on dev 8d2082 on 2026-10-24.

Work owed: one S73 sentence and the List.sort and sort_desc doc text. Also owed: an example with golden output showing label order and the sort_by spelling.
options.technical: Order law: lexicographic over members sorted by label (bytewise), each member by its own order; the same law already orders tuple Map/Set keys (ir_ordered_type .Tuple).
options.code:
pairs := [(key: "c", index: 0), (key: "a", index: 1), (key: "b", index: 2)]
&pairs.sort()
loop p in pairs { print("{p.key} {p.index}") }   // c 0, a 1, b 2
&pairs.sort_by((l, r) -> l.key <=> r.key)
loop p in pairs { print("{p.key} {p.index}") }   // a 1, b 2, c 0

options.name: No plain sort for labelled tuples
options.detail:
Named tuples with two or more members stop being Comparable. That covers <, <=, >, >=, <=>, sort, sort_desc, min, max, min_max and binary_search. Map and Set keys of tuple type keep label order internally. So the compiler carries two notions of order.

The diagnostic gets a new E-code from the registry at landing. Message: `error: \`sort()\` needs an order, and named tuples have none you wrote`. Why: `(key, index) and (index, key) are the same type, so the written order is lost`. Fix: `say which member decides: \`&xs.sort_by((l, r) -> l.key <=> r.key)\``.

Compiler sites to migrate: BuildMerge.jet:239 and BuildStatic.jet:460/467. The BuildStatic sites move to sort_by under any ruling.

options.name: Alphabetical, with a warning
options.detail:
This keeps A's rule and adds a warning. It fires at every plain ordering use of a named tuple with two or more members: sort, sort_desc, <, <=>, min, max and binary_search.

The checker cannot tell whether the user meant label order, because the written order is not part of the type. So the warning fires on correct code too. One example is the compiler's own BuildMerge.jet:239, which wants key first and gets it.

The diagnostic gets a new W-code at landing. Message: `warning: named tuples compare by label order: index, then key`. Fix: `if that is the order you want, keep it; otherwise say it with sort_by`.

comparisons.note: Positional tuples are comparable; records are not, and sorting them needs sortBy with a field. https://package.elm-lang.org/packages/elm/core/latest/List#sort

Labelled tuples compare in written order because the labels' order is part of the type; Jet's S73 made the opposite identity choice, so this law is not available. https://github.com/apple/swift-evolution/blob/main/proposals/0015-tuple-comparison-operators.md
derive(Ord) on a struct compares fields in declaration order; reordering fields silently changes the order, a known footgun. https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/cmp/trait.Ord.html#derivable
comparisons.code: #[derive(PartialOrd, Ord, PartialEq, Eq)] struct P { key: String, index: i64 }

recommendation.why: The type already forgets the written order, so label order is the only stable rule. Documenting it keeps map keys and existing sorts working.
gains: One rule for sorting, comparing, map keys and set keys.
No migration.

losses.loss: A reader can still expect the first written label to win.
losses.mitigation: The List.sort docs and a tested example show label order and the one-line sort_by fix.

whyNot.reason: It breaks working code and still needs label order for map keys, so users learn two rules.
It warns on correct sorts, so the warning becomes noise people ignore.

recommendation.tradeoff: Some readers need the docs once; sort_by states any other order in one line.

decisions.checkInstructions: Build and run a program that sorts [(key: "c", index: 0), (key: "a", index: 1)] with sort() and with sort_by on key. Under A the docs and golden example show index-then-key and key order. Under B sort() gives the new error. Under C it gives the new warning.

Sorting and < compare the parts in alphabetical order of their labels. Users expect the first written part to win. Whichever option wins, sort_by still picks any order explicitly.

current.note: This looks like a no-op: the list is sorted by index, because "index" comes before "key" alphabetically.

wild.code:

List.sortBy .key records          -- records: say the field

gains: No code changes; existing sorts keep their results.

options.gist: Keep A's rule, and warn at every plain sort or < of a named tuple with two or more labels.
gains: Nobody is surprised silently.
Code keeps working.
losses: Warns on correct code too, which teaches people to ignore it.
