decisions.title: A text-pattern hole that reuses a name already in scope
decisions.situation: In Jet, x == "v{major}.{minor}" is not a plain comparison: it checks that x has that shape and creates new names, major and minor, for the parts in braces. If a brace reuses a name that already holds a value, such as {hash}, it still creates a new name and matches any text. So selector == "hash:{hash}" is true for every selector starting with hash:, a silent bug already found in at least eight places in Jet's own tools. You are deciding what such a reused name means; we recommend a compile error that shows how to compare instead.
decisions.gist: When a text-pattern hole reuses a name that already holds a value, should Jet refuse it or compare against that value?
decisions.lesson: In Jet, x == "v{major}.{minor}" checks a shape and creates new names for the parts in braces, called holes. A hole that reuses an existing name, like {root}, also creates a new name, so it matches anything. A refuses that hole and shows two fixes. B compares an existing name with its value. C adds a pin mark, {=root}, for comparing.
decisions.explainer:
A string is text. Interpolation puts a value into text: "hi {name}" with name set to Ann is "hi Ann". The braces are a hole.

A pattern is a shape a value may or may not have. On the right of ==, Jet reads a string with holes as a pattern. The fixed text must match, and each hole creates a new name holding the text it covers. So version == "v{major}.{minor}" checks the shape and gives you major and minor.

The trap: if root already holds "/usr/", then symbol == "{root}jet" does not compare with "/usr/jet". It creates a fresh root and matches any text ending in jet.

Jet already has a rule that one name means one thing inside a function, so declaring a second root is normally an error. Holes slip past that rule in some places.

Only a hole that is a bare name, optionally with a type such as {id:Int}, is a pattern hole. A hole with a dot or a call, such as {cfg.root}, already makes the whole thing a plain comparison.
decisions.story: Lena writes path == "{trimmed}/" to check that a path is a folder inside an allowed root. Every path ending in a slash passes, including ones outside the root. The check looks right and compiles without a warning, but it is a security hole.
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-04. The parser turns `subject == "…"` into a pattern test when every hole is a bare name with an optional type (Compiler/JetParser/Source/Parser/Expressions.jet:270-273, Parser/Patterns.jet:373 and 406-418). Only == does this; != stays plain inequality. The checker binds each hole as a new name with no look at existing names (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Patterns.jet:635-659).

Today a reused name reaches E0118 only when the test is the whole if condition or a link in an && chain. Only those bindings are declared (Sema/Expressions/Control.jet:1325-1344 and 1459-1465). Even there, a hole named after an immutable `String?` local is taken as a D-FLOWTYPE1 refinement instead (Control.jet:1462-1469, 1490-1494).

Under || and in value positions, such as `return a == "{b}"`, nothing is declared. D-CHOOSE-TEST1=A says a test with no miss route binds nothing. So no E0118 fires and the hole silently matches anything. E0118's law is in Docs/spec/spec.md:244 and Sema/Diagnostics.jet:199-206. It protects locals, parameters and module constants; module function names stay free (Sema/Scopes.jet:1393-1396).

Live cases where comparison was meant. Compiler/JetEval/Source/EvalValues.jet:1865 returns `left_decimal == "{right_number}"`, which is true for every text. Jetpack: TrustCommand.jet:113-114, CheckedEntries.jet:326, R.jet:55, PackageFacts.jet:303, ExternalRoots.jet:102, LuaRocksProvider.jet:456 and SourceLoader.jet:49. SourceLoader's hole names the module constant FILE_EXT. The Jet emitter already avoids the trap by building the text first (Compiler/JetCodegen/Source/Emit/Operations.jet:1078-1082).

A parenthesised right side, `x == ("{root}jet")`, starts with a parenthesis, not a string, so the parser treats it as plain comparison (Patterns.jet:364-377). `jet fmt` keeps author-written parentheses (D-FMTPARENS1=A, crates/jet-parser/src/Formatter/Expressions.rs:2017-2021). Every option migrates the live cases in the same change.

options.name: Refuse a hole that reuses an existing name
options.detail:
A pattern hole must introduce a new name. If the name already resolves at that point to a local, a parameter or a module constant (the set E0118 already protects), the compiler reports E0118 with a teaching message. The message shows both fixes: wrap the text in parentheses to compare, `x == ("{root}jet")`, or pick a new hole name to bind.

This applies in every position, including || chains and value positions where nothing is bound. A hole named after a `String?` local is refused too, not taken as a refinement. Holes that bind new names, such as v{major}.{minor}, are unchanged.
options.technical: sema_pattern_text resolves each hole name in the current scopes before binding. A hit reports E0118 with a pattern-specific what, why and fix, and the fix carries a structured edit that adds the parentheses. The rule covers text and byte patterns alike. Both checkers, the registry text, one UI fixture per position and the migration of every live case land together.

options.name: An existing name compares with its value
options.detail:
A hole whose name already holds a value matches exactly that value's text. Only new names bind. So symbol == "{root}jet" compares with root's text plus jet, and "v{major}" still binds major when major is new.

The cost is distance. Adding an unrelated `major :: 0` higher up the function silently turns a binding hole into a comparison, and the reader cannot tell which holes compare without checking every name above.
options.technical: sema_pattern_text resolves each hole; a hit lowers to an anchored literal segment built from the value's text form, a miss binds as today. Typed holes with an existing name compare after formatting that value.
options.code:
root :: "/usr/"
symbol == "{root}jet"        // true only for "/usr/jet"
version == "v{major}"        // binds major, if major is new

options.name: A pin mark compares; bare reuse is refused
options.detail:
A hole written {=root} compares with root's current text, like Elixir's pin. A bare hole that reuses an existing name is refused as in A, and the fix offers the pin.

This keeps comparison inside one pattern, for example "{=root}{rest}", which mixes a fixed value with a new binding. It adds new syntax that every reader must learn. It also puts a second `=` mark inside holes. D-FMT-INTERP2=A already makes a trailing `{x=}` print the name and value, so `{=x}` and `{x=}` would differ only by side.
options.technical: The lexer and parser accept `=` before a hole name; the checker requires the name to resolve and lowers it to an anchored literal. The marker and its formatting rules join the grammar.
options.code:
root :: "/usr/"
path == "{=root}{rest}" ?? return
print(rest)                  // text after /usr/

comparisons.note: Elixir rebinds bare names in patterns and uses the pin operator ^ to compare with an existing value.

Rust binds a new name for a bare identifier in a pattern, so such an arm always matches (the compiler warns that later arms are unreachable). A name that resolves to a const in scope compares instead, which is option B's rule limited to constants.

recommendation.why: A turns a silent always-true check into a compile error with two clear fixes, and needs no new syntax. It extends Jet's existing one-name-one-meaning rule to the place it was missed.
gains: No hole can silently hide an existing value.
Every live always-true check in the repository surfaces at compile time.
No new syntax; the comparison spelling already parses.

losses.loss: Comparing with interpolated text needs parentheses around the text.
losses.mitigation: The error offers an automatic fix that adds the parentheses, and jet fmt keeps them.

losses.loss: One pattern cannot match a fixed existing value and capture the rest.
losses.mitigation: Check the fixed part first with starts_with, then match the rest; a pin mark can be added later if real code needs it.

whyNot.reason: B lets an unrelated binding added above silently change what a pattern does, so a reader must check every earlier name.
C adds new hole syntax for a case no live code needs today; A's refusal can grow a pin later without breaking anything.

recommendation.tradeoff: A asks for parentheses when comparing with interpolated text. In return no pattern hole can silently match everything.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: BallotDraft2. Skill: rli5. Author-run pass, because this worker cannot start agents. It found interpolation, pattern, binding and shadowing undefined and the parenthesis fix unexplained, so the explainer and option A now teach each — Clarity rewrite 2026-10-04 by BallotClear0 per CLARITY-RULES.md.

It re-checked every file:line: E0118 fires today only for a whole condition or && chain, so the story now uses the real || case and A names the protected set. It added C's clash with D-FMT-INTERP2's trailing {x=} and showed the paren fix survives jet fmt.

Write UI fixtures for a reused hole name in an if condition, in a value position such as return, in a test-bind with a ?? route, and in a byte pattern. Each must report the chosen behavior with the same code, span and fix on every run mode.

Check that "v{major}.{minor}" with new names still binds, that a dotted hole still compares, and that the parenthesised form compares. Rebuild Compiler/, Core/ and Jetpack/ and confirm each listed live case is migrated, with a regression test showing EvalValues.jet:1865 now compares BigInt and Int values correctly.

A refuses that brace and shows two fixes. B compares an existing name with its value. C adds a pin mark, {=root}, for comparing.

decisions.title: What a #Transact commit checks so concurrent edits never overwrite each other
decisions.gist: What must a #Transact commit check so two tasks editing shared values never overwrite each other?
decisions.lesson: #Transact makes edits to Shared values land together. Today each transaction edits a private copy and publishes it at the end. Nothing checks whether another task changed the value first, so one transfer can erase another. This ballot amends D-CONC-STM1. The crashes listed on the card are fixed either way.
decisions.story: Omar runs a payments service. Two refunds hit one account at the same moment. Both transactions read 1000 and both write 900, so one refund disappears and the ledger no longer balances.
decisions.inWild:
-- GHC Haskell STM (Harris, Marlow, Peyton Jones, Herlihy, PPoPP 2005)
transfer from to n = atomically $ do
  a <- readTVar from
  writeTVar from (a - n)
  b <- readTVar to
  writeTVar to (b + n)
decisions.detail:
Evidence from committed code at HEAD: edit_txn copies the value at first touch and publishes the copy (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib/JetStd/MathTaskMem.rs:1884-1918). try_commit_with takes locks in order but never compares revisions (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/SharedProtocol.rs:873-960). D-CONC-STM1=A said both designs are atomic. The publish is atomic, but the body may have used stale values. Live runs were on a dirty-tree binary; see card #3967.

Owner question 2026-09-30: under A, a re-run repeats the computation, never the Shared changes. A discarded attempt writes nothing to Shared values, and only the final attempt commits, exactly once. Locals need care: today's auto-snapshot restores assigned locals but not ones changed through method calls like `list.push` (card #3978). Option A requires #3978 first, so every local change is undone between attempts.

Conflicts are not failures, and the user never handles them. Real failures (`return Err(…)` or `?`) roll back everything as today. The caller handles them with `??` or a table, and `tx.on_rollback` can print or log.

options.name: Check at commit, run again on conflict
options.detail:
Each transaction records the revision of every Shared value it reads or edits. At commit, under the ordered locks, Jet compares them. If any changed, the attempt is thrown away and the body runs again. A thrown-away attempt changes no Shared value. Every local change is undone first, which needs card #3978 so method-call changes are covered too. Output inside the block is held and written once after a successful commit. Irreversible effects stay banned (E0746).

After a few conflicting attempts, the next attempt locks everything it touched before running. So a busy transaction always finishes.
options.technical: The shared Prelude keeps a read set with revisions per participant; try_commit_with validates it after acquiring ordered permits and loops on failure with backoff. After a bounded number of conflicts, the attempt pre-acquires the previous participant set in canonical order. A new participant aborts the attempt and joins the set. Progress is guaranteed without a user-visible error. Output is buffered through the existing on_commit hook path. Every tier inherits it through the Prelude.

options.name: Lock every value before the block runs
options.detail: Sema computes the set of Shared values the block can touch. The block locks all of them in a fixed order before its first statement and runs exactly once. A participant that cannot be known before the block runs, such as a list entry chosen by an index, is a compile error.
options.technical: Sema emits a participant list per #Transact; the runtime acquires all permits up front with the existing ordered acquisition. Dynamic participants are rejected with a new diagnostic.
options.code:
#Transact { accounts[i].balance += 1 }
// new error: `accounts[i]` is not known before the block runs

comparisons.note: Optimistic transactions validate their read log at commit and re-run on conflict; I/O is banned inside by the type system. Composable Memory Transactions, PPoPP 2005: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/composable-memory-transactions/
comparisons.code: atomically $ do { v <- readTVar r; writeTVar r (v + 1) }

comparisons.note: dosync transactions may be retried, so side effects inside them are discouraged. https://clojure.org/reference/refs

recommendation.why: Only running again fixes every read-then-decide transaction, including ones over list entries. Jet already bans irreversible effects in the block, which is what makes running again safe.

whyNot.reason: B cannot lock values chosen at run time, so transactions over list or map entries stop compiling.

recommendation.tradeoff: A contended block may repeat its work so that every transaction stays correct.

surface.gist: What must a #Transact commit check so two tasks editing shared values never overwrite each other?
surface.lesson: #Transact makes edits to Shared values land together. Today each transaction edits a private copy and publishes it at the end. Nothing checks whether another task changed the value first, so one transfer can erase another. This ballot amends D-CONC-STM1. The crashes listed on the card are fixed either way.

current.note: The shipped example moves 8 x 100 from 1000. The total must stay 1000.

wild.note: The commit checks every value the transaction read. On a conflict the block runs again. Harris et al., PPoPP 2005, section 2.1.
wild.code:
transfer from to n = atomically $ do
  a <- readTVar from
  writeTVar from (a - n)
  b <- readTVar to
  writeTVar to (b + n)
-- commit checks the reads; a conflict re-runs the block

options.name: Check at commit, run again on conflict
options.gist: If a value the block read has changed, the block's code runs again; its changes apply once.
gains: Correct for any read-then-decide code.
Works when values are picked at run time.
Needs no new syntax.
losses: Under contention the block's code may run again.
Output from the block appears only after commit.

options.name: Lock every value before the block runs
options.gist: Jet finds each Shared value the block touches and locks them all first.
gains: The block always runs exactly once.
Output appears where it is written.
losses: Values picked at run time cannot be locked first.
Readers wait while a writer holds a lock.

recommendation.why: Only running again fixes every read-then-decide transaction, including ones over list entries. Jet already bans irreversible effects in the block, which is what makes running again safe.
gains: Transfers can never erase each other on any tier.

losses.loss: Under contention the block's code may run again.
losses.mitigation: Without holding locks from the first read, the only way to use fresh values is to compute again. Discarded attempts change nothing.

losses.loss: Output from the block appears only after commit.
losses.mitigation: Output from an attempt that gets thrown away must never reach the user.

whyNot.reason: B cannot lock values chosen at run time, so transactions over list or map entries stop compiling.

recommendation.tradeoff: A contended block may repeat its work so that every transaction stays correct.

decisions.title: How a #Transact block waits until shared state lets it proceed
decisions.gist: How should a #Transact block wait until shared state lets it proceed?
decisions.lesson: A Shared value is data several tasks use at once. #Transact makes a group of edits to them land together. Sometimes a transaction must wait, like taking a job from an empty queue. Today the waiter uses a Condition, and every writer must call notify. This ballot only applies if D-CONC-STM2 picks re-runs.
decisions.story: Ada writes a worker that takes jobs from a shared queue. A new code path pushes jobs but forgets `notify_one`, and workers sleep while jobs pile up.
decisions.inWild:
-- Composable Memory Transactions, PPoPP 2005: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/composable-memory-transactions/
if v < i then retry else writeTVar r (v - i)
decisions.detail:
Prerequisites: D-CONC-STM2 option A (re-runs) and card #3978 (every local change undone between attempts). If D-CONC-STM2 picks option B, a transaction can never undo an attempt, so this ballot is withdrawn and waiting stays with D-SHAREDGUARD1. Guards and `Condition` stay for expert code either way, and they still need manual notify.

Control flow: `tx.wait()` never returns, like `return`. It ends the current attempt. Commit hooks, rollback hooks, and held output from that attempt are dropped. When a watched value changes, the whole block runs again from the top. It is legal only inside the #Transact that names `tx`; a nested transaction's wait retries that nested block's owner. A block that reads no Shared value before calling wait is a compile error, because nothing could ever wake it.

Runtime: before sleeping, the attempt releases every lock it holds, including locks taken by D-CONC-STM2's escalation, so producers can write. It registers on each value it read and rechecks their revisions atomically, the same way the existing Condition protocol does (SharedProtocol.rs:1357-1410). Any change wakes all waiters on that value. Waiting is a cancellation point (D-CANCELMODEL1): cancellation or a blown deadline unregisters it and reports `.Cancelled` or `.DeadlineBlown`. It carries the same effect as `guard.wait`.

Why a method on the handle: `tx` names which transaction restarts when blocks are nested. `wait` is Jet's name for the paper's `retry`. Readiness tables (D-CONC-CHAN2) choose among channels only, not Shared values, so they do not replace C; A covers the common several-queues case in one block. Full profile: this adds a name to the syntax ledger.

options.name: A wait call inside #Transact
options.detail: `tx.wait()` ends the current attempt without effect and never returns. The task sleeps until a Shared value the attempt read changes, then the whole block runs again. One block can read several queues and wait only when all are empty.
options.technical: Diverging call typed like `return`. Uses D-CONC-STM2's read set: it releases every held permit, registers on each read value with an atomic revision recheck, and parks. A commit that bumps a watched revision wakes all waiters. Per-attempt hooks and snapshots are discarded on wait. Requires card #3978.

options.name: Keep guards and Conditions
options.detail: No change to #Transact. Waiting uses D-SHAREDGUARD1's guard_edit, Condition, and notify.
options.technical: No change.
options.code: guard.wait(ready, q => q.len() > 0)?

options.name: Wait plus an alternative block
options.detail: Adds A's wait and an `or` form. The left block runs first. If it waits, its attempt is undone and the right block runs. If both wait, the task sleeps until any value either block read changes. A failure (`Err`) in the left block is returned, not skipped. Its real value is combining helper functions that each wait on their own.
options.technical: Needs nested transaction attempts in the shared Prelude, with the read sets of both blocks joined for the wait.
options.code: job :: #Transact { take(q1) } or { take(q2) }

comparisons.note: retry and orElse make blocking composable and remove lost wake-ups. https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/composable-memory-transactions/

recommendation.why: A removes the forgotten-notify bug for waits on Shared values, and one block can already watch several queues. It needs no second block form.

whyNot.reason: B keeps the manual notify that causes forgotten wake-ups.
C only adds combining helpers that wait on their own; plain A already waits on several queues, and `or` can be added later.

recommendation.tradeoff: One new wait call in exchange for waits on Shared values that need no notify.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: BeginnerTxnWait. Skill: rli5. The beginner pass found undefined terms, no timeline showing why A beats B, and an unstated D-CONC-STM2 dependency. The lesson, current code, and option examples were repaired.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Claude. Adversarial model family: Claude. Fresh agent: AdversaryTxnWait. The review found an undefined wait control flow, a lock deadlock risk, an overbroad local-restore claim, an unfair C comparison, and a retired example. All were repaired, #3978 was filed, and A survives.

surface.gist: How should a #Transact block wait until shared state lets it proceed?
surface.lesson: A Shared value is data several tasks use at once. #Transact makes a group of edits to them land together. Sometimes a transaction must wait, like taking a job from an empty queue. Today the waiter uses a Condition, and every writer must call notify. This ballot only applies if D-CONC-STM2 picks re-runs.

current.note: D-SHAREDGUARD1: the worker sleeps on a Condition. Every producer must remember to notify it.
current.code:
// worker
guard :: queue.guard_edit()
guard.wait(ready, q => q.jobs.len() > 0)?   // sleep until notified
job :: guard.value.jobs.pop()

// producer
queue.jobs.push(job)
ready.notify_one()   // forget this and the worker sleeps forever

wild.note: `retry` means: undo this attempt and sleep until something I read changes. Nobody has to notify. Harris et al., PPoPP 2005.
wild.code:
take q = do
  xs <- readTVar q
  case xs of
    []       -> retry          -- sleep until q changes
    (x:rest) -> writeTVar q rest >> return x

-- producer just writes q; the sleeper wakes by itself

options.name: A wait call inside #Transact
options.gist: `tx.wait()` ends this attempt and sleeps until a value it read changes (the paper's `retry`).
gains: Producers of values waited on this way never notify.
One block can wait on several queues at once.
losses: Needs transactions that can undo a local change (card #3978).

options.name: Keep guards and Conditions
options.gist: Waiting stays with D-SHAREDGUARD1's explicit Condition and notify.
gains: No new surface.
Works without re-runs.
losses: A missing notify leaves a waiter asleep.
Waiting on two queues needs a Condition both producers share.

proposed.code:
guard :: queue.guard_edit()
guard.wait(ready, q => q.len() > 0)?
job :: guard.value.pop()

options.name: Wait plus an alternative block
options.gist: A, plus `or`: if the first block waits, run the second instead.
gains: Helper functions that each wait can be combined.
losses: A second block form to learn beside plain A.

recommendation.why: A removes the forgotten-notify bug for waits on Shared values, and one block can already watch several queues. It needs no second block form.
gains: Blocking code reads as the condition it waits for.

losses.loss: Needs transactions that can undo a local change (card #3978).
losses.mitigation: A waiting attempt must leave nothing behind, including local list edits, before it runs again.

whyNot.reason: B keeps the manual notify that causes forgotten wake-ups.
C only adds combining helpers that wait on their own; plain A already waits on several queues, and `or` can be added later.

recommendation.tradeoff: One new wait call in exchange for waits on Shared values that need no notify.

decisions.title: Which number types Core ships beyond whole and decimal
decisions.gist: Whether Jet ships a complex number type and an exact fraction type.
decisions.lesson: Jet ships four number types today: Int for whole numbers, Float for measured numbers, BigInt for whole numbers of any size, and Decimal for exact base-ten money. The Core surface ledger compares Jet against eleven languages. Four operations it scores as missing are not missing functions at all. They are accessors on types Jet does not have: the real and imaginary parts of a complex number, and the top and bottom of an exact fraction. This choice decides whether those types exist.
decisions.story: Ravi ports a signal filter. Every step multiplies complex numbers, and the textbook writes them as one value. In Jet he carries two Float variables through every function and writes the multiply rule out by hand each time. One sign error in the middle of it costs him an afternoon.

options.name: Ship both, as ordinary Core types
options.detail: `Complex` and `Fraction` join Int, Float, BigInt and Decimal. Complex carries two Floats and answers the arithmetic operators. Fraction carries two whole numbers, stays exact, and reduces itself. Gain: signal, control and geometry code reads like its textbook, and exact ratios stop drifting the way Floats do. Loss: two more types every beginner sees in the Core listing, and two more sets of operator rules to learn.
options.technical: `Complex` is a struct of two Float fields, `real` and `imaginary`, with `+ - * /`, `abs`, `conjugate` and `polar`. `Fraction` is a struct of two Int fields, `numerator` and `denominator`, kept reduced with a positive denominator, with `+ - * /` and exact comparison. Division by a zero denominator is refused where every other zero divisor is. Neither is a default; both are opt-in by naming them.
options.code:
use core.math as math

filter :: Complex.{ real: 0.5, imaginary: -0.5 }
print(filter * filter)          // Complex(0.0, -0.5)
print(filter.abs())             // 0.7071067811865476

third :: Fraction.{ numerator: 1, denominator: 3 }
print(third + third + third)    // 1/1, exactly
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)         // false, the Float answer

options.name: Ship Complex only
options.detail: `Complex` joins Core. Exact fractions stay out, because `Decimal` already answers the money case that most people reach for. Gain: the numeric work that most obviously needs a type gets one, and the Core listing grows by a single name. Loss: exact ratios still drift. A program that adds a third three times still does not get one, and the workaround is to carry two whole numbers by hand.
options.technical: `Complex` as in option A. `numerator` and `denominator` are recorded as declined against this decision id, so the ledger stops scoring them.

options.name: Ship Fraction only
options.detail: `Fraction` joins Core. Complex numbers stay out, on the grounds that they belong with the compute and signal libraries rather than in the Core every program loads. Gain: exact ratios for schedules, gearing, sampling rates and probabilities, which are common in ordinary programs. Loss: complex arithmetic stays hand-written, and the textbook formula and the Jet code stop looking alike.
options.technical: `Fraction` as in option A. `real` and `imaginary` are recorded as declined against this decision id, and complex support is left to a later compute library.

options.name: Ship neither, and record the decline
options.detail: Core keeps four number types. Both are recorded as deliberate declines with this decision id, so they stop being scored as gaps and stop resurfacing. Gain: the beginner surface stays as small as it is now, and neither type has to answer the hard questions about operators, ordering and printing. Loss: Jet stays behind eleven compared languages on both, and anyone doing signal or exact-ratio work writes the type themselves.
options.technical: No new Core types. `real`, `imaginary`, `numerator` and `denominator` are marked declined against this decision id in the Core surface ledger. A user-written struct is the answer, and nothing in Core blocks that.

comparisons.note: Complex is built into the language with its own literal. Exact fractions are a standard-library module.
comparisons.code:
z = 1 + 2j
from fractions import Fraction
Fraction(1, 3) * 3   # Fraction(1, 1)

comparisons.note: Both are built in, and both take part in the ordinary numeric tower.
Neither is in the standard library. Both live in widely used external packages.
Complex is built into the language with two widths. Exact fractions are in the big-number package.
Neither is in the standard library. Complex is in the official numerics package.

recommendation.why: Both types answer a question a program cannot answer well by hand. Complex arithmetic written out at every call site is where sign errors hide, and Float ratios drift in exactly the places people assume they will not. Neither type costs the beginner anything until it is named, and both are ordinary structs with ordinary operators.

whyNot.reason: It leaves exact ratios drifting. Sampling rates, gearing and probabilities are ordinary programs, not specialist ones.
It leaves the textbook formula and the Jet code looking different, which is where sign errors in signal code come from.
It keeps Jet behind eleven compared languages on both, and hands every user the same hand-written multiply rule to get wrong.

recommendation.tradeoff: Two more names in the Core listing, and two more sets of operator rules to document. That is accepted because neither appears until a program names it, and the alternative is hand-written arithmetic in the places most likely to be wrong.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft framed the choice as four ledger rows that are accessors on absent types rather than missing functions. It compared shipping both, either one alone, and neither.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review also tested a single numeric-tower type covering both, and shipping them outside Core in a compute package. The tower was dropped because it hides two different sets of operator rules behind one name, and the package split was folded into option D, whose answer is already a user-written type.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review tested shipping Complex in Core and Fraction in a compute package. It was rejected because exact ratios turn up in ordinary scheduling and sampling code, not in specialist numeric work.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review strengthened every option, giving D a full worked user-written type and giving B and C an explicit decline id so a declined row stops being scored.
reviewPasses.adversarial: The adversarial review attacked the recommendation on beginner surface. Both types survive because neither appears until a program names one, and both behave as ordinary structs with the operators already ratified.

decisions.title: Whether the formatter collapses short blocks onto one line
decisions.situation: The formatter rewrites code into one standard layout so every project looks the same. Today it squeezes any short block onto a single line, even when the author wrote it across several lines, which differs from what the docs show. A user's first format check on a new project fails, and small edits cause large diffs. The owner decides whether short blocks stay as written; we recommend keeping multi-line blocks as the author wrote them, which reverses an earlier vote.
decisions.gist: Should the formatter keep a short multi-line block as written, or squeeze it onto one line?
decisions.lesson: A formatter rewrites code into one standard layout. Jet's formatter puts every block that fits onto one line. The docs and new-project files show those blocks across several lines, so they disagree. Whichever option wins, `jet new` output and the docs must match the formatter.
decisions.story: Eva runs `jet fmt --check` on a brand-new project and it fails. She did not change anything yet.
decisions.detail: Audit 2026-10-28 FMT-01 (fmt_probe.sh): jet new output fails jet fmt --check. Reopens D-FMTCOLLAPSE1=B (collapse every fitting block). Host card 17 fixes the round trip whichever option wins.

options.name: Keep as written
options.detail: A block written across lines stays across lines; a one-line block stays one line. Gains: Docs, `jet new` and the formatter agree. Small edits give small diffs. Losses: Two layouts of the same block can exist.
options.technical: The formatter preserves the author's line break after `{` for blocks that fit; everything else stays canonical.

options.name: Collapse every fitting block
options.detail: Keep today's rule; docs and templates change to the one-line form. Gains: One layout per block. Losses: Diffs grow when a block crosses the width limit.
options.technical: D-FMTCOLLAPSE1=B as ratified.
options.code:
fn run() { print("hi") }
// jet fmt output

comparisons.note: rustfmt keeps function bodies on their own lines by default (fn_single_line = false). Source: https://rust-lang.github.io/rustfmt/?search=fn_single_line

recommendation.why: It matches the docs and what authors write, so new projects pass the format check and edits stay small.
gains: A fresh project passes the format check.

losses.loss: Two layouts of the same block can exist.
losses.mitigation: Only the line break after `{` is kept; all other spacing stays fixed.

whyNot.reason: Forces rewriting docs and causes large diffs on small edits.

recommendation.tradeoff: A little layout freedom in exchange for stable, readable diffs.

decisions.title: How a test checks the message of an expected stop
decisions.situation: A Jet test can require that a block of code stops, meaning it fails at run time with a panic or similar error. It can name the stop's code but cannot check the message, and every panic shares one code. So a test that expects one panic still passes when the code panics for an unrelated reason. You are deciding where a test states the expected message; we recommend a message check on the existing must-stop block.
decisions.gist: Where should a Jet test say which message it expects a stop to carry?
decisions.lesson: A stop is a run-time failure, such as a panic, with a code and a message. Inside a test, .expect_fail { } marks a block that must stop, and it may name the code. Every panic shares one code, so the code alone cannot tell two panics apart. A adds a message check to that block. B adds an expected message to the whole test, as Rust does.
decisions.explainer:
Plain words first. A test is a small program that checks other code. Jet writes one as #Test("name") { ... }.

A stop is a run-time failure that ends the current work. panic("text") is the common one. Every stop has a code, such as E3001 for any panic, and a message, the text that explains it.

Inside a test, .expect_fail { ... } marks a block that must stop. If it stops, the test carries on after the block. If it finishes normally, the test fails. It may name one stop code, as in .expect_fail(E3010) { ... }.

That block is different from #Test("name", expected_fail: true), which marks a whole test as a known bug that should be fixed later.

A substring match means the expected text appears somewhere inside the real message. Rust's should_panic(expected = "...") works this way.
decisions.story: Chen ports a Rust test that must stop with "fingerprint collision". In Jet he can only require some panic, so when a broken check makes the code panic earlier, his test still passes.
decisions.detail:
Code facts, checked 2026-10-04. Docs/spec/spec.md:3214-3217 defines the .expect_fail region: it requires a runtime stop, may name one E30xx code, and a clean finish or a different stop fails the claim. The runtime keeps only the code (crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Core.rs:717-760). Its frame stores an optional expected code, and jet_test_record_stop records a code string. Registry row E0617 still says .expect_fail takes no arguments. That row, at Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Registry/DiagnosticRows.jet:6399, is stale.

The whole-test form is separate. crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/Markers.jet:187 declares #Test(name, faults, expected_fail: Bool). The Jet AST stores only that Boolean (Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/AST/Items.jet:620-634). The unit harness compares failed-or-not with it and never reads the message (Compiler/JetCodegen/Source/Emit/Harness.jet:418-427). syntax-decisions.md:7480-7486 says this is a known-bug mark, not the region.

E3001 covers panic, assert and other program-side stops (DiagnosticRows.jet:7437-7439), so the code alone cannot separate them. Three Rust tests in crates/ use should_panic with expected text today, including crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/Bundle/GenericModules/InstanceCollisionTests.rs:164.

D-TEST-XFAIL1=A settled how a test records a known failure. It did not cover checking a stop's message. Card #4510 asks for a canonical #Test form that checks the message through the existing receipt on every run mode. It says new marker syntax needs an owner ballot, which is why this ballot exists.

A third design was left off the ballot: a Core function that captures a stop as a value, as JUnit's assertThrows does. The card asks for a form that works through the existing test receipt, and Core has no capture API, so it is not a real alternative here.

options.name: A message check on .expect_fail
options.detail:
The region gains an optional named argument: .expect_fail(message: "fingerprint collision") { ... }. The region passes only if it stops, with the named code when one is given, and the stop's message contains the text. The code stays optional, so .expect_fail(E3001, message: "...") also works.

The text is a non-empty string literal matched as a plain, case-sensitive substring, not a pattern; an empty string is E0617. A wrong message fails the test with a report showing the expected text and the real message. For example: expected a stop whose message contains "fingerprint collision", got E3001: assertion failed: modules.len() > 0. The whole-test expected_fail mark is unchanged. A ported should_panic test becomes one region around the call.
options.technical:
The region frame stores the expected message beside the expected code. jet_test_record_stop records the message with the code. Leaving the region compares by substring on the stop's message text, without the rendered frame or the panic: prefix. Every stop site must pass that raw text; the scheduler stop path holds only a rendered report today (Core.rs:1312-1313).

The marker registry row, E0617's text, the spec paragraph, both checkers and every run mode's runtime change together. Fixtures cover match, wrong message, wrong code, empty text and clean finish.

options.name: An expected_stop field on #Test
options.detail:
The #Test marker gains a field: #Test("name", expected_stop: "fingerprint collision"). The whole test body must stop with a message containing that text, like Rust's should_panic.

This copies the Rust shape closely. It gives Jet two ways to require a stop, the region and the field. The field sits beside expected_fail, which means something different, a known bug, so readers can confuse the two.
options.technical: Markers.jet adds expected_stop: String? to Test; the AST, harness and receipt carry it; the harness compares the stop message after the body ends. The marker registry row and its owner gate change.

comparisons.note: Rust checks a panic message with should_panic(expected), a substring match on the whole test.
pytest checks an expected exception inside a block and matches its message with a pattern.

recommendation.why: A extends the block Jet already uses for expected stops. There stays one way to require a stop, and it now checks the reason too.
gains: A panic for the wrong reason fails the test.
Still one way to require a stop, around the exact call that should stop.
Ported Rust tests keep their message check.

losses.loss: Ported Rust tests wrap the stopping call in a block instead of marking the whole test.
losses.mitigation: The rewrite is mechanical, and a block around one call catches fewer accidental stops than a whole-test mark.

losses.loss: A message that contains the text by accident still passes.
losses.mitigation: Authors pick a distinctive phrase, as Rust tests do. Naming the stop code as well narrows the match further.

whyNot.reason: B adds a second way to require a stop, next to a look-alike field that marks known bugs.

recommendation.tradeoff: Wrapping one call in a block buys one stop check that also checks the reason.

reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: BallotDraft2. Skill: rli5. Author-run pass that found stop, region, marker, substring and receipt undefined and expected_fail confusable with the region; the explainer now teaches each and separates the two.
reviewPasses.adversarial:
Author model family: claude. Adversarial model family: claude. Fresh agent: BallotRev1-2. It re-checked each file:line, fixed overstated card claims and the bounds-check example, made A's match case-sensitive with empty text refused, and named the scheduler stop path.

Check that .expect_fail(E3010) without message behaves as today, that E0617's text matches the new shape, and that the whole-test expected_fail mark is unchanged. Port the CompW20 GenericModules should_panic test and show it fails when the collision message changes.

decisions.title: What an unchanged build is allowed to skip
decisions.gist: Whether a module whose inputs did not change may reuse its recorded check result and warnings instead of being checked again.
decisions.lesson: D-INCR-UNIT1 (ratified) says no path skips sema or diagnostics on a cache hit that still needs checking. The library-reuse plan text is stricter: no cache path skips parsing, sema, policy, or diagnostics. A memoized check stores the full result of checking a module, keyed by the digest of the module's own bytes plus every other input the check read. The choice is whether reusing that stored result counts as checking. It decides how fast an unchanged jet build can be and where its warnings come from.
decisions.explainer: Terms: checking a module means parsing it, understanding its meaning, applying the package's policy, and producing its warnings and errors. A digest is a fingerprint of exact bytes, so two inputs with the same digest are the same bytes. A module's interface is the part other modules can see. A record is a saved result with its key; a node is one build step; memoized means saved for reuse.
decisions.story: Dana runs jet build, gets two warnings, reads them, and runs jet build again ten seconds later without changing anything. She expects the same two warnings and an answer in well under a second. On a large program a fresh check of every module costs seconds even when nothing changed.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet build
Warning [L2510] (hidden_cost_in_loop): this implicit clone of `String` repeats inside a loop.
Warning [L0514] (same_subject_dispatch): adjacent categorical guards over `ch` can be one ordered subject table
✓ shop built in 4.1s · 3 of 21 units compiled, 18 reused · release · ./build/shop

$ jet build      # nothing changed
# question: re-check all 40 modules, or reuse the recorded result?
decisions.detail: Owner tradeoff pass, 2026-09-02: option A names the ratified `--no-cache` as the written expert hatch the owner asked for. It adds `--verify` with one contract shared with D-RECORD1 and seals the whole check-time closure, so the record is checked by machines instead of trusted.

options.name: Memoized module checks count as checking, with --no-cache and --verify as the expert hatches
options.detail:
A module reuses its recorded check result when its own bytes, the interfaces it imports, the package policy and settings, the target and profile, and the compiler version are all unchanged. Every generated or external input it read must also be unchanged. Changed modules and modules that import a changed interface are always checked for real.

The recorded warnings are stored as typed diagnostics with their source positions and are drawn again for the current terminal, so color, width, and --json all render correctly. An unchanged jet build verifies digests, redraws the warnings, confirms the output is still in the store, and prints the receipt line in tens of milliseconds. This option ships only with an audit test that fails if a check reads any input outside its key.

The expert hatch is the ratified `jet build --no-cache`: every step runs from source for this one invocation, for a deliberate full rebuild or a suspected stale record. It writes a record only for a key that has none. A key that already has a record must match the fresh digest; a mismatch keeps both artifacts, quarantines the key, and fails as a compiler defect.

`jet build --verify` is for CI and investigation: it recomputes every step without reuse and compares, reporting identical, or the first changed input, or a same-key mismatch as that defect. Every check-time read, in sema, the loader, comptime, and generated inputs, goes through one reader capability, and a structural test forbids any other host read there. So a record cannot omit an input, and a nightly `--verify` in CI finds a defect before a person does.
options.technical:
Check(module) key = raw source bytes + module path + imported interface digests + package policy/authority facts + lint settings + target/profile facts + compiler identity. It also includes digests of generated or external inputs read. Canonical-AST, interface, and body digests are derived outputs used by later nodes, not the Check key. Diagnostics are stored typed (code, message, spans, severity) and rendered per invocation; `--json` records are byte-identical under a versioned schema.

Input audit: every file, environment, and facts read during a check goes through one instrumented reader. An undeclared read fails the test suite, and any node kind that fails the audit checks fresh until fixed. Snapshot coherence: read through stable handles, compare metadata before and after hashing, retry on change, and bind every node of one invocation to one source snapshot. Records are verified by digest and schema at use time; corruption is quarantined. This reading treats D-INCR-UNIT1's 'still needs checking' as 'has a changed input'.

`--no-cache` (D-BUILDCACHE1): bypasses every read and publishes only absent keys. On an existing key the recomputed digest must equal the record; otherwise both artifacts are kept, the key is quarantined, and a registered compiler-defect diagnostic exits nonzero. `--verify` is one contract shared with D-RECORD1. It selects the recorded receipt, tells changed or unavailable inputs from a same-identity mismatch, recomputes every node, compares node and final digests, and quarantines only corruption or a same-key mismatch.

Reader seal: one `CheckInputReader` capability passes through the whole check-time closure, which is jet-sema, the loader, jet-comptime, and generated-input loading. A source test forbids `std::fs` and `std::env` there. An executor not yet sealed forces fresh checking until it is.
options.code:
$ jet build      # nothing changed
Warning [L2510] (hidden_cost_in_loop): this implicit clone of `String` repeats inside a loop.
Warning [L0514] (same_subject_dispatch): adjacent categorical guards over `ch` can be one ordered subject table
✓ shop up to date · 38 ms · 40 checks reused, 21 units reused, link reused · release · ./build/shop

$ jet explain-build shop --why src/net/client.jet
check shop/net/client   reused   key: bytes 4f2a…, imports 3 (unchanged), policy 91c0…, compiler 0.9.1, target x86_64-linux/release

$ jet build --no-cache   # expert hatch: everything from source; only absent keys are written
✓ shop built in 4.1s · 40 checks fresh, 21 of 21 units compiled · release · ./build/shop

$ jet build --verify     # recompute and compare; CI runs this nightly
✓ shop verified · 40 checks, 21 units, link: fresh results match the records
// or, a same-key mismatch:
Error: check shop/net/client recomputed differently under the same key (record 4f2a…, fresh 9b10…); record quarantined
  fix: report this as a compiler defect with `jet explain-build shop --why src/net/client.jet`

options.name: Always re-check the package being built
options.detail: Dependency packages restore from the store, but every module of the package being built is parsed and checked again on every build, even when nothing changed. Warnings are always freshly produced. Compile and link work is still reused. This is the safe fallback if any check input turns out to be missing from the key.
options.technical: Check nodes for the root package never hit; Emit, Compile, and Link nodes reuse. Equivalent to today's behavior with a faster backend.
options.code:
$ jet build      # nothing changed
Warning [L2510] (hidden_cost_in_loop): this implicit clone of `String` repeats inside a loop.
Warning [L0514] (same_subject_dispatch): adjacent categorical guards over `ch` can be one ordered subject table
✓ shop up to date · 1.9s · 40 checks re-run, 21 units reused, link reused · release · ./build/shop

options.name: Replay without any content check
options.detail: Trust file timestamps alone: if no file looks newer, reuse the last result. Fastest possible, but a file rewritten with a preserved timestamp would reuse stale results and stale warnings. This is the failure Cargo users know from stale-fingerprint reports.
options.technical: Stamp-only invalidation; no content digest on the hot path. Violates the one-key law of the proposal and the anti-goal 'a cache purge that fixes errors is a compiler bug'.
options.code:
$ cp -p other/client.jet src/net/client.jet   # different bytes, same timestamp
$ jet build
✓ shop up to date · 12 ms
# wrong: the binary still has the old fetch_all, and the old L2510 warning still shows

comparisons.note: Cargo replays recorded warnings for fresh crates and skips rustc when its fingerprint matches. The fingerprint covers compiler, features, target, dependencies, and build-script inputs; local source freshness uses file timestamps, which is the narrow source of its stale-build reports.
comparisons.code:
$ cargo build
warning: unused variable `x`   # replayed from the last run
    Finished `dev` profile in 0.04s

comparisons.note: Bazel treats an action with identical input digests as already done and never re-runs it; content digests, not timestamps, decide. Diagnostics are part of the recorded action result.
comparisons.code:
$ bazel build //shop
INFO: 0 processes.
INFO: Build completed successfully

recommendation.why: A stored result keyed on exact bytes and every other input the check read is the result of checking. The sealed reader and the audit test make that sentence true rather than assumed. It gives the fastest honest unchanged build and keeps warnings the same, which is what people expect from a repeat run. `--no-cache` and `--verify` keep the from-scratch build one flag away.

whyNot.reason: It spends seconds re-deriving a result the key already proves and makes the unchanged build slower than Cargo's. It remains the fallback for any node kind whose inputs are not yet sealed by the audit.
Timestamps cannot prove content, so it would reuse stale results and stale warnings.

recommendation.tradeoff: Nothing in the memoized path rests on faith: the sealed reader bounds what a check can read, `--verify` recomputes and compares in CI, and `--no-cache` rebuilds everything on request. The remaining cost is one nightly full recompute in CI, which is machine time.

reviewPasses.base: The first draft compared memoized checks, always re-checking the root package, and timestamp-only reuse, and recommended memoized checks.
reviewPasses.boilOcean: The breadth review tested a partial variant that re-checks only the entry module and a variant that stores rendered text instead of typed diagnostics. The first buys nothing the digest proves; the second breaks when terminal width, color, or output mode changes; typed diagnostics with per-invocation rendering became part of option A.
reviewPasses.hybrid: The hybrid review kept memoized checks, made importers of a changed interface always check fresh, and kept option B as the fallback for any node kind that fails the input audit. The owner's tradeoff pass added `--no-cache` write rules, `--verify`, and the reader seal.
reviewPasses.cooperative: The cooperative review gave option B its strongest form as the safe fallback while inputs are unproven, and option C its honest speed number. Neither survives the stale-warning and stale-binary cases.
reviewPasses.beginner: Fresh agent: Rli5Build. Skill: rli5. The first pass found checking, digest, and interface undefined; the lesson defines them. The second could not tell when to type `--no-cache` versus `--verify`; A now says the first rebuilds on request and the second is what CI runs nightly.
reviewPasses.adversarial: Author model family: Anthropic. Adversarial model family: OpenAI. The first rival pass found a misattributed no-skip rule and a key on canonical AST; the ballot now keys on raw bytes with an audit test. The second, on the owner's revision, found the seal missing comptime, a new flag duplicating `--no-cache`, and two meanings of `--verify`; A now seals the closure and shares one contract.

decisions.title: Types for UI preview values
decisions.situation: The core.ui module exports preview and playground functions. Their return names have no declared type in the checker, and the Rust runtime has no matching type. The spec lists these names in its table of public functions, so they are documented behavior. Removing them would break that documentation. We recommend declaring real types for them, so the checker can check preview values.
decisions.gist: The preview functions return values whose type is not declared. What type should they be?
decisions.lesson: A public name needs a real type. Otherwise the checker cannot tell preview values apart from any other value.
decisions.story: Mia calls core.ui.preview with a name. The checker accepts the value without knowing its type, so a wrong argument passes until it fails at run time.
decisions.inWild: pub fn preview(name: &str) -> UiPreview
decisions.detail: Source: Core/Ui/Ui.jet declares enums UIPreviewDevice (line 21) and UIPreviewKind (line 27), and functions returning UIPreviewViewport (lines 116-118, 197). The spec at Docs/spec/reference/core-library.md:3381-3383 lists preview and playground returning UIPreview, and desktop, phone and tablet returning UIPreviewViewport. Failing test: compiler_owned_core_ui_registry_has_nominal_rows (GoldenFix4, 2026-10-01). Option A adds three declarations: UIPreview, UIPreviewViewport, and the two enums. Usage of these names outside Core was not checked [INFERENCE: small].

decisions.title: Typed live data, and when a write wakes its readers
decisions.situation: Live data is a server value that a page keeps current, like a list of open tickets. Today a program names live data with a text label and carries its value as text, so a mistyped label silently stops updates. The helpers that skip an unchanged value accept only whole numbers. This vote picks how live data is named and typed, and whether a write of an unchanged value wakes its readers.
decisions.gist: Should live data be named by its function, and should a write that changes nothing wake readers?
decisions.lesson: Live data is a server value that a page keeps current. Jet already decided that a live query is a function that only reads the database. It also decided that data held by a link redraws its readers when written. Today the other live calls still use text labels and text values. The helper that skips an unchanged value works only on whole numbers.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: write a function that reads the tickets and pass it to app.live. The page gets a typed loading state that refreshes when the tickets change. Nothing is named twice.

Expert path: data from outside the database, like a load feed from another server, is still named by the function that fetches it. app.subscribe polls it, app.push hands every reader a new value, and app.invalidate fetches again now. Each call is checked against that function's result type.
decisions.story: Mia builds a support dashboard with open tickets and a server load feed. One call says "ticket" where the others say "tickets", and the page silently stops refreshing. Named by its function, that typo is a build error.
decisions.detail:
Today, core.web and app name live data by String and carry String payloads. The calls are live(key, data), live_get, subscribe(key), invalidate(key), signal_push and transact_invalidate (Core/Web/Web.jet, Core/App/App.jet:89-103). Eight core.reactive helpers take Int only: update, set_if_changed, changed, computed_update, effect_run, effect_run_if, effect_last and effect_changed (Core/Reactive/Reactive.jet:47-84, core-library.md:3585-3594).

A probe on dev shows the silent typo. A program calls app.live("tickets", "[]") and then app.invalidate("ticket"). It compiles, runs, and live_stats prints invalidations=0. Separately, passing a Signal<Int> literal to reactive.set_if_changed hits an internal compiler error at IR build. That is card #6197; it is not a ballot input.

D-LIVEQUERY1=A: app.live(query, args) takes a function whose effects stay inside DB.Read. A committed #Transact re-runs exactly the subscriptions whose read footprint it touches. No invalidation keys exist. app.subscribe and app.invalidate stay as the expert floor for sources outside the tracker, with an every: interval.

D-REACT-REF1=A: reads through an @ link in a tracked context subscribe, and writes notify those readers. Signal<T> becomes @T; computed and effect stay. It does not say whether an unchanged write notifies. D-DX-SERVERFN1=A: an App action is registered once, and the compiler derives its typed client and stable endpoint. D-MEMREF1=A: @Inbox{...} makes data held by a link.

So two things are open: the typed shape of the expert floor, and the write rule that replaces the Int-only helpers. Naming by function is the only shape that keeps D-LIVEQUERY1's rule that no keys exist. A text-key LiveKey<T>, as the card's wording suggests, would bring keys back. It is therefore not offered. The real owner choice is the write rule, so A and B share the naming and differ only there.

Convex uses the query function reference as the subscription's identity (docs.convex.dev/client/react). useQuery(api.tickets.open, args) is typed end to end and re-runs when data it read changes. There are no keys to keep in sync. TanStack Query names cached data with array keys matched by prefix. Its queryOptions() helper keeps the key, the fetcher and the result type in one object (tanstack.com/query, query-options guide).

Recoil atoms needed a unique text key, and a duplicate key was reported only at run time (recoiljs.org, atom API). Phoenix PubSub uses text topics, with the same typo risk. Solid and Vue skip a signal write equal to the old value, so redundant writes redraw nothing. Both compare by identity only. A replaced object that is equal in content still redraws there.

The write rule in A is one rule for every type: a write notifies only if the stored value changed. Text, lists and structs compare by content. Floats compare by bits, so NaN over the same NaN is no change, while 0.0 over -0.0 is. Links and function values compare by identity. A write through an inner link notifies on its own. No user-written == runs inside a write.

The cost is engineered in four steps. First, the compare runs only when the link has a subscriber; D-REACT-REF1 already null-checks there. Second, it stops at the first difference, and a length change is found before any element. Third, when old and new share storage, the compare stops at once. Fourth, a write the compiler proves changes the value skips the compare, such as x.n += 1 or a push onto a list.

The worst case was measured on dev with jet run -O2 on a 10,000-row list of {id: Int, title: String}. Two equal lists built separately compared in 0.33 ms. Lists that differ only in the last row took 0.29 ms. The same list against itself took 0.10 ms today, and the shared-storage stop makes that O(1). Building one such list took 4.4 ms, so the worst compare costs about 7% of making the value.

What the compare saves is larger. An invalidation that re-runs a query with an unchanged result sends nothing over the socket and redraws no reader. Under B, every such re-run redraws every reader. With a tracked footprint, many invalidations touch rows a query reads without changing its result.

The other losses found while designing, with their fixes. Sources with inputs: the arguments after the function are that function's own arguments, checked as a call, as in app.live(query, args). Pushed feeds: app.push(source, args..., value: v) checks v against the source's result type. The required source function answers a reader who joins between pushes; a push-only key cannot.

Invalidation has exactly two forms. app.invalidate(load) re-runs every binding of the source, and app.invalidate(load, "db1") re-runs exactly that argument list. There is no partial match. Renaming a source changes its wire name between deploys. That is shared with every compiler-derived endpoint under D-DX-SERVERFN1, where the build id reloads an old page. invalidate and push return nothing, so a bare call is not an E0433 discard as it is today.

Probe of A. The A program with its run body cut to the database open passes jet check on dev. With the feature, the only diagnostics are the four new app calls (E0104, E0764, E0102, E0112) and the ratified @ link spelling (E0003). Load{cpu: 0.4} runs today and prints 0.4. DBScope, SQL{...}, db.decode<T>, http.get, json.decode<T> and the 5s literal are today's Jet.

options.name: Named by function; only changes wake
options.detail: Live data is named by the function that produces it, the way live queries already are. The result is a linked loading state of that function's result type, so a wrong name or type fails the build. A write wakes readers only when the stored value changed, for every type. So an unchanged query result redraws nothing, and the number-only helpers become plain writes.
options.technical:
These are compiler-checked calls in the same family as app.live. The arguments after the function are that function's own arguments, checked as a call.

```
app.live(query, args...) -> @Loadable<T, E>      // query: fn(args...) -[DB.Read]> T E!
app.subscribe(source, args..., every: Duration?{None}) -> @Loadable<T, E>
app.push(source, args..., value: T)              // every subscriber of that binding
app.invalidate(source)                           // every binding re-runs
app.invalidate(source, args...)                  // exactly this argument list re-runs
app.live_stats() -> String
```

T and E must be Encode and Decode, proved before code generation as D-DX-SERVERFN1 does for actions. A source may carry any effects. Its stable wire name comes from its module path. A closure is a compile error, since only a named function can be a source.

Deleted from core.web and app: LiveQuery, live(key, data), live_get, live_show, subscribe(key), invalidate(key), signal_push and the public transact_invalidate. The #Transact commit hook stays internal.

core.reactive keeps computed<T>, effect and unsubscribe. It deletes update, set_if_changed, changed, computed_update, effect_run, effect_run_if, effect_last and effect_changed with the Signal box (D-REACT-REF1). Their jobs become x.n += d, x.n != v and x.n = v.

Write rule added to D-REACT-REF1's notify: notify only if the stored value changed. Content compare for text, lists and structs, bits for floats, identity for links and functions. The compare runs only with a subscriber, exits at the first difference, and stops at once on shared storage. A write proven to change the value skips it. The server applies the same rule before pushing a re-run result.

options.name: Named by function; every write wakes
options.detail: Live data is named and typed by its function, exactly as in A. The difference is the write rule. Every write wakes its readers, whether or not the value changed. A write costs no compare, and an author who wants to skip an unchanged value guards the write by hand.
options.technical:
The app calls, the deletions and the core.reactive surface are identical to A.

Write rule: D-REACT-REF1's notify runs on every write that has a subscriber, with no compare. A re-run live query pushes its result over the socket even when it is unchanged, and every reader redraws.

An author skips an unchanged write with if x.n != v -> x.n = v. That compare uses the type's ==, and it is written at each site that needs it.
options.code:
fn run() {
    conn :: db.open_memory()
    tickets :: app.live(open_tickets, conn, "web")      // same typed result as A
    feed :: app.subscribe(load, "db1", every: 5s)
    app.push(load, "db1", value: Load{cpu: 0.4})
    app.invalidate(load, "db1")
    inbox := @Inbox{unread: 0}
    inbox.unread = 3                                    // readers redraw
    inbox.unread = 3                                    // readers redraw again
    if inbox.unread != 3 -> inbox.unread = 3            // skip by hand
}

comparisons.note: The query function reference is the subscription's name and type; it re-runs when data it read changes. https://docs.convex.dev/client/react
Array keys name cached data; queryOptions() keeps the key and result type in one object. https://tanstack.com/query/latest/docs/framework/react/guides/query-options
A signal write equal to the old value notifies no one by default; the check is identity only. https://docs.solidjs.com/reference/basic-reactivity/create-signal

recommendation.why: A names live data by its function, so names and types cannot drift. One write rule, wake only on change, keeps an unchanged query result from redrawing the page.
gains: A wrong name or value type fails the build.
An unchanged result sends nothing and redraws nothing.
Eight number-only helpers become plain writes.

whyNot.reason: B redraws every reader whenever a re-run returns the same result, and makes authors guard writes by hand.

recommendation.tradeoff: A spends one compare on a subscribed write. The worst case, 10,000 equal rows, measured 0.33 ms, about 7% of building them. It saves the redraw.

surface.gist: Should live data be named by its function, and should a write that changes nothing wake readers?
surface.lesson: Live data is a server value that a page keeps current. Today it is named by a text label and carried as text. The helper that skips an unchanged value works only on whole numbers.

current.note: Labels and values are text. This typo compiles and nothing refreshes.
current.code:
q :: app.live("tickets", "[]")
print(app.live_get(q))              // text, decode by hand
_hit :: app.invalidate("ticket")    // typo: 0 refreshed
unread = reactive.set_if_changed(unread, 3)   // Int only

wild.note: The query function is the subscription's name and type.

options.gist: Live data is named and typed by its function, and a write wakes readers only if the value changed.
gains: Wrong names and types fail the build.
Unchanged results redraw nothing.

feed :: app.subscribe(load, "db1", every: 5s)
app.push(load, "db1", value: Load{cpu: 0.4})

inbox := @Inbox{unread: 0}

options.gist: The same naming as A, but every write wakes readers, changed or not.
gains: Wrong names and types fail the build.
A write never compares.
losses: Unchanged results redraw every reader.
Authors guard writes by hand.

inbox := @Inbox{unread: 0}
inbox.unread = 0                          // readers redraw
if inbox.unread != 0 -> inbox.unread = 0  // skip by hand

gains: Typos and wrong value types fail the build.
Unchanged results redraw nothing.

whyNot.reason: B redraws every reader on unchanged results and needs hand guards.

decisions.title: Where the shared SQL engine is exposed
decisions.situation: Jet's command-line tool needs the same SQL engine that Core uses to query rows, but the engine was private to Core. A public module was introduced during the self-host repair so the tool could reach it, adding names that ordinary programs can also use. Those public names become an API commitment, while a private toolchain exception would introduce a special access rule. You choose the public module, a toolchain-only door, or one public query function; we recommend retaining the small named module.
decisions.gist: Should the shared SQL engine remain a public Core module?
decisions.lesson: A private module can only be used inside Core. The command-line tool also needs the SQL engine. A publishes a named engine module, B grants the toolchain private access, and C exposes one text-to-rows function. Every choice must keep one shared implementation.
decisions.explainer: Public engine types allow the CLI to parse and execute using the same representation as Core. A smaller text-only entry point reduces exposed names but must still satisfy all CLI requirements.
decisions.story: Doris runs a query from the terminal. She wants the CLI to use Core's real engine without inventing a separate SQL implementation or an unexplained private access privilege.
decisions.detail: The source ballot describes the public surface as six types, eight functions and three methods in core.db.sql. Names include JetSQLQuery, JetSQLValue, JetSQLResultRow and execute_sql_rows. This vote preserves the original module choice; it does not authorize a second SQL engine. Proposed import paths below express the ballot's exposure alternatives.

options.name: Public SQL module
options.detail: Retain the engine's named public module with its six types, eight functions and three methods. Keep the rest of the engine private and the CLI on the same implementation.
options.technical: core.db.sql exposes the engine types and named execution helpers. Confirm the exact exported-name list and remove unused names before finalizing that list.
options.code:
use core.db.sql as sql
// CLI and user programs share this public engine module.

options.name: Toolchain-only private access
options.detail: Keep the engine private. Add a loader rule allowing only the toolchain package to import those private Core modules; user programs cannot use that access.
options.technical: Private core.db.runtime imports are accepted only when the importing package is the toolchain.
options.code:
use core.db.runtime as runtime
// Accepted only under the proposed toolchain access rule.

options.name: One public query entry point
options.detail: Expose one function taking SQL text and input rows and returning result rows. Keep the engine's internal query and value types private, subject to checking the CLI's needs.
options.technical: Proposed core.db.query_rows(text, rows) replaces access to parse and execution helpers. Its returned rows require a usable public representation.
options.code:
// Proposed single entry point:
rows :: core.db.query_rows(text, data)

decisions.title: An opened connection queries directly, meaning every row; row policies stay for code that serves users
decisions.situation: A script that opens a database and counts rows can't query today. The connection has no `query`; every query goes through a row-policy scope, and most programs write a policy of `"true"` that keeps every row. Python and Bun do it in three lines. The vote decides whether a plain connection can query. We recommend yes: `c.query(...)` means every row, and D-SQL-HANDLER1 keeps policies required where users are served.

decisions.title: A web handler that queries every row fails to compile: connection queries carry `DB.AllRows`, which the handler type leaves out
decisions.situation: A web handler that queries every row shows one user's data to another. Today Jet prevents that by making every query pick a row policy. Once a plain connection can query (D-SQL-CONNQUERY1), handlers need their own guard. A route's handler type already lists the effects it may use: `-[Net, FS.Read]>`. The vote decides how a handler is kept to a row policy. We recommend an effect: connection queries carry `DB.AllRows`, and the handler type leaves it out.
decisions.gist: How should Jet stop a web handler from reading every user's rows by accident?
decisions.lesson: A web page shows one person's data, so a handler must say whose rows it reads. `c.with_policy(policy, req.user)` narrows to that user. If every user really should see every row, write `c.all_rows()`. A handler that does neither won't compile.
decisions.story: Sam copies a script's query into a route. It compiles, and every logged-in user now sees every other user's notes.
