decisions.title: Whether the Jet install ships the Core library already checked
decisions.situation: Every check of a program that imports the http client rereads and rechecks about seventy Core library files, so even an unchanged one-file program takes about a second. Core changes only when the compiler or its Core files change, so its checked results could be made once and reused by every later run. The open choice is where those first results come from: the install, the first run on each machine, or a download signed by the Jet release key. The choice decides install size, how slow the very first check is, and whether a laptop with no network checks fast. The recommendation is to ship the results inside the install and build them locally when no shipped copy matches.
decisions.gist: Should the Jet install carry Core already checked, or should each machine check Core on first use?
decisions.lesson: Checking a library means reading its source and working out every type, effect and signature. The result can be saved as check records that later runs read instead of the source. Rust ships its standard library already compiled in every toolchain. Here the saved records cover checking only; building still compiles and links as today.
decisions.story: A student installs Jet on a train and writes a six-line program that fetches a web page. Today each check takes about a second, because Core is rechecked every time. With Core shipped checked, the first check takes an estimated tenth of a second, with no network. A compiler developer who rebuilds jet pays one longer check after each rebuild, then runs fast again.
decisions.inWild:
$ ls ~/.rustup/toolchains/stable-*/lib/rustlib/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/lib/ | grep libstd
libstd-46ee58edabb6fcaa.rlib
libstd-46ee58edabb6fcaa.rmeta
libstd-46ee58edabb6fcaa.so
# Rust installs its standard library precompiled, so a first build never compiles it.
decisions.detail:
Where Core comes from today. A Jet host reads Core from the toolchain root, JET_TOOLCHAIN_ROOT, using the files listed in CORE_SOURCE_OWNED_ROWS (Request.jet:196-201, :769-778). CoreSources.jet holds only the effect vocabulary. The record path exists but is dead: JetDriverRecordStore (Identity.jet:279), jet_driver_load_record (:921) and jet_driver_publish_record (:935). The CLI passes record_store: None (Request.jet:804).

Key and identity. The record key is the one D-BUILD-NOCHANGE1=A fixes: compiler identity, Core source digest, target and profile facts, lint and policy facts, and schema versions. Compiler identity is name@version#source id, a SHA-256 over the compiler and Core sources (compiler-packages.mjs:82-123). A compiler built from released sources therefore shares the release identity.

A compiler with no identity has no key. jet build Compiler sets no JET_COMPILER_IDENTITY (Request.jet:196-201), and the check key returns None without one (Identity.jet:904-916). Such a compiler checks the Core it reaches on every run, as today, and saves nothing. Rebuilding the compiler after a Core edit changes its identity, so every record misses once.

Measured today on the r14 jet, at a load average of 5-6. jet check fetch.jet prints ok: `fetch.jet` has no problems, with a median of 962 ms over seven runs. jet build fetch.jet takes 1178 ms, and checking a hello program that imports no Core module takes 11 ms. The kitspeed medians for the same shape (http_get.jet) are 860-933 ms before #6032 stage 0 and 561-587 ms after it.

Where the time goes. The single base trace spans 830 ms: load 340, register 190, sema.finalize 230 and sema.bodies 150 ms, with a peak of 652 MB. After stage 0 it spans 570 ms with a peak of 413 MB. The loader reads 70 Core modules: 34,482 of Core's 74,463 lines (46%). They hold 8.3 of its 10.0 MB (83%), because the set includes the large Unicode tables in Text.

The one program every option is measured against:
```jet
package { name: "fetch", authority: { allow: [IO, Mem.Alloc, Net] } }
use core.http as http
fn run() {
    resp :: http.get("http://127.0.0.1:8080/") ?? panic("request")
    print(resp.body().text(1024) ?? panic("body"))
}
```

How the warm estimate is built. A warm run still starts jet and reads the user file, which the 11 ms hello check bounds. Confirming that Core sources are unchanged costs about 1 ms by file stamps, or 11-45 ms if every file is hashed, per a Node scan of all of Core. Reading the Core records the program needs is estimated at 10-50 ms. The user package and the program phase add about 15-40 ms. The sum is about 40-150 ms.

How the build estimate is built. Today jet build fetch.jet takes about 0.2 s more than jet check (1178 against 962 ms), for lowering, code generation and linking. Records remove checking work only, so a warm build is estimated at about 0.25-0.35 s. Building and running still lower, compile and link as they do today.

How the cold estimate is built. All of Core is 167 files, 74,463 lines and 10.0 MB; the http set is 46% of the lines and 83% of the bytes. Scaling the 561-587 ms post-stage-0 check by lines gives about 1.2-1.3 s, and by bytes about 0.7 s. Before stage 0 it is about 1.9-2.0 s by lines. The estimate is 0.7-2.0 s, with a peak of about 0.9-1.4 GB, paid once per compiler identity, target and Core edit.

Size of option A. Today the install is about 105 MB: the jet binary is 76.6 MB and the runtime directory about 28 MB. Core's records hold declarations, signatures, effect rows and summaries, layouts, templates, package facts and checked bodies. They are estimated at 10-30 MB per host target on disk and 3-8 MB compressed. The plan's Core-records stage measures the real figure.

Only checking gets fast. The records replace checking only. Building and running still lower, compile and link as today, about 0.2 s for fetch, and the runtime they link already ships in the install. Offline, a shipped install checks fast and builds no slower than today.

Read-only install layer under the hatches. Recompute-and-compare rechecks Core against the shipped record. If the fresh digest differs, both are kept: the fresh record goes to the quarantine of the machine-wide store under the same key. Later runs skip that shipped record, check Core locally and report the compiler-defect diagnostic until a new install replaces it. If the store is read-only too, the run reports the defect and exits non-zero.

Reproducibility and trust. A release test rebuilds Core's records on a second machine with a different --threads value and compares digests byte for byte; any difference blocks the release. Shipped records are trusted exactly as the jet binary beside them is. Their checksum detects corruption, not tampering, and whoever can rewrite the install can rewrite jet. Only option C adds a signature.

Relation to #5476. Its approved S3 bakes the always-loaded Core state, Prelude, Errors and the effect tables, into the jet binary as static data, built in the same chain so it cannot go stale. That serves its 2 ms hello target under every option here. S3 does not cover imported modules such as http; these ballots do. Its S4, checking Core bodies only when reached on each run, is the per-run form of option C of D-BUILD-COREUNIT1.

Depends on D-BUILD-COREUNIT1. Option A assumes Core is one package, so one record set ships. Under COREUNIT1=B it would ship about 145 group record sets. Under COREUNIT1=C nothing fixed exists to ship, so A falls back to B. Sealed Core data for exact diagnostics is sized in COREUNIT1; shipped records carry the same data.

Edge cases. A corrupt shipped record fails its checksum and is a miss, never an error. A read-only or full store still works: the check runs and publishing is skipped. Cross-compiling to a target without shipped records checks Core once for that target. The examples use the ratified --no-cache spelling; D-BUILD-REUSESET1 may rename it to --cache=off.

Fixed by ratified decisions and not reopened here. The user reuse unit is the package (D-INCR-UNIT1=A; D-INCR-PARK1=C retired item reuse). Records live in the machine-wide store with its cap, reserve and jet cache commands (D-BUILD-STORE1=E). D-BUILD-NOCHANGE1=A fixes two hatches: ignore saved work, and recompute and compare, with byte-identical replay. D-BUILD-REUSESET1 decides their spelling. Persistence is disk records plus the opt-in jet dev --serve session, with no daemon (D-BUILD-SESSION1=A).

Beginner path: install Jet and run jet check; Core is already checked, with no setting and no network. Expert path: jet cache status shows the store, and recompute-and-compare proves a shipped record against a fresh check. A compiler developer sees one slower check after each rebuild. Under B every user sees one slow first check per install or upgrade. Under C a fast first check needs the network.

options.name: The install carries Core already checked
options.detail:
Release installs include Core's check records; when none match, the first run checks Core and saves them locally. Beginners notice only speed. Experts keep the ratified hatches: ignore saved work for one run, or recompute and compare.

Gains: The first check after install is already fast. Fast checking works offline, with nothing to download. A release test proves the shipped records reproduce.

Losses: The install grows an estimated 10-30 MB on about 105 MB. Developer compilers still check Core once per rebuild.

Estimated end effect. First and later checks of fetch: about 40-150 ms, against 962 ms today. Build of fetch: about 0.25-0.35 s, against 1178 ms. Small check: about 11-20 ms, as today. Ignoring saved work: about 0.7-2.0 s, because all of Core is rechecked and compared. A developer compiler pays one 0.7-2.0 s check per rebuild. Install: about 10-30 MB more on disk and 3-8 MB more to download. All figures are estimates; the detail gives the reasoning.
options.technical: The release step that already builds the prebuilt runtime (prebuild-runtime.mjs, architecture.md:1442-1452) checks Core with the release compiler for each shipped target. It copies Core's PkgCheck, Iface, Diags and Body records into the install. The record store reads this read-only install layer before the machine-wide store. A compiler with another identity, or none, never matches it.
options.code:
$ jet check fetch.jet     # fresh install, offline: about 40-150 ms (estimate)
ok: `fetch.jet` has no problems
$ jet check fetch.jet --no-cache   # all of Core rechecked: about 0.7-2.0 s (estimate)
ok: `fetch.jet` has no problems

options.name: Each machine checks Core on first use
options.detail:
Nothing ships; the first run that reaches Core checks all of it and saves the records. Beginners meet one slower check after each install or upgrade. Experts see the same hatches and store as in A.

Gains: The install stays exactly as large as today. One code path for release and developer compilers.

Losses: The first Core check after each install or upgrade is slower. A read-only store never saves, so it stays slow.

Estimated end effect. First check of fetch after install or upgrade: about 0.7-2.0 s, because all of Core is checked once. Later checks: about 40-150 ms, as in A. Warm build of fetch: about 0.25-0.35 s. Small check: about 11-20 ms. Install size: as today. All figures are estimates.
options.technical: The release ships no records. The first compile whose program reaches Core misses, checks Core as one unit, and publishes its records into the machine-wide store under the same keys as A. Concurrent first runs race safely, because publication is atomic and identical records have identical digests.
options.code:
$ jet check fetch.jet     # first run after install: about 0.7-2.0 s (estimate)

decisions.title: How the Core library is divided into units that are checked and reused
decisions.situation: Jet reuses checked work one package at a time, so the next question is how the Core library counts as packages. A program that imports the http client reaches seventy Core modules, nearly half of Core's lines, and some Core modules import each other in cycles. If Core is one package, it is checked whole once per compiler, and later runs read back only what they need. Splitting Core along its import cycles makes first checks smaller, while checking only what each program reaches avoids a whole check but reopens a settled rule. The recommendation is one Core package, checked whole once and read back on demand.
decisions.gist: Should Core be reused as one package, one package per import cycle, or only as far as each program reaches?
decisions.lesson: A unit is the piece a compiler checks once and then reuses. Go makes each standard library directory a package and forbids import cycles. Jet already made the user package its unit. Core ships with the compiler, and some of its modules import each other.
decisions.story: A web developer writes fetch, a six-line program that calls the http client. With one Core package, the first check on a new developer compiler checks all of Core in an estimated one to two seconds. After that, every check reads back only the Core parts fetch needs. A Core contributor who edits the text library rechecks all of Core once, then is fast again.
decisions.inWild:
$ go build ./a
package example/a
	imports example/b
	imports example/a: import cycle not allowed
# Go refuses import cycles, so each package stays its own unit.
decisions.detail:
Measured import structure. A throwaway scanner read the use lines of the 164 module files listed in CORE_SOURCE_OWNED_ROWS, resolving names and aliases, and kept private parts with their owner module. It finds 145 groups of modules that import each other, of which 7 hold more than one file. The largest has 10 files and about 8,500 lines: Encoding with its Cbor parts, Process, Sys and Files. Next is Crypto, with 6 files and about 5,800 lines.

Without joining parts to owners the scan finds 148 groups, the largest being Crypto at 6 files. The adversarial review counted about 155 groups with a largest of 4 files; the difference is how parts and aliases are joined. Either way, the 70 Core modules in the http trace span 54 groups, so option B saves little for fetch.

Measured today on the r14 jet, at a load average of 5-6. jet check fetch.jet prints ok: `fetch.jet` has no problems, with a median of 962 ms over seven runs. jet build fetch.jet takes 1178 ms, and checking a hello program that imports no Core module takes 11 ms. The kitspeed medians for the same shape (http_get.jet) are 860-933 ms before #6032 stage 0 and 561-587 ms after it.

Where the time goes. The single base trace spans 830 ms: load 340, register 190, sema.finalize 230 and sema.bodies 150 ms, with a peak of 652 MB. After stage 0 it spans 570 ms with a peak of 413 MB. The loader reads 70 Core modules: 34,482 of Core's 74,463 lines (46%). They hold 8.3 of its 10.0 MB (83%), because the set includes the large Unicode tables in Text.

The one program every option is measured against:
```jet
package { name: "fetch", authority: { allow: [IO, Mem.Alloc, Net] } }
use core.http as http
fn run() {
    resp :: http.get("http://127.0.0.1:8080/") ?? panic("request")
    print(resp.body().text(1024) ?? panic("body"))
}
```

Key and identity. The record key is the one D-BUILD-NOCHANGE1=A fixes: compiler identity, Core source digest, target and profile facts, lint and policy facts, and schema versions. Compiler identity is name@version#source id, a SHA-256 over the compiler and Core sources (compiler-packages.mjs:82-123). A compiler built from released sources therefore shares the release identity.

A compiler with no identity has no key. jet build Compiler sets no JET_COMPILER_IDENTITY (Request.jet:196-201), and the check key returns None without one (Identity.jet:904-916). Such a compiler checks the Core it reaches on every run, as today, and saves nothing. Rebuilding the compiler after a Core edit changes its identity, so every record misses once.

How the warm estimate is built. A warm run still starts jet and reads the user file, which the 11 ms hello check bounds. Confirming that Core sources are unchanged costs about 1 ms by file stamps, or 11-45 ms if every file is hashed, per a Node scan of all of Core. Reading the Core records the program needs is estimated at 10-50 ms. The user package and the program phase add about 15-40 ms. The sum is about 40-150 ms.

How the build estimate is built. Today jet build fetch.jet takes about 0.2 s more than jet check (1178 against 962 ms), for lowering, code generation and linking. Records remove checking work only, so a warm build is estimated at about 0.25-0.35 s. Building and running still lower, compile and link as they do today.

How the cold estimate is built. All of Core is 167 files, 74,463 lines and 10.0 MB; the http set is 46% of the lines and 83% of the bytes. Scaling the 561-587 ms post-stage-0 check by lines gives about 1.2-1.3 s, and by bytes about 0.7 s. Before stage 0 it is about 1.9-2.0 s by lines. The estimate is 0.7-2.0 s, with a peak of about 0.9-1.4 GB, paid once per compiler identity, target and Core edit.

Owner direction and settled rules. Owner direction on #5084 says every file of the program and its packages is still checked, errors anywhere are reported, and only emission follows reachability. D-INCR-PARK1=C and D-INCR-UNIT1=A, amended 2026-09-30, make the package the only reuse unit. A and B keep both rules. C makes a reached set the unit, so it needs both amended.

Demand-driven loading. The loader already walks imports from the entry (Loader.jet:3825-3871). Under A and B a warm run walks the same way but reads saved records instead of source. How much of each record it reads is the separate ballot D-BUILD-CORELOAD1, which keeps this ballot to three options.

Relation to #5476. Its approved S3 bakes the always-loaded Core state, Prelude, Errors and the effect tables, into the jet binary as static data, built in the same chain so it cannot go stale. That serves its 2 ms hello target under every option here. S3 does not cover imported modules such as http; these ballots do. Its S4, checking Core bodies only when reached on each run, is the per-run form of option C of D-BUILD-COREUNIT1.

Exactness. A warm run enters each reached Core function into the whole-program checks as a sealed node read from its record. For E0749 and E0725 the node carries its solved effect row and panic sites (Effects/Checks.jet:744-766). E1264 needs one bit: whether the function reaches a secret (:1819). E0743 needs a bit plus the first unbounded dispatch reached: callee, file, line and column (:1856-1862), because a warm run has no Core source to locate it.

E0921 needs the most. For alloc and rc each function carries its first event: operation, span, owning file and the next call on the path. The arena check also needs the byte bound, or the unbounded witness and reason (:2104-2142). Following next-call links through records rebuilds the printed path. Core declares about 6,100 functions; at 100-300 bytes each this adds an estimated 1-2 MB. Storing every whole path instead costs an estimated 5-10 MB.

Risk and test. Inside a recursion cycle the source walk and the record walk could choose different first paths. The differential test therefore includes a Core cycle; if it diverges, the records store whole paths. A diagnostic whose span points into Core reads that one Core file to draw its snippet. E1220, reflection and generic templates read package facts, full declarations and checked templates, as the incremental design says.

The unit ladder. Below a package there is no reuse rung: block, function and module are checking scopes, not reuse units. A one-file program with an inline package block is its own package, as fetch.jet is. Promoting a module to a workspace member package makes it a unit. Core under A is one more package on that ladder. This ballot adds no user setting; reuse obeys D-BUILD-REUSESET1.

The mitigation depends on D-BUILD-CORESHIP1. Release users skip the whole-Core check only if CORESHIP1=A ships the records. Under its B every install pays the check once, and under its C an offline machine pays it.

Edge cases. A Core edit changes the Core source digest, so Core's records miss, and rebuilding the compiler changes every key once. An interrupted cold run publishes nothing. A program that imports nothing beyond the always-loaded part reads only that part. Core itself denies no memory effects, so E0921 fires only from user denials that reach into Core.

Fixed by ratified decisions and not reopened here. The user reuse unit is the package (D-INCR-UNIT1=A; D-INCR-PARK1=C retired item reuse). Records live in the machine-wide store with its cap, reserve and jet cache commands (D-BUILD-STORE1=E). D-BUILD-NOCHANGE1=A fixes two hatches: ignore saved work, and recompute and compare, with byte-identical replay. D-BUILD-REUSESET1 decides their spelling. Persistence is disk records plus the opt-in jet dev --serve session, with no daemon (D-BUILD-SESSION1=A).

Beginner path: nothing to learn; checks are fast after the first. Expert path: jet cache status shows the store, and recompute-and-compare proves the Core records. Core contributors pay a whole-Core recheck per edit under A, one group and its importers under B, and one set per program under C.

options.name: One Core package, checked whole once
options.detail:
Core is checked whole once per compiler and target; each warm run reads back only what its program needs. Beginners see one fast check after another. Experts working on Core see a whole-Core recheck after each Core edit. How much a warm run reads back is D-BUILD-CORELOAD1.

Gains: One record set and one key for all of Core. Lets the install ship Core already checked. No change to Core's modules or imports.

Losses: A new developer compiler checks all of Core once. Any Core edit rechecks all of Core.

Estimated end effect. Warm check of fetch: about 40-150 ms, against 962 ms today. Warm build of fetch: about 0.25-0.35 s, against 1178 ms. Small check: about 11-20 ms, as today. Edit then recheck: only the user package, about 40-150 ms. Cold, once per compiler, target or Core edit: about 0.7-2.0 s, with a peak of about 0.9-1.4 GB. All figures are estimates; the detail gives the reasoning.
options.technical: Core gets one package identity, keyed as the detail says. On a miss the driver loads and checks every Core module, publishes PkgCheck, Iface, Diags and Body records, and frees Core bodies. On a hit, registration enters Core declarations from Iface as sealed modules, and comptime decodes only the Body sections it runs. Lowering keeps today's reachability prune (Pipeline.jet:2634).
options.code:
$ jet check fetch.jet     # new developer compiler: about 0.7-2.0 s (estimate)
ok: `fetch.jet` has no problems
$ jet check fetch.jet     # warm: about 40-150 ms (estimate)
ok: `fetch.jet` has no problems

options.name: One package per import cycle
options.detail:
Each Core module, or each group of modules that import each other, becomes its own reused package. Beginners see about the same warm speed as A. Experts working on Core recheck only the edited group and the groups that import it. Each group is a package, so this fits the package-only reuse rule.

Gains: A first check covers only the groups a program reaches. A Core edit rechecks one group and importers.

Losses: About 145 record sets to track. Http still reaches 54 groups and nearly half of Core. A new cycle in Core merges groups and changes keys.

Estimated end effect. Warm check of fetch: about 50-190 ms, slightly above A because 54 records open instead of one. Warm build of fetch: about 0.25-0.4 s. Small check: about 11-20 ms. Cold for fetch: about 0.56-0.93 s, today's cost for its reached groups. A Core edit rechecks one group and its importers. All figures are estimates.
options.technical: Each strongly connected group of the Core module import graph becomes an internal package with its own key and records; private parts stay with their owner module. Jet has no package-private visibility, so no Core item changes visibility, and use core.http resolves as today. A user key names the interface digests of the groups it reaches.
options.code:
$ jet check fetch.jet     # new developer compiler: about 0.6-0.9 s (estimate)
ok: `fetch.jet` has no problems
$ jet check fetch.jet     # warm: about 50-190 ms (estimate)
ok: `fetch.jet` has no problems

options.name: Check only what each program reaches
options.detail:
Core is never checked whole; each run checks the Core code its program reaches and saves that set. Beginners see a slower first run for each new import set. Experts see many Core records in jet cache status.

Gains: No whole-Core check, ever. Each first check costs about today's check.

Losses: Unreached Core code is never checked on user machines. Every new import set is a slow first run again. Reopens a settled rule; nothing fixed can ship.

Estimated end effect. Warm check of fetch: about 40-150 ms for a seen set, and 0.56-0.93 s for each new set. Warm build of fetch: about 0.25-0.35 s. Small check: about 11-20 ms. Edit then recheck: the user package only, unless the edit adds an import. Store use grows with distinct sets. All figures are estimates.
options.technical: This covers stage 2 of PLAN-6032, one record per reached module set keyed by the set, and S4 of #5476, which checks Core bodies only when a per-run worklist reaches them. Both make a reached set the reuse unit, which reopens D-INCR-PARK1=C and D-INCR-UNIT1=A.

ok: `fetch.jet` has no problems

ok: `fetch_json.jet` has no problems

decisions.title: One on/off `cache` setting, like Rust's incremental, settable from the workspace root
decisions.situation: Jet will save checked work and reuse it when nothing relevant changed. You asked why reuse needs three values when Rust has one switch. It does not. Rust's `incremental = false` rebuilds from scratch. Jet's agreed rebuild already compares each fresh result with any saved result for the same inputs. A mismatch fails as a compiler bug. So a separate verify value adds nothing. Today a workspace root also cannot set a value for all its packages. The vote decides two things. Is reuse one on/off setting? May a workspace root set settings for its members?
decisions.gist: Should reuse be one on/off `cache` setting, like Rust, that a workspace root can set for every member?
decisions.lesson: Yes. `--cache=off` rebuilds everything and checks it against saved work, and a workspace root may set it once for all members.
decisions.story: Ana suspects stale results, so she runs `jet build --cache=off`. Everything rebuilds, and any result that differs from the saved one is reported as a compiler bug. Her CI sets `cache: false` once in the workspace root.
decisions.inWild:
Option             Spelling                  Root sets it   Like
A on/off + root    --cache=off, cache: false yes            Rust, Zig, Bazel
B three values     --cache=on|off|verify     yes            Turborepo
C on/off, no root  --cache=off               flag only      Gradle
decisions.detail:
OWNER QUESTION (q99gmgrh)
On means reuse saved work. Off means rebuild from scratch, like Rust's `incremental = false`. Verify meant rebuild and compare with saved results. Cargo has no such mode; only rustc's unstable `-Zincremental-verify-ich` checks hashes. Jet's ratified `--no-cache` already compares every fresh result with any saved record of the same key. So off already verifies, and the third value is gone.

WHAT WE BUILD
- Setting `cache` (Bool, stock true) joins the one settings table. Forms: `--cache` / `--cache=off`, `b.cache(false)`, `cache: false` in package.jet (top level, per D-MARK-SCOPE1=A). Bool spelling follows D-SETTING-ORDER1=A.
- Off runs every step from source. Each fresh result is compared with any saved record of the same key; a mismatch keeps both and fails as a compiler bug (D-BUILD-NOCHANGE1=A).

- `jet build --verify <receipt>` (cli.md:189; Front.jet:221-227) keeps its receipt meaning (D-RECORD1).
- Workspace root package.jet becomes a layer between stock and each member, for every setting. Order for package P: flag, entry code, P's package.jet, workspace root, stock. A dependency outside the workspace takes the importing build's value.
- `jet explain build` names the layer that set each value. The settled `--session` and `--offline` settings gain the same root level.

CUTOVER
Renames the unbuilt `--no-cache` to `--cache=off` and folds the unbuilt whole-run `--verify` into it. Neither is built, so no user code changes.

EVIDENCE (r14 jet)
- `jet check fetch.jet --no-cache` gives E2102; `jet build --verify abc fetch.jet` gives E2104.
- `jet check fetch.jet`: median 962 ms over seven runs. Warm estimate 40-150 ms; cold 0.7-2.0 s.
- The workspace audit lists the missing root level (L-03, root settings not inherited).

IDS
Amends D-BUILD-NOCHANGE1=A (spelling; whole-run verify folds into off) and D-SETTING-ORDER1=A (workspace root layer). Fixed: D-INCR-UNIT1=A, D-BUILD-STORE1=E, D-BUILD-SESSION1=A, D-RECORD1, D-MARK-SCOPE1=A, D-AUTOPIN1. Consistent with D-MANIFEST-ONE1 and D-TEST-PROFILE1.

decisions.title: Dispatch by type: branching on a generic type parameter, union arms without a binding, and whether Jet adds an Any type
decisions.situation: Code sometimes needs one path for whole numbers and another for every other type, which Jai writes as a branch on the type itself. Jet refuses that branch today because a type is not a value, and a union match must bind each member's value even when it goes unused. The vote decides how a generic function branches on its type, how strictly each branch is checked, and whether a value of any type can be switched at run time. We recommend an ordinary type table, `if T == { Int -> … else -> … }`, that checks every arm with that arm's type.
decisions.gist: How does code branch on a type: per generic use while building, and also on any value at run time?
decisions.lesson: A generic function is written once for many types, with a type parameter such as `T`. Type dispatch runs a different branch for each concrete type. A union is a value holding one of a few listed types, such as `Int | String`. An `Any` value could hold a value of every type, with its type recorded beside it.
decisions.story: Kai writes a generic `describe` helper for a debug overlay. Whole numbers should print one way, decimals another, and anything else through its usual text. Today he writes a trait and three impls, and still has no fallback for other types. With the recommendation he writes one `if T == { … }` table, and a typo in the Float arm stops the build at once.
decisions.detail:
ALREADY RATIFIED, NOT ON THIS BALLOT
- Run-time dispatch over mixed values uses unions: `v: Int | Float | String` with `if v == { .Int(n) -> … }` (D-UNIONTYPE1=A). It works today.
- A general `Any` top type was refused (D-ANY-JAI1=A). Mixed argument lists use trait-bounded variadics such as `parts: ...Renderable`. Option C reopens that refusal.
- A union match names every member, and `else` over it is an error (card #6175).

- `comptime if subject == { … }` keeps only the chosen arm; the others get name checks only (D-PREP-BRANCH1=A, spelled `comptime` per D-COMPTIME-WORD1).
- Derive templates already branch with `comptime if T.$kind == "enum"`.
- `Dyn` is the one dynamic data value, closed to null, Bool, Int, Float, Text, Bytes, DateTime, Array and Object (D-ENC-DYN1). It cannot hold a user type.
- The generic header spelling is not on this ballot; examples use today's `<T>`.

MISSING TODAY (card #6180 probes)
- `if T == { Int -> … else -> … }` in a generic function is E0107: T is not a value. `T.$name` outside compile-time code is E0302.
- A union arm without a binding, `.Int -> …`, is E0306.

SHARED BY ALL OPTIONS
- A union arm may name a member without binding it: `.Int -> "a number"`. `.Int(n)` still binds. Inside a bare arm the value keeps its union type.
- Union dispatch stays exhaustive: every member is named, with no `else`.

- A type table ends with `else`, because types are an open set. A missing `else` is a build error that names it.
- Matching is exact type identity. A `Float` arm does not match `Meters :: distinct Float`, `F32` or `Float?`.
- An alias, `Name :: Type`, is its target, so it matches its target's arm. Naming both is a duplicate-arm error.

- Arm heads are concrete types. An arm that binds a new type parameter, such as `[U] -> …` or `Map<K, V> -> …`, is not added in any option.
- Code that needs the shape of a type reads `T.$kind` and `T.$fields` facts in `comptime if`, as derives do.
- Several type parameters dispatch with nested tables; a tuple subject is not added.

OPTION A
- A type may be the subject of an `if ==` table. Each arm is checked once, at the definition, with T replaced by the arm's type. The `else` arm sees only T's declared bounds.
- In the `Int` arm, `x: T` is an Int, so `x + 1` checks. A function returning T may return `x + 1` there, because T is Int in that arm.

- Cost: none at run time. Each use of the function keeps one arm, chosen while building. The others emit no code on any tier.
- This is ordinary folding (D-COMPTIME-WORD1), so no word is needed. `comptime if T == { … }` also works, under its existing rule, for an arm that cannot check under other types.
- `if T == Int { … }` is the one-arm test form, as `if x == .A { }` is for enums. Hover shows the arm each use keeps.

OPTION B
- `comptime if T == { … }` only, under the existing build-time branch rule. The chosen arm is checked for each use of the function; the others get name checks only, as in Zig and C++.
- A plain `if T == { … }` stays an error whose fix names `comptime if`.
- Cost: none at run time, as in A.

OPTION C
- As A, plus a Core type `Any` that holds a value of any type with its type tag. It is a new type, not an extension of `Dyn`, which stays a closed data tree.
- A value passes into an `Any` parameter with no wrapping, as a plain Int passes into `Int | String` today.

- `if v == { .Int(n) -> … else -> … }` switches on the tag with the union table, and `else` is required. `[Any]` holds mixed values, and `fn log(parts: ...Any)` takes any arguments.
- Views and other values that cannot outlive their scope are refused in `Any`.

- Cost: a tag compare per switch. A value larger than two machine words is copied to the heap when it enters `Any`.
- A type mistake is found when the code runs: an `Any` list can hold a value no arm expects.

RATIFIED TEXT TO AMEND
- S26 says compile-time code "never selects a type, and never affects dispatch", and that polymorphism is traits-only. Every option chooses code per type inside one generic body, so that line needs this exception.
- D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1=A already treats types as build-time values. C also reverses D-ANY-JAI1=A's refusal of a general `Any`.

CONSIDERED AND DROPPED
- Traits only, today's rule: one trait impl per type. A fallback for every other type has no home, because Jet has no specialization. Traits stay available in every option.

RESEARCH
- Jai: `#if T == int` per instance, and a run-time switch on an `Any` value's type info. Branches not taken by `#if` are not checked.
- Zig: `if (T == i64)` and `switch (T)` on comptime types; untaken branches are not analyzed. C++: `if constexpr`, whose discarded branch is not instantiated.

- Go: a type switch `switch v := x.(type)` refines `v` in each arm at run time. Before generics, Go APIs leaned on `interface{}` and moved type errors to run time.
- Rust: traits only, with specialization unstable for years. `dyn Any` with `downcast_ref` works at run time for `'static` types.
- Lesson: refinement per arm reads well, unchecked branches hide mistakes, and a general `Any` pulls APIs toward run-time checks.

RATIFIED DECISIONS
- Builds on D-UNIONTYPE1=A, D-ANY-JAI1=A, D-ENC-DYN1, D-PREP-BRANCH1=A, D-COMPTIME-WORD1=A, D-GENERIC-TYPEFN1=A, the D-IF1 and D-IF3 tables, S26, #6175 and #6176. Card #6180.

options.name: Ordinary type table, every arm checked
options.detail: A type can be the subject of an `if ==` table. Each arm is checked at the definition with T as that arm's type, and each use keeps only its arm, at no run-time cost. Mixed values at run time use unions. Gains: a mistake in any arm stops the build at once; inside an arm, values of type T act as that type; no new keyword. Losses: the `else` arm sees only T's bounds; a build-time choice looks like an ordinary `if`.
options.technical: Sema: a type-valued subject in an if-table; each arm body is checked under a substitution of T by the arm type, and `else` under T's bounds. Monomorphization folds the table to one arm.

options.name: Build-time branch only
options.detail: Type dispatch is written `comptime if T == { … }`, using the existing build-time branch, at no run-time cost. The chosen arm is checked for each use; the others get name checks only. Gains: one rule for every build-time branch; the `else` arm may use anything the concrete type has. Losses: a mistake in an arm waits for the first caller of that type; one more word.
options.technical: Sema: allow a type subject in `comptime if`; the selected arm is checked per instantiation, as for `$build.os`.

options.name: As A, plus an Any type
options.detail: Everything in A, plus a Core `Any` that holds a value of any type with its type tag, switched at run time with the union table and a required `else`. Gains: mixed lists and printf-style APIs without a trait; Jai's run-time form works as written. Losses: a tag check and possible heap copy at run time; type mistakes found only when code runs; APIs drift toward `Any`.
options.technical: Core type: a type tag plus the value, inline up to two words, otherwise heap-boxed. Sema: implicit entry into `Any` parameters; tag dispatch reuses union arms with an open `else`.

comparisons.note: Comptime type comparison; untaken branches are not analyzed; source ziglang.org/documentation/master/#comptime.
if constexpr; the discarded branch is not instantiated; source en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/if.
comparisons.code:
if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, int>) { return "int"; }
else { return "other"; }

comparisons.note: dyn Any with run-time downcasts; source doc.rust-lang.org/std/any.

recommendation.why: A type table reuses Jet's own `if ==` table and checks every arm where it is written, at no run-time cost. Mixed values at run time already have unions, which stay checked and need no boxing.
gains: A mistake in any arm stops the build at once.
Inside an arm, values of type T act as that type.
No new keyword and no run-time cost.

losses.loss: The `else` arm sees only T's declared bounds, which limits code meant to be generic over everything.
losses.mitigation: Add the needed trait to T's bounds, or write `comptime if`, which checks only the arm each use keeps.

losses.loss: A choice made while building looks like an ordinary `if`.
losses.mitigation: A type has no run-time test to confuse it with; hover shows which arm each use keeps.

whyNot.reason: B checks an arm only when a caller uses its type, so a mistake in the Float arm waits for the first Float caller.
C moves type checks to run time and adds boxing, while unions already hold a known set of types checked and unboxed.

recommendation.tradeoff: A fallback arm limited to T's bounds and no `Any`, in exchange for every arm checked where it is written.

decisions.title: Tail calls never grow the stack, on every build level
decisions.situation:
You asked Jet to beat Rust, including on tail calls. A tail call is a call that is the last thing a function does. If it reuses the caller's stack space, recursion runs in constant memory, like a loop.

Two ratified decisions disagree. D-DROP-ASAP1 promises such calls never grow the stack. D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1 says only release builds may remove recursive calls. Today no level does it.
decisions.gist: Is a call that ends a function a jump on every build level, only when marked, or only in release builds?
decisions.lesson: A recursive function that ends in a call is a loop written another way. If that loop needs no memory per step on one build level, it should need none on every level.
decisions.story: Mo writes a parser state machine as small functions that call each other at the end. It passes tests in a release build. Then `jet run` stops with a stack overflow on a large file. Under A both runs behave the same.
decisions.detail:
Probed today on O0, O1 and O2. `walk(10000000, 0)` and `is_even(10000000)` stop with E3012 on every level. `walk` at 100,000 levels runs, and 1,000,000 overflows. The O2 binary still holds `call walk` followed by two Int drops.

Those drops are the blocker D-DROP-ASAP1 names: an Int may own memory freed after the call. With memory freed at last use, nothing is pending, so the call can jump.

Rust has no stable guarantee; `become` is unstable and incomplete. Clang's `musttail` and Zig's `always_tail` are guarantees that the programmer marks.

options.name: Every tail call is a jump on every level
options.detail:
A call whose result the function returns directly reuses the frame on O0, O1, O2 and in compile-time code. It needs no mark. Mutual recursion and calls through function values are covered.

When a value with visible cleanup is still open, or an argument points into the caller's own locals, the call stays a call. A lint names the value. A team can make that lint an error.

Behavior changes: runaway tail recursion now runs on like an endless `loop` instead of stopping with E3012. Backtraces skip finished tail-call frames.
options.technical:
Amends D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1: only O2 may remove recursive calls that are not tail calls. Tail calls are jumps on every tier, I9 included. Jet's own calling convention reserves argument space so any Jet-to-Jet tail call fits. Calls into C or other foreign code stay ordinary calls, and the lint says so.

`return f(x)` and a final `f(x)` are tail calls; `f(x)?` and `1 + f(x)` are not. Quick runs keep the last 16 tail calls per thread, which stop reports and the debugger list. Release builds emit DWARF tail-call records.

options.name: Only a call marked `become` is guaranteed
options.detail:
A new word, `become`, marks a tail call. A marked call is a jump on every level, or the build stops and names the reason. An unmarked tail call follows D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1: only O2 may turn it into a jump.

The expert states intent at the call. A beginner who writes plain recursion still gets E3012 in `jet run` on deep inputs.
options.technical: `become f(x)` is valid only in tail position, with the same rules as A for what blocks a jump. A blocked `become` is a build error rather than a lint. Unmarked calls keep today's rule, so the same unmarked program can stop on O1 and finish on O2.

options.name: Only release builds may turn tail calls into jumps
options.detail:
D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1 as written. Quick runs and O1 builds keep every call, so deep tail recursion stops with E3012. O2 may turn it into a jump, but nothing promises it.

D-DROP-ASAP1's promise of flat tail calls is withdrawn.
options.technical: No new rule. O2 may perform sibling-call optimization as an optimizer choice. Output can differ between levels for deep recursion, as D-RESOURCE-LIMIT1 allows.

comparisons.note: R7RS section 3.5 requires every implementation to be properly tail-recursive. Source: small.r7rs.org/attachment/r7rs.pdf.
comparisons.code:
(define (walk n acc)
  (if (= n 0) acc (walk (- n 1) (+ acc n))))

comparisons.note: `@call(.always_tail, f, args)` guarantees a jump or fails to compile. Source: ziglang.org/documentation, @call.
`[[clang::musttail]]` on a return guarantees a jump or fails to compile. GCC 15 accepts the same attribute. Source: clang.llvm.org/docs/AttributeReference.html.
`become` is nightly only and marked incomplete. Stable Rust makes no promise. Source: doc.rust-lang.org/std/keyword.become.html.
comparisons.code: become walk(n - 1, acc + n); // nightly only

recommendation.why: A keeps D-DROP-ASAP1's promise and gives one meaning on every level, which I9 requires. It needs no new word, so beginner recursion just works. Experts can make the lint an error to get B's check.
gains: Deep tail recursion runs in constant stack on every level, `jet run` included.
One program, one result on O0, O1 and O2.
State machines and interpreters can be written as functions that jump to each other, which stable Rust cannot promise.
No new keyword; the lint names any call that cannot jump.

whyNot.reason: B leaves plain recursion stopping on O1 but finishing on O2, the split I9 forbids, and adds a keyword.
C withdraws a ratified promise and keeps quick runs crashing where release builds finish.

recommendation.tradeoff: A tail recursion that never ends now runs until stopped, exactly like a `loop` that never ends.

decisions.title: Expert GPU kernels reach a chip's matrix units through library operations with one meaning
decisions.situation: Jet already marks a function as a GPU kernel and checks every device against the main processor's answer. Experts also want a chip's special units, such as matrix units that multiply small blocks of numbers many times faster. In Mojo, kernel code asks which chip it is built for, so one kernel can print different digits per chip. We recommend library operations whose plain Jet meaning fixes the answer on every device.
decisions.gist: How should an expert's GPU kernel use a chip's matrix units?
decisions.lesson: A kernel is a function that runs on many GPU threads at once. A matrix unit is a part of a GPU that multiplies small blocks of numbers in one step. A plain meaning is ordinary Jet code that gives the answer more slowly; tests compare the chip with it. Whichever option wins, beginners keep calling `compute.matmul` and never see this choice.
decisions.story: Priya writes one tiled multiply kernel. Her laptop has an NVIDIA card, the office has an AMD card, and the test machine has none. Under A, all three runs are checked against the same plain body, so a wrong answer on any chip fails the test she already runs.
decisions.detail:
Today. `#Kernel(.parallel)` marks a safe kernel (Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Policy/PreludeMarkers.jet:43). Called on the CPU, a marked `axpy` prints 7.0 on o0, o1 and o2 (probe g15). Nothing reaches a device yet. `compute.launch` is E1004, "core.compute has no item launch" (probe g2b). `compute.from_list` and `compute.add` stop with an internal compiler error, exit 101, at every level (probe g3, known-failing rows for #5454).

Ratified law this builds on. D-COMPUTE-KERNEL-SURFACE1=B makes the marker the only way into a kernel. D-COMPUTE-BACKEND1=D makes F32Strict plus Reproducible the default and requires named, recorded profiles for looser math. D-COMPUTE-RAWBOUNDARY1=A keeps raw vendor code inside `#Unsafe` (Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:6912-6967).

More ratified law. D-CORE-BOUNDARY1=A puts chip instructions in the library as typed entries with a plain Jet body. D-ACCEL-LIB1=A makes devices libraries over a public kernel IR, checked against the CPU result. D-HOST-CAPS1=A lets code branch on `$build.hardware` facts.

What is open. No ratified rule says whether kernel code may ask which device is compiling it, or how safe code names a matrix unit. Draft scope ballots for tiles and subgroups were written but never ratified (Docs/research/mine-for-jet-2026-09-12.md:3082-3088).

Peer evidence. Mojo's `sin` branches on the compile target. NVIDIA F32 uses the PTX `sin.approx.ftz.f32` instruction, Apple uses `llvm.air.sin`, and other targets use `llvm.sin` (Mojo std/math/math.mojo:1771-1788, commit 85356f65). Mojo's `exp` uses `exp2(x * log2e)` on GPUs and a Mojo polynomial on CPUs (math.mojo:638-658).

Triton's `tl.dot` uses tensor cores in TF32 by default on NVIDIA. Its documentation warns that F32 inputs "may be truncated to TF32 format (19-bit floating point) without rounding" (triton-lang.org, triton.language.dot). So Triton and Mojo both let the chip change the digits by default.

Matrix units round their own way. Float matrix units do not promise the rounding of a plain loop (Fasi, Higham, Mikaitis and Pranesh, Numerical behavior of NVIDIA tensor cores, PeerJ Computer Science 7:e330, 2021). Integer units that multiply 8-bit values into 32-bit sums are exact while the sums fit, so they match a plain loop bit for bit.

What A means. Matrix units are library operations, such as a tile multiply-add, each with a plain Jet body. A device library lowers the operation to the unit when the chip has one and the profile allows it. Kernel code sees `$build.hardware` facts, which are the same for every device build, but never asks which device compiles it.

What B means. Kernel code may branch at compile time on the device being compiled, as Mojo does. Each branch may call that chip's operations directly. What C means. Matrix units stay reachable only through raw vendor code in `#Unsafe`, as today's law allows.

Beginner and expert paths. A beginner calls `compute.matmul(a, b)` under every option and never names a unit. An expert writes a `#Kernel` with tiles under A or B, or unsafe vendor code under C. Under every option, a precision profile looser than the default is named at the launch and recorded in the receipt.

Amends. A adds one rule to D-COMPUTE-KERNEL-SURFACE1: kernel bodies see build facts but no per-device compile fact. It extends D-CORE-BOUNDARY1's instruction entries to kernel IR operations declared by Core or a provider package. B adds a `$device` fact plane inside kernels. C changes nothing.

Research. Docs/research/2026-10-30-gpu-one-meaning.md. Review: author Claude (MemDesign-2 lane); no fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft yet.

options.name: Library operations with a plain meaning
options.detail:
Matrix units are reached through library operations, such as a tile multiply-add. Each has a plain Jet body that defines the answer. A device library lowers it to the matrix unit when the chip has one and the precision profile allows it.

Kernel code sees the build's hardware facts, which are the same on every device, but never asks which device compiles it. Raw vendor code stays in the unsafe tier.

Behavior change: under the default strict profile, float matrix units are not used, because they round differently from the plain loop. A kernel gets them by naming a looser profile at launch, which the receipt records. Integer matrix units are exact while their sums fit, and are used under the default.
options.technical:
A device operation is a D-CORE-BOUNDARY1 instruction entry over the public kernel IR, declared by Core or by a provider package. Its body is the plain meaning with a fixed summation order.

Integer units are used only when the tile shape bounds every sum within I32. Conformance compares chip and body: bit-equal for integer units and the default profile, within the named profile's stated bound for float units. `$build.hardware` folds identically into the CPU reference and every device build. `Tile` and `tile.mma` spellings are illustrative until their rows land under I7.

decisions.title: Printing an empty optional shows `None`, the word Jet code writes for it
decisions.situation: When Jet prints an optional that holds nothing, it shows `null`. That is the JavaScript and JSON word, and Jet code never writes it: the source says `None`. Debug output already says `None`. The text `null` also looks the same as a present string "null". We recommend that printing and interpolation show `None`. A present value still prints bare, so `Val(3)` shows `3`.
decisions.gist: When you print an optional that holds nothing, should Jet show `None`, `null`, or refuse to print it?
decisions.lesson: An optional either holds a value or holds nothing. Jet writes the empty case as `None` in code. Printing turns a value into text for people, so the printed word should match the word they write. Languages disagree here: Python prints None, Kotlin prints null, and Rust refuses to print an optional at all.
decisions.story: Sam checks a sum with `checked_add` and prints the result. The screen says `null`, and he searches the Jet docs for a null that does not exist. Under A it says `None`, the word from his own code.
decisions.inWild:
# Python: the printed word is the source word
nick = None
print(nick)          # None
print(f"{nick}")     # None
decisions.detail:
Today, measured on dev 03c64ad0c4. `print(x)` and `"{x}"` show an empty optional as `null`. A present one shows its value bare, so `Val(3)` prints `3`. `{x:Debug}` shows `None` and `Val(3)`. A struct prints `User { name: Ann, nickname: null }`, while its Debug form prints `nickname: None`.

The mismatch was found on `checked_add`, which returns an optional. Every optional prints the same way, so the vote covers them all. About 49 expected-output files contain the word null, and some of those come from JSON text rather than printing. Exact counts come from the golden run after the change.

Law. The spec says Display is user-facing and Debug is auto-derived (syntax-decisions.md:2310). No ruling sets the display word for an empty optional. The names `Val` and `None` are ambient Core names.

What A does. Display of an empty optional is `None` everywhere, in print, interpolation and the display of containing structs and lists. Present values stay bare. Debug is unchanged.

What B does. Nothing changes: print says `null` while source and Debug say `None`. What C does. Optionals get no display text. Printing one is a compile error that suggests `x ?? fallback` or `{x:Debug}`, as Rust does.

Linked vote. How encoders such as JSON write an empty optional field is a separate ballot, because JSON's own word for nothing is `null` whatever print shows.

Review. Author: Claude (SurfaceDesign lane). Probes: probes/m-null/show.jet and debug.jet in the lane. No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft.

decisions.title: Encoders leave out an empty optional field; a field marked `#Codable(.Null)` writes `null` instead
decisions.situation: When a struct field holds an empty optional, Jet's JSON encoder leaves the key out today. One expected-output file says it should write `"nickname":null` instead, so that test stays red. Decoding already accepts both a missing key and `null`. TOML has no null at all, and in JSON patches `null` means delete. We recommend leaving the key out everywhere, with a field marker that writes `null` where an API needs it.
decisions.gist: When an optional field is empty, should Jet's encoders leave the key out, or write it as null?
decisions.lesson: A data format can say a field has no value in two ways. It can leave the key out, or write an empty marker such as JSON's `null`. Most readers treat them alike. Some do not: a JSON merge patch reads `null` as delete this field. TOML has no empty marker, so it can only leave the key out.
decisions.story: Ada exports her app config to JSON and TOML from one struct. Under A both files leave out the unset nickname, and reading them back gives the same struct. Under B the JSON says `null`, the TOML says nothing, and a merge patch built from the JSON would delete her saved nickname.
decisions.detail:
Today, measured on dev 03c64ad0c4. `json.to_string` leaves out an empty optional field. Decoding accepts a missing key or `null` for an optional field. The case corelib/generated_struct_codecs_preserve_option_and_computed_fields expects the key left out and passes. Examples/features/serde/field_metadata_edges expects `"nickname":null` and fails.

Law. Field options are `#Codable(.Skip)` and `#Codable(.Flatten)`, ratified with the move of serialization options onto #Codable. One command exports a typed config as JSON, YAML or TOML from the same codec. In JSON merge patches, `null` deletes a member (RFC 7396). No ruling says how an empty optional is written.

What A does. Every encoder leaves an empty optional field out. A field marked `#Codable(.Null)` writes the format's empty marker instead; TOML refuses that marker at compile time because it has none. Schema export lists optional fields as not required.

What B does. Formats with an empty marker write it, so JSON writes `null` and YAML writes `null`. TOML leaves the key out. What C does. Leave the key out by default, and add a per-call setting `nulls: .Write` to the encoders.

Decode error wording, which follows from law rather than this vote. A wrong `null` input reports `found null` today, matching Core's other input words such as `found text "three"`. The golden that expects `found Null` should change to match.

Separate finding, not part of this vote. The same golden expects declaration order, but its output sorts keys. That example flattens a nested struct, and plain structs keep declaration order. This is a bug for the golden's card.

Linked vote: how print shows an empty optional. Review. Author: Claude (SurfaceDesign lane). Probes: probes/m-null/debug.jet in the lane. No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft.

decisions.title: Lists stay 0-based; the compiler teaches the off-by-one cases, and word methods cover first and last
decisions.situation: Jet counts list positions from 0, like C, Python, JavaScript and Rust. You asked whether it should count from 1, like Lua, Julia, MATLAB and R, citing the view that 0 confuses beginners. Changing would touch about 3,260 of Jet's 17,685 source files and every foreign call. Jet already lets most code avoid raw positions through paired loops, open slices and first and last methods. We recommend staying at 0 and teaching the remaining off-by-one cases at compile time.
decisions.gist: Should Jet count list positions from 0, as today, or from 1, like Lua and Julia?
decisions.lesson: Counting from 1 matches how people number things, so the first item is item 1. Counting from 0 matches memory, where a position is a distance from the start. Dijkstra argued that 0 with half-open ranges gives the fewest plus-or-minus-one corrections. Most beginner off-by-one errors vanish when code names the item it wants instead of computing its number.
decisions.story: Lena wants the last name in a list. In Lua she writes `names[#names]`. In Jet today she writes `names[names.len() - 1]`, and forgetting the minus one crashes. Under A she writes `names.last()`, and the compiler explains `names[names.len()]` before the program runs.
decisions.inWild:
-- Lua: tables count from 1
names = {"ada", "bo", "cy"}
print(names[1])        -- ada
print(names[#names])   -- cy
decisions.detail:
Today. Lists, fixed arrays, text views and byte buffers count from 0. Ranges come inclusive or half-open (D-RANGE-EXCL1=C), and slices may leave out an end (D-SLICE-OPEN1=A). Paired loops and `xs.indexes` keep code away from bound arithmetic. The methods `xs.first()` and `xs.last()` return an Option.

Census at dev 03c64ad0c4, over 17,685 tracked .jet files. 3,261 files contain a spelling whose meaning depends on the base. There are 6,763 literal `[0]` reads and 4,404 other literal indexes. There are 1,986 indexes of the form `[x + 1]` or `[x - 1]`, and 1,248 uses of `.len() - 1`. There are 5,316 ranges from 0 and 1,398 slices.

More of the census. 1,191 paired loops would print different numbers, and 1,184 calls such as `insert`, `remove` and `swap` take a position. 2,273 foreign or unsafe pointer sites count from 0 because C and machine memory do. The compiler itself is 3,320 of the `[0]` reads, so a change rewrites the compiler that builds it.

What can be rewritten by tool. Literal indexes and `.len() - 1` shift mechanically. Positions computed from data cannot: byte offsets from files, editor protocol columns, JSON and C offsets, and GPU `at.linear` positions are all 0-based. Each crossing needs a reviewed plus or minus one.

Evidence for 1. Lua, Julia, MATLAB, R, Fortran, COBOL and Smalltalk count from 1, and SQL substrings do too. Lua's history paper says its first users were Petrobras engineers, many with a Fortran background. These languages serve scientists and scripters who number rows as people do.

Evidence for 0. C, C++, Java, C#, JavaScript, Python, Go, Rust, Swift, Zig and Odin count from 0. Dijkstra's note EWD831 (1982) shows that 0 with half-open ranges writes N items as 0 ≤ i < N, with no plus one anywhere. Julia added OffsetArrays for other bases, and mixing bases has caused correctness bugs.

What A does. The base stays 0. The compiler gains a teaching error when it can prove an index equals the length, such as `xs[xs.len()]`, naming `xs.last()` as the fix. Guides teach paired loops, first and last, and open slices before raw positions, as D-RANGE-EXCL1 already does for ranges.

What B does. Every position counts from 1, including bytes and text. C calls and memory views convert at the boundary. What C does. Lists and text count from 1, but bytes, pointers and foreign memory count from 0, so the rule depends on the type.

Review. Author: Claude (SurfaceDesign lane). Census script: census/index-census.mjs in the lane. No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft.

options.name: Stay at 0; teach the off-by-one cases
options.detail:
Positions keep counting from 0. The compiler explains a provable one-past-the-end index before the program runs and names the word method that fits.

Guides lead with paired loops, `first`, `last` and open slices, so beginners rarely write a number.

decisions.title: Hosts run Jet extensions through a small runtime for checked, portable Jet
decisions.situation: You want Jet to replace Lua for editor plugins, game mods and app config. Today a program can load a Jet extension only after someone builds it ahead of time. Lua wins because a host links a small library and loads a script file directly. The question is what a host program carries to run Jet extensions. We recommend a small runtime that runs checked, portable Jet, with the compiler only on the author's machine.
decisions.gist: When an editor or game runs Jet extensions, what should it carry: a small runtime, the compiler, or nothing?
decisions.lesson: An extension language lives inside someone else's program. Hosts pick Lua because the library is small, starts at once and loads a plain script file. A safe host must also limit what an extension may touch. Jet can check those limits before the extension runs, because effects are part of every function's type.
decisions.story: Mia writes a save hook for her editor in init.jet. Under A the editor loads it at startup, and a changed file is rechecked by the jet she already has. Under B the editor download grows by the whole compiler. Under C each hook call crosses a pipe to another process.
decisions.detail:
Today. A Jet library can be exported to a foreign host as a native C library or a sandboxed component (D-EMBED1=E, D-EMBED2=C). Both need `jet build` first. Jet programs load sandboxed components with authority checks and fuel, memory and time limits (D-CORE-PLUGINPATH1=A, D-CORE-PLUGINLIMITS1=A).

No route lets a foreign host load a `.jet` file or a portable bundle at run time. D-PORTABLE1=A ratifies a verified portable form, an interpreter and a local native cache, which A reuses.

Measurements on this dev compiler. An 8-line config program ran in 286 ms cold and 8 ms with a warm cache. The `jet` toolchain binary is 81 MB. Lua's interpreter with all libraries is 293 KB, and its library is 484 KB (lua.org/about).

What A does. A host links a small runtime library with three calls: create, load, call. The runtime verifies portable Jet and grants only the effects the host's API trait offers. When `jet` is installed, the runtime asks it to check and compile a changed source and caches the result. Without `jet`, it loads shipped bundles.

What B does. The host links the full compiler, so it checks `.jet` source itself, as Lua does. The host binary grows by tens of megabytes. What C does. Extensions always run as child processes over a pipe, as Neovim's remote plugins do.

Neovim. Neovim embeds LuaJIT and talks to other languages over msgpack-RPC. A Jet plugin host can start with C and move to A once the runtime exists. That plan is a card, not part of this vote.

Review. Author: Claude (SurfaceDesign lane). Full comparison of Lua, Nix, Starlark, Dhall, CUE, Nickel, KCL, Pkl, data formats and WASM hosts: the proposal linked from card 6380. No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft.

decisions.title: Bit operations as sigils: `&`, `|`, `~`, `&~` and their updates, with `~` as complement and exclusive-or
decisions.situation: This month Jet replaced bit operators with method names such as bit_and and bit_xor, and left the tilde with no meaning. You now find the long names messy, and suggest tilde for not and complement, plus tilde-equals and and-not. Jet's own code makes 2,595 bit method calls in 465 files. Choosing a sigil option reopens both recent rulings. We recommend one small set of bit sigils for integers, with tilde as complement and exclusive-or.
decisions.gist: Should bit operations go back to short sigils, and what should the tilde mean?
decisions.lesson: Bit code is dense: hashes, codecs, flags and graphics combine several operations per line. Sigils keep such lines short enough to read as one formula. Words read better for rare use. C, Java, Python and JavaScript spell complement with a tilde. Odin and Lua also use tilde for exclusive-or, since complement is exclusive-or with all ones.
decisions.story: Sam ports a hash function from C. Today each line becomes nested calls such as `(h << 5).bit_xor(b)`. Under A he writes `(h << 5) ~ b`. Under B he keeps the xor word, but `~mask` and `&~` read as in C.
decisions.inWild:
// Odin: ~ is complement and exclusive-or, &~ is and-not
perms := READ | WRITE
perms &~= WRITE
flip := perms ~ EXEC
inverse := ~perms
decisions.detail:
What this reopens. Choosing A or B reopens D-SIGIL-ALGEBRA1=B (bit arithmetic as named methods, 2026-10-04) and D-SIGIL-FREED2=A (`~` and `^` stay free, 2026-10-11). C keeps both. The card also names D-MATH-BITS1, but that decision covers correctly rounded `core.math` and no option changes it.

Today. Every integer type has `bit_and`, `bit_or`, `bit_xor` and `bit_not` (core-library reference, spec line 227). Shifts stay `<<` and `>>`. Infix `&`, `|` and `^` on numbers give E0398 with a method fix. Prefix `&` and `^` are ownership marks, `!` negates Bool only, and copying is `.copy()`.

Census at dev 03c64ad0c4. Jet code makes 2,595 bit method calls in 465 files: Compiler 1,523, Core 669, Jetpack 195, tests 107, Examples 91 and Tools 10. A `jet fix` rewrite is the reverse of today's E0398 repair and keeps grouping. Jet code also has 19,588 `!=` and about 2,271 prefix `!` uses.

Survey of `~`. Complement in C, C++, Java, C#, JavaScript, Python and Swift. Complement and exclusive-or in Odin and Lua 5.3; Go uses `^` for both. Logical not in MATLAB. Concatenation in D and Raku. Pattern match in awk, Perl `=~` and PostgreSQL. A formula in R. A destructor in C++, and a lazy pattern in Haskell.

Survey of `~=` and and-not. Not-equal in Lua and MATLAB. Append in D. Exclusive-or update in Odin. And-not is `&~` in Odin, `&^` in Go, and `a & ~b` in C. Rust writes complement as `!`.

What A does. Integers gain infix `&`, `|`, `~` (exclusive-or), prefix `~` (complement) and `&~` (and-not), with updates `&=`, `|=`, `~=` and `&~=`. Precedence follows C, with `&` above `~` above `|`, and all sit above comparisons. The four bit methods retire. On Bool, `~` is an error naming `!`, and a `~=` inside a condition is an error naming `!=`.

Why exclusive-or is `~` and not `^`. Infix `^` meant power until this month, so ported Lua, Julia or MATLAB code would silently change meaning. Prefix `^` also already marks a hand-over.

What B does. It reads your suggestion literally: `~` becomes the one not, for Bool and integers, and `~=` replaces `!=`. And-not is `&~`, with infix `&` and `|`. Exclusive-or stays `bit_xor`. That renames about 21,900 not and not-equal uses.

What C does. Nothing changes. Bit operations stay methods and `~` stays free.

Review. Author: Claude (SurfaceDesign lane). No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft.

options.name: Bit sigils for integers; `~` is complement and exclusive-or
options.detail:
Integers use `&`, `|`, `~`, `&~` and their updates, as in Odin. Prefix `~` flips every bit. Bool keeps `!`, `&&` and `||`.

A `~=` in a condition is an error that names `!=`, so Lua and MATLAB habits get a lesson.
options.technical: New tokens and BinOps: BitAnd `&`, BitOr `|`, BitXor `~`, AndNot `&~`, unary Complement `~`, compounds `&=`, `|=`, `~=`, `&~=`. Precedence: shifts, `&` and `&~`, `~`, `|`, then comparisons. Infix `&`/`|` are value-position only, distinct from prefix marks and type unions. E0398 flips direction; `jet fix` rewrites the 2,595 method calls; bit methods retire.

inverse :: ~perms                // complement

decisions.title: How the native Jet runtime does TLS
decisions.situation: TLS encrypts connections and checks who is on the other end, making HTTPS and secure email possible. Today Jet relies on Rust libraries, so removing Rust leaves native programs unable to establish these secure connections. This affects application authors whose existing HTTPS and email code must keep working without changing its public interface. You choose between a mature C library, a new Jet implementation, or a temporary Rust helper; we recommend the C library.
decisions.gist: How should native Jet provide TLS without its current Rust runtime?
decisions.lesson: TLS protects network traffic and checks certificates. Jet currently borrows Rust libraries for this work. A borrows a mature C library, B implements TLS in Jet, and C keeps the Rust library temporarily. All three must preserve certificate checks and the public API.
decisions.explainer: Using a mature library does not remove Jet's responsibility for correct integration. Certificate identity, protocol versions, encrypted reads and writes, and application protocol negotiation must retain their current behavior.
decisions.story: Maya fetches a page over HTTPS. Her native build needs the same certificate checks and encrypted connection as her current build, without depending on Jet's Rust runtime.
decisions.detail: The source ballot reports about 15 dependent test cases and one example. This vote preserves core.net.tls and chooses its native provider, not a new user-facing TLS API.

options.name: Use a C TLS library
options.detail: Call a mature C library such as OpenSSL or mbedTLS through Jet's C interface. Add one external dependency while keeping certificate checks, protocol negotiation and error behavior unchanged.
options.technical: JetRuntime C exports wrap the chosen library. Nix supplies and links it. The core.net.tls API remains unchanged.

options.name: Write TLS in Jet
options.detail: Implement TLS, certificates and the needed cryptography in Jet. Avoid an outside TLS dependency, but keep native TLS unavailable until the implementation, security audit and interoperability testing are complete.
options.technical: Native TLS 1.2/1.3 state machine and certificate validation in Core and JetRuntime.

options.name: Keep the Rust TLS library temporarily
options.detail: Link the existing Rust TLS implementation as a temporary helper for native programs. Restore TLS without replacing the implementation, but explicitly retain Rust until a replacement lands.
options.technical: A rustls static helper uses the helper-artifact path. Its scope is TLS only, with an explicit removal condition.

recommendation.why: A restores native TLS using a mature library, preserves the public API and removes Rust from Jet's runtime.
gains: Native HTTPS and secure email without a Rust runtime.

losses.loss: Jet gains one external C dependency.
losses.mitigation: Pin it through nix and isolate it behind the C interface so a later Jet provider can replace it.

C retains Rust in the runtime rather than completing its removal.

decisions.title: `crypto.wipe(&bytes)` safely zeroes a plain byte list's whole buffer, and Core uses that public name instead of `__zeroize`
decisions.situation: Keys from Core are `crypto.Secret` values, which wipe themselves when they close. Some bytes must stay plain, such as a seed handed to a C token library, and must still be erased after use. Today user code can't: the wipe is reserved for Core, and the only route is an unsafe loop. The vote decides how plain bytes are erased. We recommend a safe `crypto.wipe(&bytes)` that Core itself uses, so no reserved name remains.
decisions.gist: How should a program erase key bytes that must stay a plain byte list?
decisions.lesson: Secret keys should not stay in memory after use. Core's key types erase themselves. If you must hold key bytes in a plain `[U8]`, call `crypto.wipe(&seed)` when done. It overwrites every byte with zero, and the compiler can't skip it.
decisions.story: Noor's signing tool passes a seed to a hardware token's C library. To erase it after, she copies an unsafe volatile loop from another project and hopes it is right.
decisions.inWild:
// .NET: a safe wipe of any span.

decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0zlbj08, and card #6117, which asks for a public wipe. This is the public wipe question from the D-CRYPTO-WIPE1 package, asked alone. Keeps D-CRYPTO-API1=A (no safe raw export of Secret bytes), D-MEM-WIPE1=A (the `#Secret` duty never wipes plain memory on its own) and D-SHAPE-DUNDER2=A (E0067).

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/b4/cw/probe, on dev. w1.jet: `crypto.__zeroize(&seed)` is E0067 "`__zeroize` is reserved for Jet"; no `crypto.wipe` exists. w2.jet: the only route, an audited `#Unsafe` loop of `mem.volatile_write` over each element, runs and prints 32, 0, 0. Jetpack/Publication/Tests/Sign.jet:154-172 writes that loop by hand. Core's Secret Close calls the reserved `core.crypto.__zeroize` (Core/Crypto/Crypto.jet:198).

Reads with D-CRYPTO-ZEROSHARED1, which decides what the wipe does when another list still shares the buffer. Under D-RECEIVER-MARK1=A a function argument keeps its `&`, so the call stays `crypto.wipe(&seed)`.

options.name: A safe `crypto.wipe`
options.detail:
The wipe zeroes every element and the spare capacity past the length; the length is unchanged. It is safe because the caller already holds the list exclusively.

Core writes it as an audited volatile loop. A target without volatile stores refuses the call at build time, never building a wipe that may be skipped.
options.technical: Core/Crypto: `wipe(bytes: &[U8])`, an `#Unsafe` volatile loop checked by the sentry (#6107). Secret Close, the hasher and expert copies switch to it, and `__zeroize` retires. Byte lists only; zero is not valid for every element type.

options.name: Only through `Secret`
options.detail:
Plain bytes are moved into a Secret, which wipes when it closes.

A Secret never exports its bytes safely (D-CRYPTO-API1), so a C call that needs them can't be made without unsafe code.
options.technical: No new API; `__zeroize` stays Core-only.

options.name: Tag the value `#Secret`
options.detail:
D-MEM-WIPE1's tag carries a wipe duty through every copy.

It covers more than one erase needs, and each copy pays for it.
options.technical: Uses the ratified tag; still needs a public kernel for the duty to call.

comparisons.note: The zeroize crate; its docs warn that moves and reallocation leave copies. Source: https://docs.rs/zeroize/latest/zeroize/
A wipe that is never optimized away. Source: https://doc.libsodium.org/memory_management
A safe wipe of a span. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.security.cryptography.cryptographicoperations.zeromemory

gains: Sign.jet's unsafe loop becomes one call.

losses.mitigation: Reserve capacity first, or tag the value `#Secret`.

whyNot.reason: B leaves bytes that must stay plain with no safe wipe.
C charges every copy for a one-off erase.

recommendation.tradeoff: Plain lists get no crash scrub; long-lived keys stay in a Secret.

decisions.title: Wiping a list whose buffer another list still shares gives this list fresh zeroes and marks the old buffer "zero at last release"
decisions.situation: Jet lists share one buffer after a copy, until one of them writes. A wipe on one list must not change the other's value, but leaving the bytes for the other holder defeats the wipe. Secret adoption today has the same gap: it copies and leaves the shared buffer behind. The vote decides what a wipe does with a shared buffer. We recommend a fresh zeroed buffer for this list, and one mark on the old buffer: zero it when the last holder lets go.
decisions.gist: When a wiped list still shares its buffer with another list, what should happen to those bytes?
decisions.lesson: Copying a list in Jet is cheap because both copies share one buffer until one changes. If you wipe one copy, the other still needs its bytes. Jet gives your copy fresh zeroes and erases the shared bytes once nothing can read them.
decisions.story: Joe wipes a seed after signing. A logger made a copy earlier, so the seed's bytes stay in memory until the process exits.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0zlbj08, and card #6117, which asks for a public wipe. This is the shared buffer question from the D-CRYPTO-WIPE1 package, asked alone. Keeps D-CRYPTO-API1=A (no safe raw export of Secret bytes), D-MEM-WIPE1=A (the `#Secret` duty never wipes plain memory on its own) and D-SHAPE-DUNDER2=A (E0067).

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/b4/cw/probe, on dev. w1.jet: `crypto.__zeroize(&seed)` is E0067 "`__zeroize` is reserved for Jet"; no `crypto.wipe` exists. w2.jet: the only route, an audited `#Unsafe` loop of `mem.volatile_write` over each element, runs and prints 32, 0, 0. Jetpack/Publication/Tests/Sign.jet:154-172 writes that loop by hand. Core's Secret Close calls the reserved `core.crypto.__zeroize` (Core/Crypto/Crypto.jet:198).

JetRuntime/Source/Secret.jet:132-143 copies a shared buffer on adoption and leaves the old one. The kernel today erases the length but not the spare capacity (JetRuntime/Source/CryptoEntropy.jet:78-84).

Reads with D-CRYPTO-ZERO1, which adds the wipe. Buffers a growing list retired before the wipe are not reached under any option; `List<U8>.try_with_capacity(n)` before filling avoids them (w2.jet).

options.name: Fresh zeroes here, zero the old buffer at last release
options.detail:
An unshared buffer is zeroed in place. A shared one is left to its holders, with one bit in its count word meaning "zero me at the last release". This list gets a fresh zeroed buffer of the same capacity.

A writer that copies a marked buffer marks the copy too. Secret adoption uses the same path, closing today's gap.
options.technical: One mark bit in the count word (Refcount.jet); the free path zeroes a marked buffer before returning it, one load and branch beside header words it already reads.

options.name: Refuse a shared wipe
options.detail:
The wipe returns an error when the buffer is shared.

The other holder may be in a library the caller can't change.
options.technical: Adds an error case; no count-word change.

options.name: Zero in place, shared or not
options.detail:
The wipe writes through the shared buffer.

A list the caller never wrote to changes value, which no other Jet operation does.
options.technical: No count-word change; breaks copy-on-write.

comparisons.note: zeroize reaches only the value it is called on. Source: https://docs.rs/zeroize/latest/zeroize/
