Guarded allocations own their memory and wipe on free. Source: https://doc.libsodium.org/memory_management

recommendation.why: A erases every byte the wipe touched without changing any other list's value, at the cost of one bit and one branch on free. Copy-on-write stays intact.
gains: Covers copies made earlier.
Fixes Secret adoption too.

losses.loss: Shared bytes live until the last holder drops.
losses.mitigation: Tag the value `#Secret` so every copy carries the duty.

whyNot.reason: B fails at run time on copies the caller may not control.
C changes another list's value under it.

recommendation.tradeoff: One bit in every count word.

decisions.title: Jet ships a generated raylib binding, its own native game library, and its own font engine
decisions.situation: Jet's standard library holds a small raylib bridge and a font module that asks the host to shape text. A static Jet program cannot load the C libraries behind either, so windows never open and text is only estimated. The owner wants a raylib binding that shows off Jet's automatic C binding, and a native Jet library that beats raylib. This vote decides where each piece lives, and whether text uses Jet's own engine or FreeType and HarfBuzz. We recommend three first-party packages.
decisions.gist: Should Jet ship a generated raylib binding, its own `ray` game library, and its own `font` engine as packages?
decisions.lesson: A binding wraps a C library someone has installed; a native library is written in Jet and needs nothing installed. Drawing text needs two jobs: reading a font file into glyph shapes and pixels, and shaping, which picks and places glyphs for a script. Raylib does the first with a small built-in reader and skips shaping.
decisions.story: Omar writes a small game. With the `raylib` package he calls the real C raylib he installed. With `ray` he writes the same game in plain Jet, ships one file, and his text draws the same pixels on every machine and in every test.
decisions.inWild:
# Rust: a raylib binding crate, and pure-Rust font crates
[dependencies]
raylib = "5.5"
rustybuzz = "0.20"
swash = "0.2"
decisions.detail:
Today. core.game.raylib is Core/Game/Raylib.jet, 205 lines over raw host bindings, and core.font is Core/Font/Font.jet, 168 lines. On the static native runtime both take a no-library path (RouteAGame.jet, RouteAFont.jet). No window opens and every shaping request gets the approximate fallback.

Owner direction (2026-10-31, on this ballot): the C raylib binding should test Jet's automatic C binding, and Jet should own a native raylib-like library that beats raylib. Fonts become our own engine only if the value is real; otherwise they are a binding.

Rulings this builds on. D-RAYLIB1=A made raylib a first-party package. D-FFI-BINDER1=A lets `use "raylib.h"` read a C header directly. D-EXTEND-ARCH1=A gives Core no private powers. D-JPK-RINGSHIP1=C ships first-party packages with Jet at its version.

What A does. The `raylib` package is generated by the C binder from raylib.h and links the user's installed raylib. Its build is a binder showcase and a regression test. The `ray` package is the native library from card 5086: shapes, textures, text, input and audio mixing in Jet, over Core's window, sound and input doors (card 5035).

The `font` package is a Jet font engine. It reads TrueType and OpenType files, rasterizes glyph outlines with anti-aliasing, and shapes text with the GSUB and GPOS tables. Both `ray` and the `gui` toolkit use it. core.game.raylib and core.font retire with registered errors naming `jet add`.

Why our own font engine. First, exact pixels: FreeType output changes with its version and build flags, so headless text goldens could never be exact on every machine. A Jet engine gives the same pixels on every tier and host. Second, nothing to install: a static Jet program cannot load FreeType or HarfBuzz without a dynamic loader.

Third, safety: font files are untrusted input, and FreeType parsing bugs keep recurring. CVE-2025-27363, an out-of-bounds write in FreeType 2.13.0 and older, was reported as exploited in the wild. Fourth, the wasm and embedded targets get the same text with no C toolchain.

Peers made the same move. Chrome replaced FreeType with the Rust Fontations crates (skrifa) for web fonts in 2025 for memory safety. Rust has rustybuzz, a HarfBuzz port, and cosmic-text builds on it. Go's Fyne and Gio use go-text/typesetting, a pure Go HarfBuzz port. Raylib itself vendors stb_truetype and does no shaping.

Cost and staging. The work is one card per stage. Stage 1 is outline reading, rasterizing, kerning and simple ligatures, which already beats raylib's text. Stage 2 ports complex-script shaping for Arabic, Indic and other scripts. Stage 2 is proven against HarfBuzz's own shaping test data. The native runtime has no shaping at all today, so no program loses anything while stage 2 lands.

Edge cases. A missing glyph draws the font's notdef box, as HarfBuzz does. A program can still call FreeType or HarfBuzz through the C binder as an ordinary package. System fonts are found by path search; fontconfig is not required.

`raylib` is the generated binding to installed C raylib. `ray` is Jet's own game library. `font` is Jet's own font reader, rasterizer and shaper, used by `ray` and `gui`.

All three ship with Jet. `jet add` writes each dependency line.

decisions.title: What the Count type means in history tests
decisions.situation: The history test records (D-TEST-STRATEGY1) give case indexes, step bounds, identity values and weights the type `Count`. No decision defines Count. The language rule for aliases (D-TYPEALIAS1) forbids `Count :: Int`, because an alias may not rename a primitive. The golden tooling/test_history uses Count as an ordinary Int everywhere. We recommend A: those fields are plain Int, and the Count name is retired.
decisions.gist: Is a history count a plain Int, another name for Int, or its own type?
decisions.lesson: A history test generates a list of operations. Each operation records its index, the handles it creates, and the task and event it belongs to. Those indexes and identity values are whole numbers that are never negative. Jet's default whole number is Int, and `len()` returns an Int.
decisions.story: Ada writes a generator for booking histories. She numbers each operation with its loop index, builds `HandleID{value: next_id}` from an Int counter, and checks `operations.len()` against `max_steps`. Under A and B her code checks as written. Under C she converts at each of those points.
decisions.detail:
Today. D-TEST-STRATEGY1 (Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:3892) says `generate` receives `case_index: Count` and `max_steps: Count`. Nothing else in Docs/spec defines Count. The registry declares Count as a plain opaque type (Compiler/Prelude/Core.jet:208), so no Int value fits it and no operator applies to it.

The conflict. D-TYPEALIAS1 (syntax-decisions.md:1473-1476) allows an alias only to shorten a generic spelling. A primitive newtype must use `distinct`. A probe of `Count :: Int` gives E0324.

The golden. Examples/features/tooling/test_history/run.jet uses Count as an Int. It writes `index % 2` (line 51), `index + 1` (line 52) and `index > 0` (line 70). It passes literal 0 and 1 arguments (lines 422, 433). It builds `HandleID{value: next_id}` from an Int `next_id` (line 419). It compares `operations.len()` with `max_steps` (line 294). Today the check gives E0108, E0109, E0112, E0360 and E0915 at these lines.

The oracle. The Rust foundation had `pub type Count = usize;` (crates/jet-foundation/src/TestingHistory.rs:123-125 at c9129d174d^), documented as a non-negative source-level count. usize is Rust's length type. Jet's length type is Int (D-INTBIG1, syntax-decisions.md:1509).

Draws. HistoryRng's `next_u64()` and `below(bound)` feed `seed:` and the step count in the golden (lines 410, 411, 541). Under A and B they return Int. Under C they return Count.

Not negative. None of the three options checks at the type level that a count is not negative; Rust's usize could not be. Under every option the Jet runner rejects a negative bound or weight when it validates the strategy.

Who changes. Under A, the Count export is removed, the records use Int, and the golden's 7 `testing.Count` annotations on 6 lines (44, 98, 112, 318, 406, 407) become `Int`. Under B, the compiler resolves `Count` to Int as a named exception to D-TYPEALIAS1, and the golden is unchanged. Under C, Count becomes `#Numeric Count :: distinct Int` in Core, and the golden gains a conversion at each of the 39 type errors that cross between Int and Count today.

Review. Author: Claude (GoldC lane). No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft.

decisions.title: Jet reads Parquet with its own reader in Core, proven against the pinned test files
decisions.situation: In September you approved reading Parquet data files through the official Arrow Rust library. Since then Jet's toolchain has dropped Rust, and its runtime is C. Nothing in it can link that library, and no Parquet code exists. A data-loader test cannot pass until this is settled. Core already decodes gzip and Zstandard in Jet code. We recommend a Jet-owned Parquet reader in Core, checked against the same pinned test files.
decisions.gist: The approved Rust Parquet reader cannot link anymore: should Jet write its own, link a native one, or drop Parquet?
decisions.lesson: Parquet stores tables by column, compressed, with a small index at the end of the file. A reader decodes that index, then each column's pages. Several engines, such as DuckDB and Polars, wrote their own readers instead of linking Arrow's. A reader in Jet runs the same everywhere, including the web, with no foreign library.
decisions.story: Mina loads sales.parquet in a notebook, a server and a web page. Under A the same Jet code reads it in all three. Under B the web page needs a separate WebAssembly build of a native library. Under C she first adds a package.
decisions.inWild:
# Python with pyarrow: one call reads the table
import pyarrow.parquet as pq
table = pq.read_table("sales.parquet")
print(table.num_rows)
decisions.detail:
Reopens the September Parquet ruling. That ruling chose the pinned Rust `parquet` 59.3.0 crate and its Arrow closure behind the foreign boundary. Its rejected option was a Jet-owned reader with the same obligations. The Rust compiler and its Prelude, including the old Parquet bridge, are gone, and the toolchain builds no Rust.

Today, at dev 03c64ad0c4. `Core/Data` knows the Parquet format name, but no code decodes it. Its loader errors call such formats provider-owned. Examples/features/tooling/data_loader expects `url:bound:1000` from a pinned parquet-testing file. That example also hits an unrelated compiler fault today. Four pinned corpus files and their expected output exist in tests/fixtures/parquet_reader.

Size of the approved reader. The `parquet` 59.3.0 crate alone is 112,904 lines of Rust source. It also pulls Arrow crates, flate2, brotli, lz4_flex, a Snappy crate and more.

Jet already owns codecs in Core. DEFLATE and gzip (Core/Archive), and a full Zstandard decoder (Core/Archive/Zstd.jet, 1,010 lines). Both were ruled Jet-owned instead of wrapping C libraries, and the BSON and MessagePack codecs are Jet-maintained too.

What A does. Core gains a Parquet reader in Jet. It covers Thrift compact metadata, every page encoding, nested columns, and statistics. It also covers the logical types, including INT96 timestamps, and the codecs the Rust reader supports. A Jet Snappy, LZ4 and Brotli decoder joins gzip and Zstandard. LZO is refused with a typed error, as both Arrow readers do.

What A proves. The parquet-testing corpus and differential runs against pyarrow as a development-only oracle, never a runtime dependency. Limits on bytes, rows, nesting and allocation follow the existing data limits. A timed comparison against pyarrow is published, and any loss becomes a card.

What B does. A native Arrow reader is vendored under the dependency invariant, either a prebuilt Arrow Rust library per target or Arrow C++. Each target, including WebAssembly, needs its own build. What C does. Core drops Parquet, and an optional first-party package provides it, built on A or B.

Prior art. DuckDB, Polars, parquet-go and hyparquet each own their Parquet reader. pyarrow and Spark use Arrow C++ and parquet-mr. Review. Author: Claude (SurfaceDesign lane). No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft.

decisions.title: Web pages, forms, router and store leave Core for the first-party web package; HTTP stays in Core
decisions.situation: Core holds the whole web stack: HTTP, and the app layer of pages, forms, router, store, tables and browser storage. The owner wants every capability that can be a library to be one. A first-party package ships with Jet at the same version and needs no download. The vote decides which part of the web stack stays in Core. We recommend keeping HTTP in Core and moving the app layer into the web package that already exists.
decisions.gist: Should web pages, forms and routing move to the first-party `web` package while HTTP stays in Core?
decisions.lesson: A standard library is promised to every program forever, so it should hold what most programs share. Go and Python ship HTTP in their standard library but leave web frameworks such as Gin or Django to packages. A first-party package can still ship with the toolchain, so moving code out of Core changes its promise, not its availability.
decisions.story: Mia writes a command-line tool that fetches one JSON file. Today her program's standard library also carries forms, a router and a browser store she never uses. Under A she uses core.http alone, and her teammate's web app lists `web` once.
decisions.detail:
Today. core.web is 12 files and 5,628 lines in Core/Web. core.http is 3 files and 4,845 lines in Core/Http, beside core.net. A first-party `web` package already exists in Jetpack/Provider/Batteries/web, 252 lines over core.web.

The compiler knows the web stack by name in several places. Sema has Calls/Http.jet and Calls/HttpRouting.jet, and `web.form(...)` is expanded in sema. IR and runtime carry RouteBrowser.jet and RouteWeb.jet.

D-EXTEND-ARCH1=A (2026-10-30) already says Core gets no private powers. So those compiler rows must become ordinary markers and traits under every option. This vote decides only where the code lives.

What A does. core.http and core.net stay in Core: HTTP is how any program talks to the network. Everything in core.web moves into the `web` package: app, pages, live queries, forms, router, store, table, virtual lists, browser storage and browser tests.

A first-party package ships inside the toolchain at its version, offline (D-JPK-RINGSHIP1=C). A project lists it once, and `jet add web` writes that line. After the move, `use core.web` is an error whose fix is `jet add web`, as D-CORE-MODELDESC1=D did for models.

The Browser effect stays a machine root in Core (D-EFFTYPE-KERNEL1=A). The dev server is not part of this vote. D-DEVSERVER1=A (2026-10-24) already moves it out of the compiler and rebuilds it as a tool.

This amends the home named in D-FLAGSHIP-WEBAPI1=A, which called typed browser events a Core surface. The events keep their shape and move with the package.

Moves under A, one card each. Core/Web moves into the web package. The sema web rows become markers, and the runtime web routes move too. Examples and tests change `use core.web` to `use web`.

Peers. Go ships net/http but not a web framework. Python ships http.server but leaves Django and Flask to packages. Rust and Zig ship neither in std. Deno ships HTTP serving in its runtime and frameworks as modules.

Review. Author: Claude (SurfaceDesign lane). No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft.

decisions.title: core.term stays in Core, core.tui becomes the first-party tui package, and #Live becomes a marker declared by core.term
decisions.situation: Core has two terminal modules. core.term prints text, reads keys and switches the terminal into raw mode. core.tui builds full-screen layouts, widgets and colors on top of it. The `#Live` raw-input block is known to the compiler by name. The owner wants every capability that can be a library to be one. We recommend keeping core.term in Core, moving core.tui to a first-party package, and declaring `#Live` in core.term.
decisions.gist: Should terminal layouts and widgets move to a first-party `tui` package while printing and keys stay in Core?
decisions.lesson: Every program prints and many read keys, so those belong in the standard library. Full-screen layouts are a framework that few programs need. Rust keeps ratatui outside std, and Go keeps bubbletea outside its standard library. A marker that a library declares works like a compiler one, but anyone can write the same kind.
decisions.story: Ken writes a script that asks one yes or no question. He needs keys and raw mode, not a widget library. Under A he uses core.term alone, and `#term.Live` comes from the module he already imported.
decisions.inWild:
# Rust: terminal raw mode in a small crate, widgets in another
[dependencies]
crossterm = "0.28"
ratatui = "0.29"
decisions.detail:
Today. core.term is Core/Term/Term.jet, 665 lines: printing, line input, keys and terminal size. core.tui is Core/Tui/Tui.jet, 709 lines: events, color profiles, layout and widgets over core.ui nodes.

`#Live` is a row in the compiler's syntax registry (JetFoundation/Data/Syntax/CoreSurface.jet). It switches the terminal to raw input for its body and restores it on every exit.

D-DECL-TYPES1=A (2026-10-30) makes markers ordinary types that libraries declare. A wrapping marker implements `wrap(self, call)`. D-TERM-COMMANDS1=A (2026-10-30) gives core.term `.EnableRawMode` with automatic undo on every exit.

What A does. core.term stays in Core as the door to the terminal. core.tui moves to a first-party `tui` package, which ships with Jet at the same version (D-JPK-RINGSHIP1=C). `jet add tui` writes its one line.

`#Live` becomes `struct Live` in core.term, implementing Marker with a wrap method. The wrap turns raw mode on and lets D-TERM-COMMANDS1's undo restore it. Code writes `#term.Live { }`, and the registry row is deleted.

D-TUI-ANSI1=A's checked ANSI text lands in core.term rather than core.tui. D-TERM-COMMANDS1's `.Print` command takes it, so it must be where printing is.

Moves under A, one card each. Core/Tui moves into the tui package. `#Live` moves out of the registry into core.term. The runtime routes RouteTerm.jet and UiCarriersTui.jet follow their modules.

Edge case. A file that writes bare `#Live` gets a registered error whose fix is `#term.Live`, and `jet fix` rewrites it. Sixteen files use it today.

Peers. Rust has crossterm for raw mode and ratatui for widgets, both crates. Go has golang.org/x/term and bubbletea outside the standard library. Python ships curses in its standard library.

Review. Author: Claude (SurfaceDesign lane). No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft.

decisions.title: The UI node tree, windows and previews leave Core for the first-party ui package; OS services in core.ui.host stay in Core
decisions.situation: Core's UI module does two jobs. It builds a tree of UI nodes and opens app windows. It also reaches operating system services such as the clipboard, file dialogs and text input. The compiler knows UI values by name in many runtime files. The owner wants every capability that can be a library to be one. We recommend moving the node tree and windows to a first-party package and keeping the OS services in Core.
decisions.gist: Should UI nodes and windows move to a first-party `ui` package while OS services stay in Core?
decisions.lesson: A UI toolkit is a framework with opinions about layout and state, and it changes often. The clipboard and file dialogs are doors to the operating system that any program may need. Standard libraries tend to keep the doors and leave toolkits to packages, so the toolkit can change without breaking Core.
decisions.story: Lena writes a command-line tool that copies a result to the clipboard. Today that pulls in Core's whole UI tree. Under A she uses core.ui.host.clipboard only, and her colleague's desktop app lists `ui` once.
decisions.inWild:
// Rust: windows and widgets are crates, not std
[dependencies]
winit = "0.30"
egui = "0.29"
decisions.detail:
Today. Core/Ui is 783 lines. Ui.jet (297) holds nodes, geometry, previews and app windows. Host.jet and Host/* (486) hold the OS services D-FOUND-PLATFORM1=A placed in ui.host: file dialogs, clipboard, IME, drag and drop, shortcuts and accessibility.

The compiler knows UI by name. Sema has Calls/UiHandles.jet. The runtime has 26 Ui*.jet carrier files, and two transfer leaves are gated by `#Unsafe` (Sema/Calls/Core.jet). A first-party `gui` package (572 lines) already builds on core.ui.

D-EXTEND-ARCH1=A (2026-10-30) already says Core gets no private powers. The compiler rows become ordinary library code under every option. This vote decides only where the code lives.

What A does. core.ui.host stays in Core, unchanged: these services cross into the operating system, as core.term and core.http do. The node tree, geometry, previews, app and window handles move to a first-party `ui` package.

The runtime carriers for nodes and windows move with the package. The `gui` and `tui` packages build on `ui`. A first-party package ships with Jet at the same version, offline (D-JPK-RINGSHIP1=C), and `jet add ui` writes its line.

Edge cases. `core.ui.host` keeps its path, so OS service imports do not change. `use core.ui` after the move is a registered error whose fix is `jet add ui`, and `jet fix` rewrites imports. Jet's devtools panel (D-DX-DEVTOOLS-UX1=D) depends on the package like any tool.

Moves under A, one card each. The node tree and windows go to the ui package. UiHandles and the 26 carrier files follow, with the `#Unsafe` transfer leaves rewritten as package code. Examples and tests switch imports.

Peers. Rust, Go and Zig ship no UI toolkit in std. Python ships tkinter in its standard library. Swift and Kotlin take UI from platform frameworks outside the language's standard library.

Review. Author: Claude (SurfaceDesign lane). No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft.

decisions.title: core.db stays in Core; the SQL engine and core.auth leave for first-party sql and auth packages
decisions.situation: Core holds three pieces of data and account code. core.db opens databases, runs queries and applies row policies over a bundled SQLite. A second module is a SQL engine written in Jet that the command line shares. core.auth handles sessions, passwords, OAuth and signed tokens. The owner wants every capability that can be a library to be one. We recommend keeping core.db and moving the engine and accounts to first-party packages.
decisions.gist: Should core.db stay in Core while the SQL engine and account code move to first-party packages?
decisions.lesson: A database door is shared plumbing: many programs store data, and drivers need one interface to implement. Account flows such as OAuth are opinions about how a web app signs people in. Go and Python ship a database interface in their standard library but leave login frameworks to packages.
decisions.story: Ana writes a script that keeps notes in a SQLite file. Under A she uses core.db with no dependency line. Her teammate's web app adds `auth` once, and its login code can change without waiting for a Jet release.
decisions.detail:
Today. Core/Db is Db.jet (1,890 lines) and Sql.jet (938). The core.db module owns connections, values, row policies, pools, migrations and the private SQLite driver. The core.db.sql module is an in-Jet SQL engine that D-DB-SQLKERNEL1=A made public so the command line shares it.

The core.auth module is Core/Auth/Auth.jet, 1,351 lines: sessions, password checks, magic links, OAuth, JWT and PASETO. D-AUTH1=A (2026-07-12) asked for these batteries but did not choose Core over a package.

The DB effect is already settled. D-EFFTYPE-KERNEL1=A (2026-10-30) makes Core declare `effect DB` with the same `#FX` line a package uses. D-EXTEND-ARCH1=A removes the compiler's private rows under every option.

What A does. core.db stays in Core with its SQLite driver, row policies and the DB effect. The SQL engine moves to a first-party `sql` package, which the command line depends on. core.auth moves to a first-party `auth` package.

Both packages ship with Jet at its version (D-JPK-RINGSHIP1=C), and `jet add` writes each line. The `web` package depends on `auth` for its login helpers.

Moves under A, one card each. Sql.jet goes to the sql package. Auth.jet goes to the auth package. The Taint rows for auth become package code. Examples and tests switch imports.

Edge cases. `use core.db.sql` and `use core.auth` become registered errors naming the `jet add` fix. Typed queries, D-SQL-HANDLER1's handler effects and D-DBPOLICY-CHECK1's policy helpers stay in core.db unchanged.

Peers. Go ships database/sql as a driver interface, with drivers and auth outside. Python ships sqlite3 but leaves SQLAlchemy and Authlib to packages. Rust std has neither.

Review. Author: Claude (SurfaceDesign lane). No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft.

decisions.title: When the comptime probe and the comptime run disagree, which meaning wins?
decisions.situation: Some Jet code runs while the program compiles; Jet calls this comptime. Today the compiler type-checks every comptime piece twice. An early probe checks it only to list what it depends on, then the real run checks it again before computing the value. The speed plan removes the probe, because it costs about 41 seconds per self-compile. If a census finds code where the two checks see different things, one meaning must win. We recommend the run's meaning, because the run is where the value is computed.
decisions.gist: When the early dependency probe and the comptime run see different references or types, which one defines the comptime item's meaning?
decisions.lesson: Comptime code is checked by an early probe that only lists its dependencies, and again by the run that computes its value. The two checks see slightly different worlds: the run already knows types built by earlier comptime items, and the two treat failure handling and host hooks differently. Removing the probe is safe only if one of the two views is declared the meaning.
decisions.story: Theo builds a table type at compile time with a comptime function, then a second comptime constant reads that type's fields. The probe checks the constant before the type exists and lists one set of dependencies. The run checks it after the type exists and sees another. When the probe goes away, the compiler must know which list was right, or Theo's constant could silently change value.
decisions.detail:
Source: SPEED-500K.md section 6, row D2, and section 11, row T6. Measured cost: sema.check is 40.9 seconds, about 95 percent of it the probe (sema_comptime_probe_dependencies, CheckProgram.jet:5117). The run check is sema_check_comptime_item_in (:6164), about 72 percent of comptime's 155 seconds.

The probe's dependency set feeds only the run: it decides which constant rows are passed to each comptime program (needs_rows). The known differences come from frontend.md in the perf folder. The run sets no failure carrier, the probe withholds host hooks, and the run already has staged constant types.

So a constant reached only through a resolved type can change needs_rows. The plan first runs an instrumented census of probe references against run references over the whole self-compile. If the census finds no difference, the probe is removed and this vote changes nothing.

If it finds differences, this vote decides the meaning. Under A, each differing item is listed in the census report with its old and new dependency set. Any value change is treated as a fix and gets a regression case.

options.name: The run's view is the meaning
options.detail: A comptime item means what the check in its run sees: types built by earlier comptime items are known, and failure handling and host hooks follow the run's rules. Dependencies come from the run's own references. The probe is deleted after the census.

options.name: The probe's view is the meaning
options.detail: The run is changed to check in the probe's earlier and narrower view: no types from earlier comptime items and no host hooks. Code that needs a type built at compile time before it can be checked becomes an error. This is stricter, and some programs that work today stop compiling.

options.name: A disagreement is a compile error
options.detail: Keep both checks and compare them for every item. When they differ, the build stops with an error naming the item. This never picks a meaning silently, but it keeps the duplicate check the owner ruled out on 2026-10-17 at 12:25.

comparisons.note: Zig analyzes comptime code lazily, at the point where it is evaluated. There is no separate earlier pass with its own view.

recommendation.why: The run is where the value is computed, so its view is the only one that can match the value. It also removes the second check entirely, as the owner's no-duplicated-work rule asks.
recommendation.tradeoff: A rare item may change dependencies or value once; the census lists every such item and each gets a regression case.

whyNot.reason: It rejects programs that work today and still differs from what the run computes.
It keeps the duplicate check, about 41 seconds per self-compile, which the owner ruled out.

losses.loss: A few comptime values could change once at the cutover.
losses.mitigation: The census names every differing item before removal, and each one gets a regression test.

decisions.title: How the compiler's own lexer gets vector instructions
decisions.situation: The fastest compilers read source text 64 bytes at a time with vector instructions, which test many characters in one step. Jet's speed plan needs this in its lexer for the last milestone, one million lines per second. Jet already ratified one public set of vector tools that its runtime and users share. The question is whether the compiler uses those same tools, gets a private route only it can call, or gets a new public vector module. We recommend the same public tools, so users can write what the compiler writes.
decisions.gist: Should the compiler's vectorized lexer use the public vector tools users already have, a private compiler-only route, or a new public module?
decisions.lesson: Vector instructions test 16 to 64 bytes in one step, which is how fast lexers classify letters, spaces and quotes. Jet already ratified public tools for this: lane types, per-chip copies of a function, and typed instructions for each chip level. The compiler is ordinary Jet code. This vote decides whether it follows the same rule as Jet's runtime: one way, shared with users.
decisions.story: Ravi maintains a JSON parser written in Jet. He reads that Jet's compiler now lexes source at 2 nanoseconds per byte with byte shuffles and bit masks. He wants the same trick for his parser. Whether he can write it in ordinary Jet depends on whether the compiler used public tools or a private shortcut.
decisions.detail:
Source: SPEED-500K.md section 2 (P1 and P2, lexer data layout and SIMD) and section 11, row T7. The planned lexer classifies a 64-byte block with byte-shuffle tables, turns the result into bit masks, and walks the masks with trailing-zero counts. Target: classification at or below 1 nanosecond per byte. This is milestone M5 work, the last step of the ladder.

Ratified context. D-SIMD3=B gives the portable lane family, including U8x16 and U8x32. D-SIMD-NATIVE1=A (2026-10-04) says Jet's runtime writes its fast paths with the same tools users get. Those tools are #Multiversion per-chip-level copies, Lanes<T>, and typed core.arch instructions named under comptime if on the chip level. It also says no separate SIMD module exists.

Today's lane types offer splat, from_array, to_array, indexing, arithmetic and reduce. They do not offer byte table lookup or compare-to-mask. Under A, the lexer reaches those through typed core.arch instructions inside a #Multiversion function, with a scalar baseline copy. That uses only ratified surface.

The speed plan's own draft recommended B (an internal route first, public API later). This ballot recommends A because D-SIMD-NATIVE1 already settled the one-way rule for Jet's own fast paths. Option C conflicts with D-SIMD-NATIVE1's no-separate-module rule.

options.name: Use the public tools users already have
options.detail: The lexer is an ordinary #Multiversion function. Lane types do the plain parts. Typed core.arch instructions do the byte shuffles and masks in the chip levels that have them, and a scalar baseline copy runs everywhere else. Everything it uses is already ratified public surface. The backend work that makes these fast also makes users' code fast.

options.name: A private route only the compiler can call
options.detail: The backend gains vector operations that only compiler sources can reach, through private intrinsics. Users get nothing new, and the compiler gets a second way to use vector instructions. Bugs and speed work on that route never reach user code.

options.name: A new public core.simd module
options.detail: Add a separate public vector module with its own byte vector type, shuffles and masks, similar to Rust's std::simd. The compiler and users share it, but it sits beside the existing lane types as a second public vector surface.

comparisons.note: Rust exposes vendor intrinsics in core::arch and keeps the portable std::simd module unstable after years of work. Its compiler is written with ordinary library code.
Zig's own tokenizer uses the same @Vector builtin type that users get. There is no private compiler route.

recommendation.why: Jet already ruled that its own fast paths use the same tools users get. Following that rule in the compiler adds no surface, and every backend improvement made for the lexer also speeds up user code.
recommendation.tradeoff: The vector lexer waits for #Multiversion and core.arch to be built; it is last-milestone work, so earlier milestones are unaffected.

whyNot.reason: It creates a second, private way to use vector instructions, which the ratified one-way rule forbids for Jet's own fast paths.
It adds a second public vector surface beside the lane types, which the ratified rule also refuses.

losses.loss: The vector lexer depends on ratified tools that are not built yet.
losses.mitigation: The vector lexer is last-milestone work; the scalar lexer serves every earlier milestone.

surface.gist: Should the compiler's fast lexer use the vector tools users already have, a private route, or a new module?
surface.lesson: Vector instructions test 16 to 64 bytes in one step; fast lexers use them to sort characters. Jet already ratified public tools for this: lane types, per-chip copies of a function, and typed chip instructions. Jet's runtime must use those same tools. This vote decides whether the compiler follows that rule too.

current.note: Today's lexer reads one byte at a time. The plan needs 64 bytes per step.

wild.note: simdjson sorts 32 bytes per step with one shuffle and one mask.

options.name: Same public tools
options.gist: The lexer is ordinary Jet using ratified vector tools.
gains: Users can write what the compiler writes.
No new surface.
losses: Waits for the ratified tools to be built.

options.name: Private compiler route
options.gist: Only compiler sources can call the vector operations.
gains: No user-facing design work.
losses: A second, hidden way to use vectors.
Speed work never reaches user code.

options.gist: A separate vector module beside the lane types.
gains: Shared with users.
losses: Two public vector surfaces.

mask :: simd.swizzle_dyn(TABLE, block).simd_eq(SPACE).to_bitmask()

gains: One way to use vector instructions.
Backend speedups reach user code.

losses.loss: The fast lexer waits for unbuilt tools.
losses.mitigation: It is last-milestone work; earlier milestones use the scalar lexer.

A second public vector surface is also refused.

decisions.title: If the 1M lines per second goal is missed, do the always-on checks keep their budget?
decisions.situation: Jet's compiler is being rebuilt to compile one million lines of code per second from a cold start. Every compile also runs checks: ownership and effect analysis, failure inference, two internal consistency checkers, and debug info. Together they cost about 17 percent of the time budget at that speed. If the last milestone falls short, someone must say whether the checks keep their share or some leave normal builds. We recommend keeping every check on and accepting a landing near 900 thousand lines per second.
decisions.gist: If the cold compile misses one million lines per second, should the always-on safety and consistency checks keep their 17 percent share of the budget?
decisions.lesson: Every Jet compile runs checks that catch mistakes: ownership, effects and failure analysis for the user's code, two consistency checkers for the compiler's own work, and debug info. At the one million lines per second target they cost 2,350 of 13,600 nanoseconds of work per line. The speed plan keeps them all on, each run once. This vote fixes what happens if the final milestone lands short.
decisions.story: Mia runs the speed proof at the last milestone. The budget table shows every phase in its column except scaling, and the build lands at 910 thousand lines per second. She needs to know today whether that is a pass, or whether the two internal checkers should leave the default build to close the gap. Without a rule, the plan's last step has no finish line.
decisions.inWild:
# Go keeps its SSA checker off unless asked for:
go build -gcflags=-d=ssa/check/on ./...
# Zig keeps runtime safety checks on in Debug and ReleaseSafe builds.
zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe
decisions.detail:
Source: SPEED-500K.md in the perf discovery folder. See section 1 (budget table), section 10 (what must not be traded) and section 11, row T3. Owner rules in the plan, 2026-10-17: at 12:25, checks and debug info stay on with no duplicated work. At 12:30, about 900K is an excellent first target because Jet keeps extra work. At 12:33, the target is 1M.

The checks-on rows at 1M, in nanoseconds of work per source line: P5b ownership 700, P5c effects 300, P5d failure inference 200. Then P9 MIR consistency check 500, P11 LIR consistency check 250 and P13b DWARF debug info 400. Total 2,350 of 13,600, which is 17 percent.

Only part of that total can move. P5b, P5c and P5d are language rules: they produce the user's ownership, effect and failure errors, so no option removes them. Option B moves only P9 and P11 (750 ns per line, 5.5 percent of the work). DWARF stays on under every option, as the owner ruled at 12:25.

The plan already tries the section 9 contingency first: cache topology, pass fusion, compressed indices, search-built instruction templates, speculative scheduling and AVX-512 scans. This vote applies only to what remains after those.

options.name: Keep every check on and ship the measured number
options.detail: All checks stay in every default build, each run once. If the last milestone lands short after the contingency work, the measured speed is the result, for example about 900 thousand lines per second. The budget rows stay fixed and visible.
options.code:
$ jet build    # every check on, each run once
  ownership, effects, failure     on
  MIR check, LIR check            on
  debug info                      on
# budget table at the last milestone: 910K lines/s
# result: shipped as 910K, checks unchanged

options.name: Move the two internal checkers to verification mode
options.detail: If 1M is missed, the MIR and LIR consistency checkers leave the default build. They run only in the existing full-verification mode, which CI always uses. That frees about 750 nanoseconds per line, 5.5 percent of the work. A compiler bug could then reach a user's binary without being caught on that machine.
options.code:
$ jet build    # ownership, effects, failure, debug info on
               # MIR and LIR checkers off
# CI and compiler development turn on full verification:
# MIR and LIR checkers run once per function

options.name: Make no rule now; decide with the last milestone's numbers
options.detail: Keep every check on through the milestones and bring the question back when the final budget table exists. This decides with measured data, but the plan keeps an open finish line until then.
options.code:
# milestones M1-M5 run with every check on
# at M5: the owner sees the budget table and votes again

comparisons.note: The Go compiler's SSA checker runs only when a developer turns it on with a debug flag. Normal builds skip it.
Zig keeps runtime safety checks in Debug and ReleaseSafe builds and removes them only in ReleaseFast and ReleaseSmall.

recommendation.why: The owner already called about 900K an excellent result because Jet keeps extra safety work. Keeping the checks on makes that the rule and keeps one build mode.
recommendation.tradeoff: The final number may be about 10 percent below 1M; every build still catches compiler mistakes before they reach users.

whyNot.reason: It buys at most 5.5 percent and lets a compiler bug reach a user's binary unseen.
It leaves the plan's finish line open, although the owner already gave the deciding fact.

losses.loss: The headline speed may land near 900K instead of 1M.
losses.mitigation: The budget table publishes the check rows, so the cost is visible and every other phase still meets its column.

surface.gist: If Jet's compiler misses one million lines per second, should its always-on checks still keep their time budget?
surface.lesson: Every compile runs checks that catch mistakes: ownership, effects and failure analysis, two internal consistency checkers, and debug info. At the target speed they cost about 17 percent of the time. The plan keeps them all on, each run once. This vote decides what happens if the last milestone lands short.

One build mode for everyone.

options.name: Decide later

gains: Decides with measured data.
losses: The plan has no finish line until then.

recommendation.why: The owner already called about 900K excellent because Jet keeps extra safety work. Keeping every check on turns that into the rule.
gains: Every build stays checked.
The finish line is clear today.

losses.loss: The headline number may miss 1M.
losses.mitigation: The budget table shows the check cost on its own rows.

whyNot.reason: It saves at most 5.5 percent and lets compiler bugs through.
The deciding fact is already known.

recommendation.tradeoff: About 10 percent of speed for checked builds everywhere.

decisions.title: `.int()` is the one strict whole-number read for JSON, and typed decoding into Int follows it
decisions.situation:
Jet's JSON parser keeps every number as written. Both of Core's whole-number reads, `.int()` and `decode<Int>()`, accept `2.0` and `1e2`. `.int()` also expands the eight characters `1e999999` into a million-digit number, which ran past two minutes. Protocol code carries three private copies of a stricter check.

The last draft added a second read named `json.integer`. You asked why Jet needs a separate spelling. It does not: we now recommend making `.int()` itself strict, as Rust's serde_json and Go do, with typed decoding into `Int` following the same rule.
decisions.gist: Should `.int()` become the one strict whole-number read for JSON, with typed decoding into Int following it?
decisions.lesson: Parsed JSON keeps each number as the text that was written, such as `2`, `2.0` or `1e2`. A strict whole-number read accepts only text with no decimal point and no exponent. Rust, Go, C# and Kotlin read integers this way. A loose read also accepts `2.0` and turns it into 2.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A lexeme is the exact text of a number in the JSON document, such as `2.0`. `.int()` reads a parsed JSON value as an `Int`; `decode<T>()` reads it into a typed field. Jet's `Int` is exact and has no size limit, so `.int()` never needs a 64-bit cap.

The huge-exponent stall: `1e999999` is eight characters, but its whole-number value has a million digits. A read that values it before checking its spelling does all of that work for one field.
decisions.story: Sam's editor sends a language-server request with id 7, and Jet's server reads it with `.int()`. A broken client sends id 7.5, and `.int()` refuses it with the field and the reason. A hostile client sends id 1e999999, and `.int()` refuses it at once, because the text has an exponent.
decisions.detail:
Source: the JSON-number sweep after the parser change that keeps number lexemes (#4602). ToolsJet-34 and ToolsJet-36 repaired about 30 readers in Jetpack and the compiler with one strict helper, `foundation_json_integer`. GoldC-31's JSON schema binder and the testkit each carry their own copy.

Probes on the tree14 compiler, in ballot/jint. `.int()` gives 7 for `7.0`, 100 for `1e2` and a 401-digit number for `1e400`. It refuses `1e999999999` as "expected int". Typed `decode<Int>()` gives 7 for `7.0` and 100 for `1e2`, and refuses exponents past one million.

The stall. For `1e999999`, eight characters inside that limit, both `.int()` and `decode<Int>()` were still running when the two-minute probe timeout killed them. The strict helper refuses all of these at once.

What the best libraries do. serde_json's `as_i64` returns a number only for a written integer within i64. Go's `Number.Int64` parses the text as an integer, so `2.0` is an error. C#'s `GetInt64` and Kotlin's serializer refuse `2.0` the same way. All four refuse `2.0` in a typed integer field too.

Where Jet improves on them. Jet's `Int` is exact, so `.int()` reads any written integer without a 64-bit cap, where serde returns None past i64. The refusal is an error naming the field path and the reason, not a bare None. The value never has more digits than its text, so no input can make the read slow.

The rule. A lexeme is an integer when it is an optional minus sign and digits, as RFC 8259 writes integers. `Dyn.Int` built in code also passes. Everything else is refused: a decimal point, an exponent, text, a Bool and null.

Typed decoding follows the same rule. An `Int` field refuses `2.0`, as in serde, Go, C# and Kotlin. Fixed-width fields such as `I64` add their range check, as today. The ratified number law said `Int` rejects non-integral fractions; this ballot narrows it to integer spellings only.

Who changes. Twenty-four files call `.int()` on JSON or Dyn values. Each reads a count, a position, a size, an id, a price or a shape that its producer writes as an integer. The strict helper and both copies are deleted, and their callers use `.int()`. The full cases suite is the landing proof.

A producer that writes whole numbers as `2.0`. Python writes a float that way, and JavaScript writes 1e21 and larger with an exponent. Those values are floats at the producer, so the error message says to read them with `.float()` or declare the field `Float` or `Decimal`.

options.name: `.int()` becomes the one strict read; typed Int decoding follows it
options.detail:
`.int()` accepts a written integer of any size and refuses `2.0`, `1e2`, text, Bool and null with a field error. Typed decoding into an `Int` field uses the same rule.

The Foundation helper and the two private copies are deleted, and their callers use `.int()`. The huge-exponent hang is gone on both paths, because an exponent is refused before any valuing.
options.technical:
In JetRuntime Dyn.jet, `jet_dyn_int` accepts a Number lexeme only when it is an optional `-` and digits, then parses it exactly. The Int Decode route and the web runtime's `jet_dyn_int` use the same check. The error reads "expected an integer, got 7.0" with the field path, and its fix line names `.float()`.

Repoint `foundation_json_integer` callers, JsonSchemaBinder and testkit StepsJson to `.int()`, and delete the copies. Update the JSON numbers section of encoding-decisions.md and core-library.md.

options.name: A second Core read, `json.integer`
options.detail:
Core gains `json.integer(value) -> Int?`, the strict rule, beside `.int()`. The Foundation helper and the copies are deleted.

`.int()` and `decode<Int>()` keep the loose rule, so Core has two whole-number reads with different answers for `2.0`. The huge-exponent stall stays on both loose reads.
options.technical: Add `fn integer(value: Dyn) -> Int?` to Core/Encoding/Json.jet. It checks the lexeme for `.`, `e` and `E` before valuing it and bounds the result to i64. `.int()` and the Int Decode route stay as they are.

options.name: Keep the compiler library helper
options.detail:
Core stays as it is. The Foundation helper stays the one shared copy for the compiler and Jetpack, and the testkit keeps its own.

User programs get only the loose reads, and the huge-exponent hang stays on both.
options.technical: No Core change. `foundation_json_integer` in Compiler/JetFoundation/Source/Encoding/ProtocolJson.jet stays. JsonSchemaBinder switches to it. Testkit, Tools and user programs cannot reach it.

comparisons.note: `Value::as_i64` returns a number only when the text was an integer inside i64; a typed i64 field refuses `2.0`. Source: docs.rs/serde_json, Value::as_i64.
`json.Number` keeps the text, and `Int64()` parses it as an integer, so `2.0` is an error. Unmarshal into an int field refuses `2.0` too. Source: pkg.go.dev/encoding/json.
`JsonElement.GetInt64` throws for `2.0`, and `TryGetInt64` returns false. Source: learn.microsoft.com, JsonElement.TryGetInt64.
The parser picks the type from the text: `2` becomes an int and `2.0` becomes a float. Source: docs.python.org/3/library/json.html.
comparisons.code:
json.loads("2.0")  # 2.0, a float
json.loads("2")    # 2, an int

recommendation.why: A keeps the one spelling Jet already has, `.int()`, and gives it the rule the best libraries use. It removes all three copies, and no input can make it hang.
gains: One whole-number read, `.int()`, strict like serde_json and Go.
Any size of written integer, with a field error naming the reason.
No huge-exponent hang on `.int()` or typed decoding.

losses.loss: Whole numbers written as `2.0` are refused for Int.
losses.mitigation: Producers that write `2.0` mean a float; the error says to read `.float()` or declare the field Float.

whyNot.reason: Two whole-number reads give different answers for `2.0`, and both loose reads still stall on `1e999999`.
User programs keep only the loose reads and the stall.

recommendation.tradeoff: `.int()` and Int fields stop accepting `2.0` and `1e2`. Every reader that wants a whole number gets the strict rule with no new name.

decisions.title: package.jet holds what a dependent needs; project.jet holds how this checkout works
decisions.situation: Today one package.jet can name a package, list other packages, hold profiles, and point at tool lists. A reader cannot tell which lines matter to someone who depends on the package. A root that both names a package and lists others silently skips its own code. The vote decides where the facts of the folder you work in live, now that it is called the project. We recommend a separate project.jet for them.
decisions.gist: Should the folder you work in keep its own facts in project.jet, apart from package.jet?
decisions.lesson: A package is code others can depend on. A project is the folder you work in: its packages, profiles, tools and team rules. Someone who depends on your package never sees your project. Cargo already ignores a dependency's profiles without saying so. A separate project file makes that rule visible.
decisions.story: Mia publishes a text library. Her package.jet holds a release profile and a tool list. A user who adds the library asks whether her profile changes their build. Under A those lines sit in project.jet, which nobody who depends on the library ever reads.
decisions.inWild:
# Cargo.toml at the repo root
[workspace]
members = ["shop", "shared"]

[profile.release]   # read only at the root;
lto = true          # a dependency's profiles are ignored
decisions.detail:
Today. package.jet accepts 25 top-level fields. They mix four kinds of fact: what the package is, what it needs, what it makes, and how this checkout works. The fourth kind is profiles, members, environments, profile defaults and configs. None of it means anything to a consumer, yet it sits beside name and deps in the published file. Research doc, section 2.

Ruling in force. D-MANIFEST-ONE1=A (2026-10-30) made package.jet the one project file, with `members:` and `environments:` as fields and a root without `name:` as a virtual root. The owner then asked on #6368 for a cleaner split and ruled that workspace becomes project. A amends D-MANIFEST-ONE1 and keeps what it won: no env.jet, no workspace.jet, one field syntax.

Bug B1, probe P3. A root package.jet with `name: "p3"`, `members: ["a"]`, an app output and a broken root run.jet. `jet check .` reports only the member, as clean, and `jet run` runs the member's program. Only `jet check run.jet` finds E0107. One file meaning both a package and a group is how this happens.

What A does. One question sorts every fact: would someone who depends on this package need it? Yes goes in package.jet: name, version, deps, outputs, authority, its own policy and lints, data test suites, and which output `jet run` picks. No goes in project.jet. Only this run goes in a flag.

`project.jet` fields under A: `packages:`, `profiles:` (build and test, one namespace), `defaults:` for profiles, `environments:`, `toolchain:` and `overlays:`. It also holds `catalog:` for shared dependency versions, `policy:` as a ceiling over every package, and shared `version`, `edition` and `license`. A package that leaves one of those three out takes the project's, as D-CORE-HEADER1 already says for roots.

Roots under A. The project root is the nearest folder upward with project.jet. Without one, it is the folder of the nearest package.jet, or the lone file's folder. So a one-package program writes no project.jet. If it wants its own profile or tools, its package.jet begins with a `project { … }` carrier. A lone file begins with `package { … }` the same way (D-ECO-INLINEPACKAGE1=A). jet.lock and .jet/ sit at the project root (D-LOCKFILE1, D-WORKSPACE-CMD1).

Edge cases under A. A project.jet with no `packages:` field has one package: the package.jet in its own folder, if any. Projects do not nest: a project.jet inside another project starts its own project. Listing a package that belongs to another project is an error naming both files. Nothing in project.jet is published, and a consumer's build never reads it. The carrier never lists `packages:`, is an error under a project.jet, and is never published.

One settings order under A: stock, then project with its selected profile, then package (source markers, package.jet, build.jet), then deployment layers, then flag. A pin, or a project `forbid`, refuses a conflicting value and names both lines. This replaces three orders in force: D-CONF-MERGE1, D-SETTING-ORDER1 and D-BUILD-REUSESET1's root layer.

Migration under A. `jet fix` moves 22 workspace.jet files, 159 env.jet files, 5 `members:` roots and 38 profile blocks into project.jet. It also moves 22 committed .jet/lock files to jet.lock. 154 env.jet files sit where no package.jet exists and become project.jet files, not nameless packages. A leftover old spelling is an error naming its new home. Counts are git ls-files at e784bb1ffe.

Peers. Cargo enforces the split silently and needs a docs section on root package versus virtual manifest. Go keeps go.mod free of checkout facts and puts multi-module work in go.work. pnpm moved its package list out of package.json into pnpm-workspace.yaml, which also holds shared version catalogs. Gradle has settings.gradle beside each build file. Bazel disabled its WORKSPACE file in Bazel 8 after it grew several jobs.

Research. Docs/research/2026-10-30-project-package-config-today.md maps every file, field and word today, with the peer table. Docs/proposals/project-package-config-2026-10-30.md sections 1, 2, 4 and 6 give the model and four before-and-after projects, including the Jet compiler's own root.

options.name: package.jet for dependents, project.jet for this checkout
options.detail:
Two data files, sorted by one question: would someone who depends on this package need it? The `package.jet` file holds what a package is, needs and makes. The `project.jet` file holds how this checkout works: its packages, profiles, tools, toolchain pin and team policy.

No project.jet means the package folder is the project. Such a package.jet may begin with a `project { … }` carrier, as a lone file may begin with `package { … }`. Nothing in project.jet or the carrier is ever published.
options.technical:
project.jet: packages, profiles, defaults (profile picks), environments, toolchain, overlays, catalog, policy (ceiling), version, edition, license. package.jet drops members, build, test profiles, environments and configs. Root: nearest project.jet upward, else nearest package.jet. A leading `project { … }` carrier in package.jet goes to the project.jet parser.

The carrier cannot list `packages:` or sit under a project.jet, and publish drops it. Settings order: stock, project, package, deployment, flag; pins and forbids cross it. Amends D-MANIFEST-ONE1=A, D-TEST-PROFILE1=A and D-BUILD-REUSESET1=A.

options.name: One package.jet, as ratified today

options.name: project.jet lists the packages only
options.detail:

options.technical: project.jet: packages only. Every other D-MANIFEST-ONE1 field stays in package.jet, including build and test profiles, environments and the root settings layer.

options.name: One top-level package; nested packages are its subpackages
options.detail:
There is only package.jet, and no project. The top-level package.jet is the root package: it has its own code like any package, and it also holds the settings for the whole tree (profiles, environments, toolchain pin, team policy). Any folder below it with its own package.jet is a subpackage, found automatically, so there is no list to keep.

A subpackage says only what it is, needs and makes. Publishing drops the tree settings, so dependents never see them.
options.technical:
Root: the topmost package.jet at or above the working folder, inside the repository. Subpackages: every package.jet below the root, skipping .gitignored folders, .jet and the root's `exclude:` globs. An excluded folder with a package.jet is its own root when you work inside it.

Tree settings (`build:`/`test:` profiles, `environments:`, the `jet:` toolchain pin, policy ceilings, `exclude:`) are legal only in the root. A subpackage that writes one gets a registered error naming the root. `jet publish` strips them from the published manifest.

`members:` and the nameless group root retire. `jet check .` and `jet build` at the root cover the root's own code and every subpackage, so no code is ever skipped. Subpackages depend on each other with path deps as today. Amends D-MANIFEST-ONE1=A (no members list, no virtual root); field names stay as ratified.

comparisons.note: Profiles are read only from the workspace root; a dependency's profiles are ignored. A root Cargo.toml can be a package, a workspace or both. Source: doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/profiles.html and workspaces.html.
go.mod describes the module; go.work, a separate file, groups modules for local work. Source: go.dev/ref/mod#workspaces.
pnpm-workspace.yaml lists packages and shared version catalogs, apart from each package.json. Source: pnpm.io/workspaces and pnpm.io/catalogs.
MODULE.bazel holds identity and deps, BUILD files hold targets, .bazelrc holds named configs. WORKSPACE is disabled by default in Bazel 8. Source: bazel.build/external/migration.

decisions.title: After workspace becomes project: the list is packages:, Jetspace retires, workspace keeps only its Jai meaning
decisions.situation: You ruled that workspace becomes project, because Jai uses workspace for one compilation with its own build options. Other words hang off the old one. The field that lists a root's packages is called members, a ratified name for the whole checked graph is Jetspace, and the editor window is also called a workspace. The vote decides which words follow the rename. We recommend `packages:` for the list, retiring Jetspace, and using workspace only when explaining Jai.
decisions.gist: Which words should follow from renaming workspace to project?
decisions.lesson: A word should name one thing. Jet uses workspace for the repo root, the editor window and, through Jai, one compilation. It also has Jetspace for the checked graph of a whole project, a word no code uses. The project rename is settled; this vote picks the words around it.
decisions.story: Ana reads a Jai tutorial about workspaces and Jet's docs on the same day. Under A, Jet's docs say project for the folder and never use workspace, so Jai's meaning is the only one she meets.
decisions.inWild:
# pnpm-workspace.yaml: the list is called packages
packages:
  - "packages/*"
catalog:
  react: ^18.3.1
decisions.detail:
Today. Workspace means the monorepo root and workspace.jet (D-WORKSPACE-CMD1, D-BUILD-REUSESET1, spec "Workspace overlays"), and the Canvas editor window (Docs/spec/reference/canvas-workspace-architecture.md). In Jai it means one compilation with its own build options (`compiler_create_workspace`). The owner ruled on #6368 that the first meaning becomes project. Research doc, section 3, lists every overloaded word.

Jetspace. D-ECO-ROOTNAME2=D (2026-08-23) named the complete checked graph Jetspace. A tree grep finds it nowhere in code. Under A the graph is simply the project's, so the word retires. D-ECO-ROOTNAME1=I (the root noun is Package) is also superseded by project.

What A does. Project replaces workspace in CLI help, diagnostics, spec and Canvas's `"mode": "workspace"`. The `project.jet` list of packages is `packages:`. No Jet file, field, flag or message uses workspace. Docs use it only to explain Jai: one compilation with its own options, which in Jet is one output under one set of options (D-JAI-CONFIG1).

The two old meanings of `packages:` are gone under A. The old package.jet `packages:` map of output kinds folds into `outputs:`, and env.jet's `packages:` for tools became `tools:` under D-MANIFEST-ONE1. After the cutover, `packages:` in package.jet is an error naming both new homes, and `members:` is an error naming `packages:`, which `jet fix` applies.

Profile keeps one meaning under A: a named BuildOptions or TestProfile. A platform preset in `targets:` says `platform:`, not `profile:`. Target means the platform only, as D-TARGET-ONE1 ruled.

What B does. Only workspace becomes project. The list keeps `members:`, Jetspace stays the ratified name for the checked graph, and Canvas's mode becomes project.

Peers. pnpm's pnpm-workspace.yaml lists `packages:`. Cargo and npm call the list `members` and `workspaces`. Gradle calls each sub-unit a project, which is Jet's package; Jet's docs define project once and keep it. Bazel retired its WORKSPACE file in Bazel 8.

Migration. The words change with D-PROJECT-ROOT1's `jet fix` moves; this ballot adds the Canvas mode rename and a sweep of help, diagnostics and spec text. Amends D-ECO-ROOTNAME1=I, D-ECO-ROOTNAME2=D and D-WORKSPACE1=B.

decisions.title: fn build, fn test and fn dev live in build.jet, test.jet and dev.jet beside package.jet
decisions.situation: A package's build, test and dev code is a function that runs on the developer's machine, with powers such as running programs and writing files. Today it may sit in any file of the package, and the compiler finds it by searching. In Jet's own tree it sits in at least six differently named files. The vote decides whether each of these functions gets one fixed file. We recommend build.jet, test.jet and dev.jet beside package.jet.
decisions.gist: Should `fn build`, `fn test` and `fn dev` each live in one fixed file beside package.jet?
decisions.lesson: Build code runs before your program exists, with the power to run tools and write files. A reviewer should see from a file list that build code changed. Cargo's build.rs, Zig's build.zig and Bazel's BUILD files each give build code one fixed name for this reason.
decisions.story: Raj's package keeps `fn build` in util.jet, among ordinary helpers. A new teammate edits util.jet without knowing that part of it runs at build time and can run programs. Under A the build lives only in build.jet, so its file name says what it is.
decisions.inWild:
my-crate/
├── Cargo.toml
├── build.rs      # the build script; Cargo looks only here
└── src/main.rs
decisions.detail:
Today. D-CONF-ENTRY1=A (2026-08-06): one `fn build` per package, in any of its files, found by the compiler. D-BUILDSCOPE1=A (2026-07-19) said the unit's definition file instead. A census of top-level entries finds them in main.jet (55 files), run.jet (36), build.jet (25), workspace.jet (3), package.jet (3) and others.

Searching has costs. Examples/features/tooling/build_entry_discovery needs a README to say where its build lives. Two `fn build` in one package give two codes for one mistake: E0105 from `jet check` and E3520 from `jet build` (bug B3, probe P5).

What A does. `fn build(b: Build)` lives in build.jet, `fn test(t: Test)` in test.jet and `fn dev(d: Dev)` in dev.jet, each beside its package.jet. One of each per package, as today. A program run as one file, with or without a `package { }` block, keeps every entry in that file. Both data files, package.jet and project.jet, hold values only.

Edge cases under A. An entry in any other file of a package is a registered error naming its home, and `jet fix` moves it. Build code can still be split: build.jet imports ordinary modules and calls their functions. project.jet has no entry; a project builds its packages in dependency order (D-WORKSPACE-CMD1). A bundle made from several packages is an output of a small package that depends on them.

No new names are taken. A module already cannot be called build.jet, test.jet or dev.jet (JetCli/Source/Cli/Entry.jet:72-74).

Migration. 38 entries outside their home move: 21 in run.jet, 8 in main.jet, 3 in package.jet, 2 in tools/build_entry.jet and 4 others. Each stays in the same package, so its names still resolve. The 29 already in place and the 104 in one-file programs do not move.

Under every option, `jet new --template overrides` stubs are rewritten to D-ENTRY-SHAPE1's shape: the entry sets values, then the stock work runs once. Today they say "replace the stock default" (Host.jet:1514-1516).

What C does. The entry sits inside package.jet, as D-BUILDSCOPE1 said for pkg.jet. Then reading any field means compiling the file, so `jet env`, editors and policy checks must run project code (D-JPK-DEVCOMPOSE1 keeps them from doing that).

Peers. Cargo build.rs, Zig build.zig, Gradle build.gradle.kts, Bazel BUILD and Jai first.jai or build.jai each give build code one known file. None of them finds it by searching a package. Amends D-CONF-ENTRY1=A and D-BUILDSCOPE1=A.

decisions.title: One b.add call adds any output; each add_* helper is a one-line wrapper over it; generated code is a source value
decisions.situation: In a build, a package adds what it makes through nine helper calls such as `add_executable`. No single call adds any kind of output, so a library cannot hand back outputs for the caller to add. Generated code is passed by typing its path inside Jet's cache folder. The vote decides the build API's basic calls and how its helpers relate to them. We recommend one `b.add` call for any output, each helper one line over it, and generated code passed as a value.
decisions.gist: Should one `b.add` call add any output, with each `add_*` helper a one-line wrapper over it?
decisions.lesson: A primitive is the one call that can do everything. A wrapper is a short helper for a common case, built from the primitive. Good APIs offer both and let you see how a wrapper expands. Jai gives build code primitives only; Jet's build API today has only helpers.
decisions.story: Lee writes a web helper library that makes a browser output for each game. Today it must take the build handle and call `add_executable` for every name. Under A it returns the outputs, and the caller adds them with `b.add(...web.targets("game", "editor"))`.
decisions.detail:
Today. D-BUILD-CORE1=A (2026-10-22) made Build an ordinary Core type with nine `add_*` methods. Each takes a name and sources, then labelled options. The checker does not have that contract yet. Every label is E0764, `b.action` takes "5 or 7 to 15" positional arguments, and `add_*` takes "3 to 7" (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/Build.jet:94-96, 148).

D-TARGET-ONE1=A made one output list, written as data (`outputs:`) or code, with nine closed kinds. D-BUILD-GENVALUE1=A made generated code a `Generated` value. Sources still name its file under .jet/generated, as Examples/features/tooling/build_write_generated does.

What A adds. `b.add(outputs: ...Output) -> [Output]` adds outputs of any kind code may make. Each `add_*` becomes an ordinary Core function whose body is one `b.add` call. Its doc comment shows the expansion, and `jet explain` prints it. A wrapper has no power the primitive lacks. A `Generated` value is accepted anywhere a source path is.

One set of values. An `outputs:` entry in package.jet is the literal form of the value `b.add` takes, so a fact moves between data and code unchanged. The wrapper and the primitive build the identical plan, and `jet inspect build` cannot tell them apart.

Sources. The wrappers take sources as D-CALL-VARTAIL1 decides. Under its A they are a variadic tail: `b.add_executable("app", "run.jet", "util.jet", deps: [log])`. Otherwise they are a list, as D-BUILD-CORE1 ratified. This ballot does not depend on that vote, and the examples here use the list form.

Edge cases under A. Output names stay unique across data and code; a duplicate is a registered error naming both lines (D-TARGET-ONE1). Environment, Image, System and Fleet stay data only, because `jet env` and deploy never run code. So `b.add` refuses those four kinds with an error that names `outputs:`. `b.add` with no outputs returns an empty list.

Peers. SwiftPM builds one Package value from target values made by factories like `.executableTarget`. Bazel macros are functions over native rules. Zig gives `b.addExecutable` beside the raw step graph. Jai gives primitives only, so every Jai project rewrites the same message loop (Docs/audits/jai-parity-2026-10-16.md).

Amends D-BUILD-CORE1=A: adds `b.add` and Generated as a source; the wrappers keep its names and labels. Proposal section 5 has the full primitive list and the argument rules.

Review. Author: Claude (SurfaceDesign lane). No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft.

decisions.title: Label-only parameters may follow a variadic parameter, written after `*`
decisions.situation: A variadic parameter collects any number of trailing arguments, written `parts: ...String`. Today it must be the last parameter. So a function cannot take a run of items and also a named option, such as a separator or a list of dependencies. Callers wrap the items in brackets instead. The vote decides whether label-only parameters may follow a variadic. We recommend allowing them after the `*` marker that already means label-only.
decisions.gist: May label-only parameters follow a variadic parameter, written after `*`?
decisions.lesson: A variadic parameter, `parts: ...String`, gathers the remaining bare arguments into a list. A label-only parameter must be passed with its name, like `sep: "-"`, and is declared after a `*`. Allowing one after the other lets a single call take items typed inline plus named options.
decisions.story: Sam writes a `join` that glues words together. He wants `join("a", "b", "c", sep: "-")`. Today Jet refuses that declaration, so callers write `join(["a", "b", "c"], sep: "-")`. Under A his first spelling works.
decisions.detail:
Today. D-VARIADIC1 puts a variadic in final position (E1310). S61 makes parameters after `*` label-only (E0769). Probe v1 declares `fn f(name: String, sources: ...String, *, deps: [String]{[]})` and gets E1310, "Variadic parameter `sources` must be last". Probe v2 moves the variadic after `*`, and the call `g("app", "run.jet", deps: ["core"])` gets E0769 for both `deps` and `sources`.

Why it matters. Jet's call rules make every required input positional, a run of items a variadic tail, and every option labelled (S61, D-CALLPOS1, D-VARIADIC1). Today one function cannot have both a variadic and options. Core has only 2 variadic functions, partly for this reason.

The cases that need it are common: build helpers with `deps:`, `join` with `sep:`, and a logger taking fields as a variadic tail with `level:`. Without it, authors fall back to list parameters or sibling names.

What A does. A parameter list may continue after a variadic only with `*` and label-only parameters. Binding is D-CALLPOS1 unchanged. Bare arguments before the first label fill the leading parameters, and the variadic takes the rest. Labels bind the options. A bare argument after a label stays E0768.

Edge cases under A. Spread works as today: `join(...words, sep: "-")`. A label-only parameter after the variadic may be required; leaving it out is the usual missing-argument error. A parameter after a variadic without `*` stays E1310, whose fix now says to add `*`. A variadic declared after `*` keeps today's meaning and is label-only.

Types. Zones are already part of a function's type (S61), so function values and interface methods bind the same way. No new syntax is added: `*` and `...T` both exist.

Templates. D-META-PARAMS1's `fn $name(...$params)` pastes every parameter with its zone, so a pasted list keeps the variadic, the `*` and the options in order.

Nothing breaks. Every declaration accepted today keeps its meaning, since the new form was E1310 before. No caller changes.

What B does. As in Python, every parameter after a variadic is label-only without writing `*`, and the variadic opens the label-only zone. The API proposal for card 6367 preferred this form. This ballot recommends `*` so the declaration shows which parameters need labels.

What C does. Today's rule stays. Options go before the variadic and are passed bare and first, or the items become a list parameter.

Peers. Python's keyword-only arguments (PEP 3102) follow `*args`. Swift requires the parameter after a variadic to have an argument label. Kotlin passes parameters after a vararg by name.

Amends D-VARIADIC1 (final position) and S61's E1310 text. Review. Author: Claude (SurfaceDesign lane). No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft.
