decisions.title: Environments v3: static data by default, an expert env entry point with full control, one model up to JetOS
decisions.situation: You asked for a Jet-flavored devenv that replaces Nix and devenv. The default stays simple static configuration, and experts opt in to an env entry point with a full env API. This version keeps static `environments:` in the root package.jet as the default. An env.jet entry and the `core.env` API give experts full control, and one module model scales to JetOS.
decisions.gist: Should environments be static data by default, with an opt-in env.jet entry point and a full core.env API for experts?
decisions.lesson: A development environment says what a machine has: tools, languages, services, variables and scripts. Most projects can list these as data. Some need logic, such as picking a free port or a tool per system, so a code entry point gives full control.
decisions.story: Ada lists Node and Postgres in package.jet and runs `jet dev`; nothing else is needed. Her teammate on a Mac needs a different container tool and a free port. He adds env.jet, changes two values through `core.env`, and `jet env show` prints the result.
decisions.detail:
What you asked. Static configuration stays the easy default. Experts opt in to an env entry point with an env API and full control. Modules and the path to a whole JetOS machine stay.

The ladder. Rung one is `environments:` data in the root package.jet. Rung two is modules in `include:`. Rung three is env.jet with `env :: fn(e: &Env)`, which receives the applied data and can change anything. This matches build and test (philosophy.md pillar 4).

What already exists for A. D-ECO-DECL1 makes environments, services and systems typed values. D-ECO-EXTENSION1 makes an extension an ordinary typed function. D-ECO-COMPOSE2 combines modules without order and stops on a clash. Services, presets and the flake bridge exist (jetpack-epoch5.md:359-428).

Where it lives. Under D-PROJECT-ROOT1 D, the root package.jet holds `environments:` and `systems:`. env.jet sits beside it. dev.jet keeps the `dev` loop, as D-ENTRY-HOME1 places it.

Trust. Static data and pure modules run nothing, so Jet shows and locks them before any trust prompt. env.jet is code. Its effect row is shown in the trust prompt, and it runs only after you approve it.

options.name: Static data by default; env.jet and core.env give experts full control
options.detail:
The default is static data. The root package.jet lists each environment: tools, languages, services, processes, variables, scripts and git hooks. `include:` adds modules, which are values or pure functions such as `devkit.node(version: "22")`. Modules combine without order, and a clash stops the build naming both lines. Most projects stop here.

`jet dev`, or entering the folder with the opt-in shell hook, applies the data. No code is needed.

The expert opt-in is env.jet with `env :: fn(e: &Env)`. Jet calls it for each environment after applying the data. `e` holds the whole environment, and the `core.env` API can read, add, remove or change any part. It can also run commands, pick ports and add logic on entering the shell.

The same model scales up. A `System` value in `systems:` uses the same modules for a JetOS machine, and `system :: fn(s: &System)` is the same opt-in.
options.technical:
`Environment` keeps `tools`, `services` and `git_hooks_path`, and gains `include`, `languages`, `processes`, `vars`, `scripts` and `hooks`. Existing values keep their meaning.

`core.env` is ordinary Jet in Core (pillar 5): `Env` and `System` with handles for each part, plus `on_enter`, `run`, `fs` and `net`. The entry's effect row bounds what it may do.

Order: static data and modules are merged and locked, then `env(e)` runs, then services and processes start. `jet env show` prints the final value and the line that set each field.

System activation belongs to the JetOS track; this vote fixes that it shares the model.

options.name: Static data and modules only; no entry point (v2)
options.detail:
The previous version of this ballot. Environments are static data with modules, applied by default, and the same modules reach JetOS. `dev` in dev.jet runs after setup but cannot change the environment.

Logic that depends on the machine, such as a free port or a per-OS tool, has no place in Jet.
options.technical: As A without env.jet or `core.env`. Modules must be pure, so no module can read the machine.

options.name: The env entry point builds every environment
options.detail:
env.jet's `env :: fn(e: &Env)` builds every environment through `core.env`, and package.jet has no `environments:` field. Experts have full control.

Every project writes code, even one that needs only Node. Jet must run that code before it can show the setup, so even a simple project starts with a trust prompt.
options.technical: `core.env` as in A, with an empty starting value. Reopens D-MANIFEST-ONE1 A.

comparisons.note: Modules of static options; custom logic is Nix expressions over them. Source: devenv.sh/basics.
A shell per system from mkShell; logic is Nix code, with no services or processes. Source: nixos.wiki/wiki/Flakes.
A whole machine from modules with options and conditions; clashes are settled by priorities such as mkForce. Source: nixos.org/manual/nixos.
Static tools, variables and tasks per folder, applied on cd; logic is shell in tasks. Source: mise.jdx.dev.
comparisons.code:
# Simple: mise.toml
[tools]
node = "22"

# Complex: mise.toml
[tools]
node = "22"
python = "3.12"
[env]
DATABASE_URL = "postgres://127.0.0.1:5432/shop"
_.python.venv = { path = ".venv", create = true }
[tasks.setup]
run = "test -d .venv || python -m venv .venv"

comparisons.note: Services as static data with profiles and health checks; logic lives in images and scripts. Source: docs.docker.com/compose.
comparisons.code:
# Simple
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16

# Complex
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    ports: ["${DB_PORT:-5432}:5432"]
    healthcheck: { test: ["CMD", "pg_isready"], interval: 2s }
  web:
    build: .
    depends_on: { db: { condition: service_healthy } }
    profiles: [dev]

decisions.title: Empty text for reuse: assignment only, or a clear method too?
decisions.situation: A program can empty text by assigning the empty string, but String has no clear method like lists do. The compiler work can reuse existing storage without adding a method. This vote asks whether that familiar assignment is enough, or whether the library should also offer a named operation. Both choices produce identical text.
decisions.gist: Keep empty-string assignment alone, or also offer String.clear()?
decisions.lesson: String is Jet's text type. The empty string is written "". Capacity is space already reserved for later text. A reusable destination can keep that space when emptied; neither option promises that later text of any size will fit.
decisions.explainer:
Beginner path: write out = "", then append with +=; no new rule is needed. Expert path: pass an initialized destination as out:&String and &text at the call, or work with an initialized String field. & permits changes to the caller's existing storage. B also permits &out.clear(), a method call with explicit write permission. It changes the same destination to empty text.

Shared work: keep eligible capacity reuse as a compiler optimization, independent of this API choice. Refilling within retained capacity need not grow the destination; growing beyond it can allocate. The caller's retained storage is a real input, not an output-only dummy value. This vote does not change lists or introduce another text type.
decisions.story: Sam rebuilds a short display line each frame using the same text storage. He wants to empty it before appending the next line.
decisions.detail:
The predecessor attributes capacity reuse to .agent-worktrees/perfalloc, card #4566 slices 4 and 7b. Source inspection confirms crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/MIRRust.rs:17663-17667 recognizes a single-use empty literal into an eligible place; :19664 emits clear(). Compiler/JetCodegen/Source/Emit/Operations.jet:3098-3100 uses empty_text_or_list, appendable_place and always_initialized_place for the corresponding source emitter. Its initialization predicate is at :3375-3378. These references are within that worktree.

These source facts establish an optimization in those emitters, not a capacity guarantee for every tier or assignment. Bare locals can be uninitialized at a write, so the inspected scope excludes them. Other paths must retain the same text values. No cross-tier allocation or timing result was exercised here.

The predecessor reports E0311 for String.clear(), but this drafter did not rerun it. Tools/perf/function-boundary/list-reuse/main.jet:5-7 shows &out.clear() and &out.push(...) for lists. The predecessor's future proof-log path is not a measurement receipt. No timing numbers or claim that a queued proof passed is retained.

Decision audit: D-CORE-ONE-NAME1=A deletes duplicate public function aliases, not ordinary assignment syntax. D-CORE-STRING-HOME1=A places String behavior in Core. D-OUTPUT-RETURNS1=A preserves real reusable capacity while prohibiting output-only public dummy arguments. A adds no public API and is implementation work under those contracts. B adds a discovery-oriented method, not a foreign-name alias of another public String function.

If the owner considers B barred by the one-mechanism rule, it asks for that narrow exception rather than claiming prior approval. The ballot decides only the optional new method. It is not a gate for the optimization.

Both functions empty an initialized, caller-owned String and append "ab". Any previous text becomes "ab". Neither returns a second String, changes ownership, or affects lists. Both helpers are called refill(&text). Retained capacity is real storage input under the returned-results policy. No new memory-safety rule or uninitialized destination is admitted.

options.name: Use the existing assignment
options.detail: Add no String method. Teach empty-string assignment and appending. The compiler may keep eligible initialized storage without changing the resulting value. Beginners keep familiar code; experts reuse an existing destination.
options.technical: No syntax or Core API addition. Keep the existing String = empty-literal value contract; permit capacity-preserving lowering only when the destination is proved initialized and the transformation preserves all observable behavior. The inspected implementation handles eligible write parameters and initialized local fields, with a single-use empty literal. Do not advertise that every bare-local assignment or every tier already retains capacity. List.clear remains unchanged and outside this ballot; no later list retirement is promised.

options.name: Also offer a clear method
options.detail: Keep assignment and add one named String operation, matching how lists expose emptying. Both spellings make the text empty. Beginners may discover it through method help; experts may explicitly request clearing initialized storage.
options.technical:
Propose String.clear with a write receiver and Unit result. &out.clear() removes every character, preserves reusable capacity, and requires ordinary exclusive write permission. It allocates no replacement buffer merely to empty the value. Add it through String's canonical Core owner, not a second Rust-only owner. All execution paths must implement this contract and diagnose ownership consistently.

This is a discovery addition, not an alternative claimed to beat assignment; no speed benefit is asserted. If proposed for speed, AGENTS.md:165-168 requires a registered candidate/plain pair and strict measured win before ratification. Confirm any required narrow one-mechanism exception explicitly.

comparisons.note: Rust names the operation String::clear. This is a syntax comparison, not an execution or speed receipt.

recommendation.why: A keeps the spelling people already use. Storage reuse does not need another library method.
gains: No new method to learn or support.
Capacity reuse stays independent of API choice.

losses.loss: Method help cannot list a named String clear operation.
losses.mitigation: Teach empty assignment beside appending in String's reuse example and in help for mutating text.

whyNot.reason: Method discovery is useful, but it adds another way to empty the same text without a demonstrated speed benefit.

recommendation.tradeoff: Prefer familiar assignment over a discoverable extra method; preserve honest, scoped reuse documentation.

decisions.checkInstructions:
Run Tower's ballot validator before posting. This drafter ran that validator only, not compiler programs, tests or benchmarks. The optimization is not awaiting API ratification. After integration, exercise initialized write-parameter/local-field clearing, unchanged bare-local values, append growth, alias rejection and all execution paths.

Use PerfAlloc's complete canonical string-reuse/plain pair for performance evidence. Require the applicable strict gate, not the predecessor's at-or-below comparison. If B is ratified, update Core String, adapters, diagnostics/help, callers/examples and API tests together. If B becomes performance-motivated, require a strict candidate/plain win before ratification.

decisions.title: How a function changes module-level state
decisions.situation: A module value is a name written at the top of a file that every function can see. Today any function can change a plain one, although the owner ruled that only `#Persist` values may be changed that way. Every task sees module values, so two tasks changing one at once silently lose updates. The vote decides how functions change module state. We recommend a module link, `HITS :: @0`, with raw writes only in audited unsafe code.
decisions.gist: May a function write a plain module `:=`, or must module state a function changes be a visible `@` link?
decisions.lesson: A module value is one name every function and every task can see. Changing it from two tasks at once can lose updates. A link, written `@`, is Jet's one form for a value many holders share. When a link reaches another task, each statement on it is one locked step, so no update is lost. Whichever option wins, the checker and the spec must agree.
decisions.story: Ana counts page hits in a module `hits := 0` and bumps it from each request handler. Her server runs handlers as tasks. Under A, the build tells her to write `HITS :: @0`, her handlers keep `HITS += 1`, and the count is right under load. Under B her code builds as written and loses about one hit in five under load.
decisions.detail:
What Jet does today. A plain module `hits := 0` written from a function compiles and runs on every tier. Probe a23 prints 4 for `counter += 1` on 3. The checker treats any module `:=` as writable storage (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Statements.jet:4089-4093).

What the rulings say. D-PERSIST-DEVSTATE1=A (owner ruling 2026-08-20, syntax-decisions.md:8038-8045) makes `#Persist` the one module binding a function may write. Every other module binding is E0111. D-LIVE1=A (2026-09-02, :9978-9979) repeats it. The older D-ENTRY-SCRIPT1 text at :354-356 and spec.md:253-254 and :486 still call the plain form writable. Examples/features/basics/script_run.jet teaches that write. The newer owner ruling wins, so the code is the drift. This vote settles the law the code then follows.

Why it matters beyond style. Every task sees module state. Probe a24 runs four tasks that each add 1 to a plain module `counter := 0` 100000 times. It printed 322945, not 400000, so about one update in five was silently lost. The same workload through today's built holder, `shared Hits{count: 0}` with `HITS.count += 1`, printed 400000 (probe a25).

A module `::` holding a `shared` value is legal and runs today (probe a31 prints 5). Probe a28 found that a module-level `Cell` also loses updates across tasks. That is a separate defect in Cell's task-boundary rule, not part of this vote.

Who writes module `:=` from a function today (census 2026-10-30, same-file writes, $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/LiveUI/p3/modvar.mjs). The runtime has 59 globals in 41 files of Compiler/JetRuntime: allocator, scheduler, TLS keys, host roots and test hooks. Init functions in .init_array or expert hooks write them, and hot paths read them. The runtime already holds 351 `#Unsafe` blocks in 81 files.

Jetpack has 14 sequence counters (Store, Provider, Nix, Environment) that name temporary files. There is one example (basics/script_run.jet) and one test case (run_entry/module_globals_and_explicit_run_keep_statement_order). Compiler/JetSema/Tests/ScalarGlobalFixtures.jet has six writes. Eight `#Persist` sites are already legal under every option.

How A migrates. The 59 runtime writes move inside `#Unsafe("…")` blocks, and most already sit in one. The generated code does not change. The 14 Jetpack counters become module links such as `SEQ :: @0`, which also stops two tasks from taking the same temporary name. The example, case and fixtures use a link or `#Unsafe`, matching what each one teaches.

How B and C migrate. Under B nothing migrates, and the D-PERSIST-DEVSTATE1 and D-LIVE1 sentences change to say `#Persist` only adds survival across reload. Under C all 81 sites become `#Persist`. The runtime's scheduler, TLS and allocator roots then enter the reload store.

Beginner path under A. A beginner who writes `hits += 1` from a function gets E0111, and its fix rewrites the declaration to `HITS :: @0`. Every write site stays `HITS += 1`. A fixed `::` link can never point elsewhere, so assigning to its name can only write the value it points at. Adding `#Persist` keeps the value across a reload, and leaving it off resets it like every module value.

Expert path under A. Code that needs a raw word with no lock, such as the runtime's allocator root, writes it inside `#Unsafe("reason")`. That is the existing audited escape hatch (I1). No new keyword, marker or type is added.

One meaning on every tier (I9). Under A the check is in sema, so o0, o1, o2 and web reject the same programs with the same E0111. An `#Unsafe` write lowers to the same IR global store as today, so the runtime pack's code does not change.

Performance. A changes no generated code in the runtime or for any `#Unsafe` write. D-MEMREF-TASK1=A sets the cost of a link. A link no task reaches is a plain word with no lock. A link another task reaches takes one lock per statement, and the build reports which. `#Local` or `#Shared` pins the choice.

Paired-cell plan for the gauntlet. Cell one compares `HITS += 1` on a module link that tasks reach with Rust `static HITS: Mutex<i64>` and Go `sync.Mutex`. Cell two compares the same link in a program with no tasks against a C `static long`. Cell three compares an `#Unsafe` module write with a Rust `static mut` write. Each cell must beat or match the peer before the change lands, and any loss is carded.

Rust. Writing a `static mut` needs `unsafe`, and the 2024 edition denies references to it by default (`static_mut_refs`). The documented safe forms are atomics, `Mutex` and `OnceLock`. Source: doc.rust-lang.org/edition-guide/rust-2024/static-mut-references.html.

Swift 6. A global `var` is an error: "not concurrency-safe because it is nonisolated global shared mutable state". The fixes are `let`, an actor, or `nonisolated(unsafe)`. Source: swift.org Swift 6 concurrency migration guide, common problems.

Go, Python, Zig and C. Go package variables are freely writable, and the race detector finds races only at run time. Uber's PLDI 2022 study reports about 2,000 data races found in its Go code in six months (arxiv.org/abs/2204.00764). Python needs an explicit `global name` line before a function may rebind a module name. Zig and C leave globals freely writable with no protection.

What to borrow. Take Rust's split: safe state goes through a synchronized holder, and raw writes need the audited escape hatch. Take Python's rule that changing module state is visible at the declaration.

What to avoid. Avoid Go's and Zig's silent races. Avoid Kotlin/Native's old model, which froze top-level objects and was dropped in Kotlin 1.7.20 after wide friction (kotlinlang.org/docs/native-memory-manager.html). A never freezes anything; it only asks for the `@` link Jet already ratified. Avoid Swift 6's migration shock: E0111's fix writes the link, and the repository migrates in the same change.

Spelling. D-MEMREF1=A (2026-09-28) chose `@` for every shared live value and retires the `Shared<T>` spelling, with `View`, `Cell` and `Pin`. The `shared` keyword is still the only built holder today, and it needs a struct: `TICKS :: shared 0` with `TICKS += 1` is E0111 (probe a26). A lands with the module slice of the link build. Until then, E0111's fix writes today's `shared` struct holder, and `jet fix` respells it as `@` when links land.

options.name: Change module state through an `@` link
options.detail:
A function may read any module value but may not write a plain module `:=`; that write is E0111. Module state that functions change is a link: `HITS :: @0`. Functions write it as `HITS += 1`, and each statement on a link that tasks reach is one locked step, so no update is lost.

`#Persist` keeps working and still adds survival across a reload. Expert code may write a plain module `:=` inside `#Unsafe("reason") { … }`, the existing audited escape hatch.
options.technical:
Sema rejects an assignment to a non-`#Persist` module binding from a function body with E0111, unless the write sits inside an `#Unsafe` block. A fixed `::` link cannot be re-pointed, so assignment to its name writes its target. Storage follows D-MEMREF-TASK1=A: plain when no task reaches the link, one lock per statement when one does. `#Transact` groups several statements. An `#Unsafe` write lowers to today's IR global store.

Migration: 59 runtime writes move inside `#Unsafe` blocks, and 14 Jetpack counters become links. One example, one case and six fixtures are rewritten. The spec sentences at spec.md:253-254 and :486 and syntax-decisions.md:354-356 are corrected in the same change.

options.name: Plain module `:=` stays writable
options.detail: Any function may write a plain module `:=`, as the code does today. `#Persist` only adds survival across a reload. The owner rulings that say otherwise are amended to match the code. Nothing in the repository changes.
options.technical: No checker change. D-PERSIST-DEVSTATE1 and D-LIVE1 text change to "`#Persist` is the module binding that survives a reload and can be lent with `&`". Writes from several tasks stay unsynchronized plain stores.

options.name: Only `#Persist` is writable, everywhere
options.detail: Apply the owner ruling as written: a function may write only a `#Persist` module value. Every other write is E0111, and every current writer becomes `#Persist`, including the runtime's scheduler, thread and allocator roots.
options.technical: Sema rejects any non-`#Persist` module write. 81 sites gain `#Persist`. Scalar `#Persist` values are kept in the reload store, so the runtime's roots join it, and writes from several tasks stay unsynchronized.

comparisons.note: A `static mut` write needs `unsafe`; the 2024 edition denies references to it. Safe module state uses `Mutex`, atomics or `OnceLock`. Source: doc.rust-lang.org/edition-guide/rust-2024/static-mut-references.html.
comparisons.code:
static HITS: Mutex<i64> = Mutex::new(0);
fn bump() { *HITS.lock().unwrap() += 1; }

comparisons.note: A top-level `var` is a compile error under strict concurrency; fixes are `let`, an actor, or `nonisolated(unsafe)`. Source: swift.org Swift 6 migration guide, common problems.
A function must declare `global hits` before rebinding a module name; otherwise the write makes a new local.
comparisons.code:
hits = 0
def bump():
    global hits
    hits += 1

comparisons.note: Package variables are freely writable; races are caught only at run time by the race detector. Uber reports about 2,000 races found in six months (PLDI 2022, arxiv.org/abs/2204.00764).
comparisons.code:
var hits int
func bump() { hits++ } // races under goroutines

recommendation.why: A keeps the owner's rule that functions do not silently change module values. It uses the one ratified form for shared values, the `@` link, which never loses an update and costs nothing when no task reaches it. The runtime keeps its exact code through the audited unsafe escape hatch.
gains: Two tasks never lose an update to module state.
A beginner adds one `@` and keeps every write as written.
A program without tasks pays no lock.
Uses only ratified forms: `@`, `#Persist` and `#Unsafe`.
The runtime's generated code does not change.

whyNot.reason: B keeps a silent data race in the simplest program shape: four tasks lost one update in five.
C pushes the runtime's scheduler and thread state into the reload store and still races.

recommendation.tradeoff: A lands with the module slice of the `@` link build. Until then E0111's fix writes today's `shared` struct holder, which `jet fix` respells as `@`.

decisions.title: A record is its database table, and migrations are derived and reviewed
decisions.situation: Programs that store data describe each table twice: once as a Jet record and once as SQL text. Queries return loose rows that code reads by column name, and changes need hand-written SQL steps. This vote picks where a table's shape lives. We recommend the record: Jet derives the table, typed queries and a reviewed migration file.
decisions.gist: Should a Jet record declare its database table, with typed queries and derived migrations?
decisions.lesson: A migration changes a stored table, for example renaming a column. If the program's record and the table can drift apart, bugs appear at run time. Tools like Prisma keep one schema, compare it with the database, and write the change as a file you review.
decisions.story: Sam renames `mail` to `email` in the `User` record and marks the old name. `jet db plan` writes a migration that renames the column. A query that still says `mail` fails to compile.
decisions.detail:
Today. Queries return [[String: DBValue]] (Core/Db/Db.jet:732) and code reads columns by name (row_int, line 138). Migrations are lists of SQL text: migrate(scope, name, steps: [SQL]) at line 941. The #SQL(row:) marker names a row type for a block (Compiler/Prelude/Markers.jet:192) but checks no columns.

What A says. #Table on a record declares its table, with #Key, #Unique and #Index on fields. Typed select returns [User]. `jet db plan` compares the stored schema with the records and writes a migration file to review. A rename uses #Rename(from:), which reuses the existing #Rename marker.

Option B keeps SQL as the source and checks query results against a record. It suits teams who write SQL first. Option C keeps today's steps and adds nothing.

Cost. SQL text is built while building, and rows decode by column position, not by a name lookup. Row policies and the DB.AllRows effect (D-SQL-HANDLER1) apply unchanged.

Research: Docs/research/declarative-jet-2026-10-31.md (GoldC lane, dev 68c87ae07b).

Review. Author: Claude (GoldC lane). No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft yet.

decisions.title: One way to declare things across Jet: typed values, traits that derive code, and one view
decisions.situation: You asked for Jet to be declarative everywhere: hardware, foreign code, builds, data, screens and tests. Today each area reads its descriptions its own way, so the same idea has four readers and four sets of rules. This vote picks one shape for every description. We recommend plain typed values that the compiler reads while building, with derived code you can always print.
decisions.gist: Should every declared thing in Jet be a typed value read while building, with derived code you can print?
decisions.lesson: A declaration says what is true, like a board's pins or a table's columns. The tool then writes the code that follows from it. Jet already has typed values, build-time evaluation, markers that generate code, and a view that prints generated code. The question is whether every area must use those same parts.
decisions.story: Mia ships a sensor board. She writes the board once as a value. The compiler derives the linker regions, the pin drivers and the vector table, and it refuses a pin used twice. She runs `jet inspect expand` and sees every derived line next to the board line it came from.
decisions.detail:
Today. Jet reads its descriptions in four ways. The board is a record of plain text fields (Jetpack/Provider/Batteries/embedded/embedded.jet:22-42). package.jet is read by 54 hand-written text scanners (Jetpack/PackageModel/Source/Manifest). Environment modules have their own evaluator (Jetpack/EnvModel/Source/ModuleEval). Codec traits are known only inside the compiler (Compiler/JetSema/Source/Sema/Calls/Methods.jet:333).

What A says. A declaration is a typed constant, evaluated by the one build-time evaluator that `prep` uses. A Core trait names what it derives, such as a board's drivers or a table's queries. A marker or a `use` line runs the derive. `jet inspect expand` prints each derived item with its source line, as D-MARKER-EXPAND1 already ratified.

Why no new keyword. Every part of A is already ratified: markers that derive (D-MARKER-DECL1), build-time branches (D-PREP-BRANCH1), binders as packages (D-FFI-BINDER1), facts (D-BUILD-FACT3) and traits for every list (D-EXTEND-ARCH1). The research note walks eleven areas and finds each one expressible with these parts.

Option B adds a `declare` keyword with its own block form. It reads nicely in small files. It is a second way to write a value, so tools, the formatter and errors must learn it.

Option C keeps each area's own file format, such as devicetree for boards and TOML for settings. Each format gets its own reader and its own errors. Nothing ties a board file to the code that uses it.

Research: Docs/research/declarative-jet-2026-10-31.md (GoldC lane, dev 68c87ae07b).

Review. Author: Claude (GoldC lane). No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft yet.

decisions.title: Chips, boards, registers and interrupts as typed Jet values, read from vendor files
decisions.situation: Firmware talks to a chip through registers at fixed addresses. Today Jet's one board is a record of text, and its registers are plain numbers with nothing checked. This vote picks how a chip and a board are described. We recommend typed Jet values, generated from the vendor's chip file, so a wrong register write fails to compile.
decisions.gist: How should Jet describe a chip, its registers and a board, so wrong hardware use fails to compile?
decisions.lesson: A chip vendor publishes a file listing every register, its address, its bit fields and whether it can be written. Tools can turn that file into typed code. A board then says which pins and parts of the chip it uses. Jet ratified typed target profiles and hardware descriptions but has not built them.
decisions.story: Leo writes `uart.state.tx_full.write(true)` by mistake. The build stops: the field is read-only on this chip. He also tries to use pin A5 for two things, and the build names both lines.
decisions.detail:
Today. The only board is embedded.board() in Jetpack/Provider/Batteries/embedded/embedded.jet:64. Its memory kind, access, linker, allocator and panic fields are all text (lines 7-42). Registers are plain U32 fields (lines 133-162). The #Interrupt marker exists (Compiler/Prelude/Markers.jet:184), but the battery says no vector table seam exists (embedded.jet:255-257).

What is ratified. Typed profile modules (D-TARGET-SURFACE1), checked memory regions (D-TARGET-MEMORY1), linker input generated from facts (D-TARGET-LINKER1), and hardware descriptions that packages extend (D-HOST-CAPS1). This vote picks the library shape that builds them.

What A says. `core.hw` has chip, peripheral, register, field, pin, clock and interrupt types. A register type carries its width and access. `use svd.stm32f411 as chip` runs a reader package that turns the vendor file into those values. A board is a value built from a chip, and it derives pin drivers, linker regions and the vector table.

Option B keeps today's records and hand-written register structs. It needs no new library, but nothing checks access or overlap. Option C reads devicetree files with a separate tool. It reuses Linux and Zephyr board files, but Jet code sees only generated names.

Cost. A field write lowers to a masked volatile read and write, with the mask built at build time. A constant write is one store. The board value exists only while building.

Research: Docs/research/declarative-jet-2026-10-31.md (GoldC lane, dev 68c87ae07b).

Review. Author: Claude (GoldC lane). No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft yet.

A board implements the D-HOST-CAPS1 hardware trait and feeds the target profile, linker regions (D-TARGET-LINKER1) and dossier. #Interrupt(board.uart.rx) builds the vector table.

decisions.title: A screen is a function from state to a view value, and the runtime mounts and updates it
decisions.situation: Jet programs that draw screens today call mount inside a change handler, and one example compares old and new screens by hand. On the web build, the counter app builds but draws nothing. This vote picks who owns drawing and updating. We recommend that a view is a plain function from state to a view value, and the runtime does the rest on every target.
decisions.gist: Should a Jet screen be a function from state to a view value, with the runtime mounting and updating it?
decisions.lesson: SwiftUI, Elm and Compose let you describe what the screen shows for the current state. When the state changes, the framework works out what changed and updates only that. You never call mount or compare screens yourself.
decisions.story: Ana writes a counter as a function that returns a column with a label and two buttons. She runs it natively, in the terminal and in the browser without changing a line. A list without stable keys fails to compile with a clear fix.
decisions.detail:
Today. The gauntlet counter calls ui.mount inside ui.reactive_render (Tools/gauntlet/entries/web-app/jet/run.jet:9-21). Examples/features/ui/ui_view_tree.jet:10-27 compares old and new leaves by hand. The web build ships no DOM host, so the counter builds and draws nothing.

What A says. A view is fn(state) -> ui.Node. ui.app(view, state: …) mounts it, tracks which state each node reads, and updates only those nodes. Native, terminal and web use the same call. List rows need a key.

Option B keeps effects that call mount, and adds a helper for diffing. Option C uses an Elm-style message loop with an update function. C is clear but needs a message type for every action.

Cost. Static parts of the tree are built once while building. Only nodes that read changed state run again, from the signal graph core.reactive already builds.

Research: Docs/research/declarative-jet-2026-10-31.md (GoldC lane, dev 68c87ae07b).

Review. Author: Claude (GoldC lane). No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft yet.

decisions.title: What `jet inspect explain-build` shows before any build has been recorded
decisions.situation:
`jet inspect explain-build` lists each step of the last build with its measured time and the reason it ran. When no build has been recorded, there is nothing measured to show. The Rust host printed the planned steps with 0.000 ms each, which looks like a real measurement. The Jet port refuses with E2104 instead, and since Jet does not write build records yet, it refuses every time.

We recommend that the command always lists the planned steps, which the compiler already knows, and lists measured steps only when a record exists. Nothing is invented, the output has no empty or null time fields, and the command works before the first build.
decisions.gist: Before any build has been recorded, should `jet inspect explain-build` list the planned steps, refuse, or print zero times?
decisions.lesson: A build is a set of steps such as check, compile and link. The compiler knows the planned steps of every program before it runs them. Times and reasons exist only after a run, and only the build record holds them.
decisions.explainer:
Words used here. A step, or node, is one unit of build work, such as checking main.jet or linking the program. The planned steps are the ones the compiler would run now; each has a kind, a key, a subject and its inputs. The build record is what a finished build writes: the steps that ran, how long each took, and why each ran.

The JSON form is the document named `jet.explain-build/v1`. Its `nodes` list holds recorded steps.
decisions.story: Ana opens a new project and runs `jet inspect explain-build app.jet` to see what a build will do. Today the Jet port stops with E2104 and a fix line she cannot follow, because no Jet build writes the record yet. The Rust host would have shown 0.000 ms for every step, and she would have thought the build was instant. Under A she sees the check, compile and link steps with their inputs, under a line saying no build has been recorded yet.
decisions.inWild:
$ go build -n ./app
# prints the commands a build would run; nothing runs and nothing is timed
decisions.detail:
Source: card #4893, found while porting the build-graph CLI rows. The Rust host (Source/CmdCompile.rs:807-856) printed the checked planned steps with duration_ms 0.000 and why_ran first-run for every step. The 2026-10-08 log adds Check-step times (CmdCompile.rs:15103-15152), which were also 0.0.

What the Jet port does today. Compiler/JetCli/Source/Cli/InspectBuild.jet:421 refuses with E2104, "build execution-node evidence is unavailable". Measured on the tree14 compiler with a three-line hello.jet: the refusal prints in text and as a jet.status/v1 error in JSON.

Who writes the record. Today no Jet build writes one: `jet_cli_build_compile_observation` is called only from Compiler/JetCli/Tests/InspectBuild.jet. So under B, the command refuses for every program until native build timing lands, and its fix line names a runtime that does not exist yet.

The planned steps already exist. `jet_driver_query_build_nodes` returns them for every program, with or without `fn build`. For a one-file program they are check main.jet, compile main and link main, each with a stable key and its inputs (InspectBuild tests, lines 83-91). A program with two executables has one check step and a compile and a link step per executable.

Earlier rulings. The card cites a build-query ruling that was never filed in Tower. No ratified ruling covers the case with no record, so this ballot decides it.

The design in A. The JSON document keeps its name and gains one list, `planned`, which is always present. Each planned entry has the four fields the compiler knows: kind, key, subject and inputs. It has no time and no reason fields at all, so nothing is null and nothing is zero.

`nodes` holds recorded steps, as today, and is an empty list when no build has been recorded. The text form prints the recorded rows when a record exists. Otherwise it prints one header line and the planned rows. The exit code is 0 in both cases, because the command answered the question.

A record that belongs to another program still gets E2104. That case means the record store is damaged, not that no build has run.

options.name: Always list the planned steps; list measured steps only when recorded
options.detail:
The command always lists the planned steps that the compiler knows: kind, key, subject and inputs. When a build record exists, it also lists the recorded steps with their measured times and reasons, as today.

With no record, the text form prints one header line and the planned rows, and the JSON form has an empty `nodes` list. No time or reason is printed for a step that has not run, so there is no zero and no null to misread. The exit code is 0.
options.technical:
In InspectBuild.jet, `jet_cli_build_nodes_host` stops refusing when the record is None and passes the planned nodes from `jet_driver_query_build_nodes` to the report.

`jet_cli_build_nodes_report` takes the record as optional plus the planned nodes. JSON gains a `planned` array of {kind, key, subject, inputs} beside `nodes`; the schema name stays `jet.explain-build/v1`.

Text prints the recorded rows when a record exists, else the line "no build recorded for <program> yet; planned steps:" and one row per planned step. A record for another program keeps E2104. The CLI reference gets one paragraph for the `planned` list.

options.name: Refuse with E2104 until a build is recorded
options.detail:
The command stops with E2104 when no record exists and prints no steps. This is the Jet port's behavior today.

Because no Jet build writes a record yet, the command refuses for every program until native build timing lands.
options.technical: No change: `jet_cli_build_nodes_host` keeps returning E2104 for a missing record, and the planned steps stay reachable only through tests.

options.name: Print the planned steps with zero times, as Rust did
options.detail:
With no record, the command prints every planned step with 0.000 ms and the reason first-run, the same row shape as a measured run.

A reader cannot tell these rows from a build that ran in no time.
options.technical: `jet_cli_build_nodes_host` builds a stand-in record from the planned nodes with duration_ms 0.0 and why_ran "first-run", and passes it to the existing report.

comparisons.note: `go build -n` prints the commands a build would run without running or timing any of them. Source: `go help build`.
`bazel aquery` lists the planned actions of a target with their inputs, and has no time fields. Times come only from a profile written by a real build. Source: bazel.build/query/aquery.
`cargo build --timings` writes a report only after a build runs; there is no report before the first build. Source: doc.rust-lang.org/cargo, Reporting build timings.

recommendation.why: A shows what the compiler knows, the planned steps, and adds measured steps only when a build recorded them. Nothing is invented, and the command works on a fresh project.
gains: Works before the first build, and today, with no record writer.
No zero or null times for steps that never ran.
One document shape whether or not a record exists.

whyNot.reason: It hides the planned steps the user asked about and refuses for every program until build timing lands.
Zero times read as measurements, and scripts comparing runs see false slowdowns.

recommendation.tradeoff: The JSON document gains one always-present list, `planned`. In return the command answers on a fresh project and never prints a time it did not measure.

decisions.title: Build the expert memory tools now, by calling the runtime code Jet already has
decisions.situation: Experts can manage memory by hand with arenas, pools, pins and raw pointers. The rules for these tools are settled, and `jet check` accepts them. But `jet build` cannot build an arena yet. So a program copied from the manual passes the check, then the build fails. The safety checks that catch bad pointer use in development never run either. The runtime code for both already exists: about 1,000 lines that nothing calls. The vote decides whether to build these tools now, refuse them until later, or drop them.
decisions.gist: Should Jet build its expert memory tools now, by calling runtime code it already has?
decisions.lesson: Yes: build them now, so every example in the manual that checks also builds.
decisions.story: Kai copies the arena example from the manual. `jet build` makes a program, and it prints 42.
decisions.inWild:
Option          Manual example   Expert control   Like
A build now     builds, runs     full             Zig, C++, Odin
B refuse        refused          none for now     Rust (unstable)
C drop arenas   no such code     pointers only    Go
decisions.detail:
WHAT WE BUILD
- JetIR: cases for AllocNew, RawAddressOf and PtrFromAddr (they fall to ir_fail_slot at Compiler/JetIR/Source/BuildExpr.jet:1503-1505). `.Deref` and `.RawOf` already lower (:1501-1502).
- Each case calls the runtime memory code: Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/MemStorage.jet (467 lines) and Sentry.jet (555 lines), which have no JetIR caller today.
- Sentries: emit them in dev builds, silent in release (D-MEM-SENTRY1=A). Today BuildExpr lowers .SentryPolicy, .Unsafe and .UnsafeBlock to plain scopes.
- Core/Mem/Mem.jet:34-38: remove the INTERIM panic in mem.from_addr (#4971).

- Fix the E1004 position error on `mem.address_of` that stops Examples/features/memory/pin.jet and unsafe_sentries.jet at check.
- Done when every Examples/features/memory example builds and passes golden output on every tier (I5, I9).
- Spec card #5892 (spec describes these as working) closes with this work.

EVIDENCE (r14, ballots2/redo/probe/)
- arena.jet (copy of the manual example): `jet check` ok; `jet build` E2104 "expression AllocNew".
- m_rawptr.jet: `jet build` exit 0, so raw reads already lower.
- m_pin.jet and m_unsafe_sentries.jet: E1004 "`core.mem` exposes `address_of`, but not in this position".
- A backend refusal of checked code breaks I2 (it should never be a user error), so the trap is a defect under every option.

- The earlier claim that B would "write the lowering twice" on a rebuilt core found no backing: JetIR is the shipping backend (#4599, #5993).

IDS
Keeps D-RAWPTR2=A, D-MEM-SENTRY1=A, D-AUTHORITY-MEM2=A, D-MEM-GUARANTEE1=A, D-MEM-HARDEN1, D-EFF-FIXED-FIT1, D-ALLOC1. Cards #5534, #5535, #5536, #4971, #4889, #4894, #5840, #5892.

options.name: Build them now
options.detail: The compiler turns each memory tool into a call to the existing runtime code. Development checks switch on. Gains: Every manual example that checks also builds. Reuses about 1,000 lines of runtime code. Pointer misuse is caught while developing. Losses: The largest job of the three. Development builds run pointer checks, which slow memory-heavy code.
options.technical: The compiler gains three missing cases. They are arena allocation, taking a raw address, and turning an address into a pointer. Reading through a pointer already builds. Each case emits a call to the runtime memory code that exists today. Development builds add the pointer checks, which stay silent in release builds, as already decided. The checker keeps its rules that stop arena values from escaping. `mem.from_addr` loses its temporary panic. Done means every memory example builds and passes on every tier.
options.code:
// A: the same program builds and runs
arena :: mem.Arena.new()
x :: arena.alloc(42)
print(x)          // 42
close(^arena)

options.name: Refuse them until built
options.detail: `jet check` refuses each tool with a clear error, and shows a list-and-index form instead. Gains: No pass-then-fail trap. Cheap to ship. Losses: Experts cannot use any of these tools. The manual describes features that are refused.
options.technical: One refusal per tool, at check time. Removing a refusal turns its tool back on once it is built. This matches how Rust refuses unstable features.

options.name: Drop arenas and pools
options.detail: Remove the allocator tools from the language, as Go did with its arena experiment. Raw pointers stay. Gains: Less to build and to teach. Losses: Experts lose control over where memory lives. Undoes settled decisions on arenas and pools.
options.technical: Deletes the allocator types and their checks. Code that needs bulk freeing uses lists and indexes.

comparisons.note: Arenas are a standard library allocator. Source: https://ziglang.org/documentation/master/std/#std.heap.ArenaAllocator
A monotonic buffer is the standard arena. Source: https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/memory/monotonic_buffer_resource
Unfinished features are refused on stable with error E0658. Arenas come from crates. Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/error_codes/E0658.html
Go tried arenas behind a flag, then put the proposal on hold. Source: https://github.com/golang/go/issues/51317
Arenas are library allocators, passed through a context. Source: https://odin-lang.org/docs/overview/#allocators
comparisons.code:
// Odin: arena as a context allocator
arena: virtual.Arena
context.allocator = virtual.arena_allocator(&arena)
x := new(int)

recommendation.why: The rules and runtime code already exist. Only the compiler step between them is missing. Building it removes the trap and keeps expert control.
gains: A program that checks also builds.
Experts get the full settled tool set.
Development builds catch pointer misuse.

losses.loss: It is the largest job of the three.
losses.mitigation: The runtime code exists, so the job is three compiler cases plus the checks.

losses.loss: Development builds run pointer checks, which slow memory-heavy code.
losses.mitigation: Release builds drop the checks, as already decided.

whyNot.reason: It hides a missing piece behind an error and leaves experts with nothing.
Jet promises experts full control, and arenas are a core part of it.

recommendation.tradeoff: More work now, instead of a refusal or a smaller language.

decisions.title: Memory left behind by each run inside a long-lived Jet session
decisions.situation: During a long development session, the helper process that runs build scripts and re-runs keeps growing by every run, and nothing gives that memory back. A one-shot program skips freeing memory at exit, because the operating system reclaims it all at once. The long-lived helper never exits, so every run leaves its memory behind. The vote decides how each run returns its memory, and what that costs.
decisions.gist: Should each run inside a long-lived Jet helper give its memory back when it ends?
decisions.lesson: When a program ends, the operating system takes back all its memory, so skipping cleanup is safe. A helper that runs many programs never ends, so skipped cleanup piles up. This vote picks how each run's memory is returned.
decisions.explainer: Under A each run in the helper gets its own memory region. When the run ends, the whole region is handed back in one step, without visiting each value, after the run's last output. One-shot programs keep the fast exit. If the helper still grows past a limit, Jet replaces it and says so. B only replaces the helper at a limit. C changes nothing.
decisions.story: Noor re-runs her program 300 times in `jet dev`. Under A the helper stays the size of one run, and the re-runs feel no slower.
decisions.detail:
What exists today, read at dev 8d2082ea63. At normal exit, main_process_ending makes jet_rt_free a no-op (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Alloc.jet:938-939). It also makes jet_rt_rc_release return false (Refcount.jet:44-50), so no drop walk runs.

The flag is cleared only at the end of the entry (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Main.jet:179-183). Its comment notes that loaded-image hosts run another entry in the same process. Compile-time batches, fn build and fn dev entries, and jet eval run in long-lived children (Compiler/JetEval/Source/IR/Native.jet:1-21).

Resident sessions are ratified in D-RUN-SESSION1 and D-BUILD-SESSION1. So each entry abandons its live heap in that child. [INFERENCE: review 2026-10-23 gap G9; not yet measured.] D-ALLOC-DEFAULT1=A already promises that empty pages return to the system.

Separately, the inlined release in Compiler/JetIR/Source/X64Select.jet:869-887 ignores the flag and still walks drops at exit. That is review gap G8, and it only wastes time today.

Beginner path. Nothing to do; sessions stay small. Expert path. The session report names a replaced helper and its size, so a leak in user build code is visible rather than silent.

Edge cases. A value the compiler reads back from a compile-time call lives in a result cell. It must be read before the run frees, which today's call protocol already orders. Secrets alive at the end of a run are still scrubbed. A run that ends by a fatal stop or an explicit exit already replaces the child.

Globals that persist across runs by design, such as #Persist values in jet dev (D-LIVE1), are not freed between runs.

Pauses or reclaim cost under A. The program never pauses for cleanup: its region is released after its last output, before the next run starts. The cost is proportional to the region's pages, not its values, because no value is visited. [INFERENCE: a run-scoped heap needs allocator work in Alloc.jet; the page release itself is one system call per region.]

Downsides engineered away. The per-value cleanup walk of the earlier design is removed by releasing the region in one step. Resources are still closed, because the runtime's list of open files and sockets is walked, not every value. Secrets are still wiped, because they live on their own pages. The only cost left is the page release between runs, which the user never waits on inside the program.

Option B alone keeps every leak until the limit, then pays a full restart and warm-up. Option C leaves the growth unbounded, which matters on a machine that already ran out of memory once from compiler processes.

options.name: Give back each run's region at once, with a size limit as backstop
options.detail: Each run in a helper allocates from its own region. When the run ends, after its last output, the whole region is returned in one step, so there is no per-value cleanup walk. Open files and sockets are still closed. One-shot programs keep the fast exit. A helper that still grows past a limit is replaced, with a report line.
options.technical: Loaded-image hosts give each entry a run-scoped heap in Alloc.jet. At entry end, Close runs for live resources from the runtime resource list, secret pages are wiped (D-MEM-WIPE1), and the region's pages are released. Results read back by the compiler are copied out first. main_process_ending is set only for one-shot images, and the inlined release reads the same flag (G8). The session host replaces a child past an RSS limit via the existing respawn path.

options.name: Keep the fast exit; replace the helper at a limit
options.detail: Runs keep skipping cleanup. When a helper passes a size limit, Jet replaces it with a fresh one.
options.technical: No runtime change; the session host checks child resident size after each entry and respawns past the limit.

options.name: Keep today's behaviour
options.detail: Each run leaves its memory in the helper until the helper ends for another reason.
options.technical: No change.
options.code:
// jet dev, after many re-runs
// helper memory grows each run, with no limit

comparisons.note: PHP-FPM replaces a worker after a set number of requests to bound leaks: https://www.php.net/manual/en/install.fpm.configuration.php#pm.max-requests.
Gunicorn restarts a worker after a set number of requests for the same reason: https://docs.gunicorn.org/en/stable/settings.html#max-requests.

recommendation.why: A keeps the helper the size of one run at a cost tied to pages, not values, paid after the run's output. No program sees a pause, and the limit catches any leak.
gains: Helper memory stays flat across runs.
No per-value cleanup walk and no pause in the program.
One-shot programs keep the fast exit.

losses.loss: Each run's region is released after its output, which takes time per page.
losses.mitigation: It happens after the program finishes, so the program itself never pauses.

whyNot.reason: B bounds growth, but keeps every leak until the limit and then pays a full restart.
C leaves the helper growing without limit.

recommendation.tradeoff: A page release after each run instead of unbounded growth.

Time the gap between a run's last output and the next run's start, against today. Confirm an open file is closed and a secret page is wiped at run end. Force a leak and confirm replacement at the limit. One-shot exit time must not regress in a same-run A/B.

decisions.title: Start replacing views, shared handles, cells and pins with @ links
decisions.situation: Users would have to rewrite code that uses five older reference tools, and this vote decides how much that costs them. Jet chose one spelling, the at sign, for a link: a field or name that points at a live value instead of holding a copy. The five older tools that do parts of this job are read views, write views, shared handles, local cells and pinned fields. No link is built yet, so learners meet all five.
decisions.gist: Should Jet start replacing the five older reference tools with @ links now, one tool at a time?
decisions.lesson: A link points at a live value, so a change through one name is seen through every other. Jet has five older tools that each do part of this job. This vote decides when and how users move to links.
decisions.explainer: Under A read views move first, because a read-only link compiles exactly like today's view. Each later step retires one old tool. `jet fix` rewrites the user's code for each step automatically, and the error for an old spelling shows the exact new one. B switches everything in one change later. C keeps the five tools.
decisions.story: Ana has a project full of read views. When step one lands she runs `jet fix` once and her code uses links, with the same speed and no manual edits.
decisions.detail:
What exists today, read at dev 8d2082ea63. D-MEMREF1=A, ratified 2026-09-28, spells live links as @T and @x. It replaces the View, ViewMut, Shared, Cell and Pin-field spellings (Docs/proposals/memory-model-2026-10-05.md:140-150).

Its family is ratified too: D-MEMREF-LIFE1, D-MEMREF-EXCL1, D-MEMREF-TASK1, D-LINK-DEBT1, D-LINK-ITEM1 and D-REACT-REF1. None is built. Team{captain: @p} reports E0107, and @Node{...} reports E0119 (memory-model-2026-10-05.md:152-156).

The lexer reserves prefix @ for links (Compiler/JetFoundation/Data/Syntax/Spellings.jet:25; Docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md:34). The five old tools are built and documented; see Docs/spec/spec.md:1294-1314 for views and Shared<T>. Later APIs use the old spelling: D-ITER-VIEWCOLLECT1, D-COLLECTION-TOPK1 and D-FOUND-VIEW1. The 2026-10-23 review counts five built mechanisms plus one ratified replacement as an I8 breach.

Beginner path. Under A a beginner learns @ once the first step lands. If they copy an old spelling, a teaching error shows the exact rewrite. Under C they keep learning five tools. Expert path. Experts keep every denial and pin from the ratified family, such as !Mem.Check, #Local and #Shared. jet inspect reports how each link was lowered.

Edge cases. A link with no proven value write during its life lowers exactly like today's read view, so the first step costs nothing at run time (memory-model-2026-10-05.md:186-192). A stored link into a growable list must point at an object, per D-LINK-ITEM1.

A link that crosses into a task switches to thread-safe storage, per D-MEMREF-TASK1. A link to a value that owes a job is generation-checked, per D-LINK-DEBT1. Pool and Id stay as a data structure for entity systems, not a reference tool.

Migration cost to users under A. Each step changes one old spelling. The compiler error for the old spelling shows the new one, and `jet fix` applies it across a project, so the cost of a step is running one command. Step one changes no generated code, because a read-only link lowers through today's view path. Jet's clean-cutover rule means no old spelling lingers as a silent alias.

Downsides engineered away. Manual rewrites are removed by `jet fix`. Mixed old and new code is removed within a step, because each step migrates the examples, tests and Core APIs in the same change. A speed change is removed for step one. The only cost left is running `jet fix` once per step, which cannot be merged without making users wait for B.

Option B migrates once but delays links until after the core rebuild. Option C needs no migration but keeps five overlapping tools and amends D-MEMREF1.

options.name: Start now, one old tool per step, with automatic rewrites
options.detail: Build links in steps. Read views move first, because a read-only link compiles exactly like today's view. Write views, cells, shared handles and pinned fields follow. Each step retires its old spelling, and `jet fix` rewrites user code for that step automatically.
options.technical: Slice 1: parse and check `@T` fields and `@x` for read-only use, lowered through the existing view path; retire View in that change with a machine-applicable fix. Later slices: ViewMut (lend checks from D-MEMREF-EXCL1), Cell, Shared (task switch from D-MEMREF-TASK1), Pin fields. Examples, tests and Core APIs migrate in the same change.

options.name: Switch everything at once, later
options.detail: Wait until the compiler core rebuild is done, then build the whole link family and retire all five old tools in one change.
options.technical: One cutover after the flat core lands: parser, checker, lowering and Core API migration together, with the full ratified family.

options.name: Keep the five tools
options.detail: Keep views, write views, shared handles, cells and pinned fields as the built answer. Withdraw links and the rulings that build on them.
options.technical: Amend D-MEMREF1 and its family; drop the `@` link reservation in Spellings.jet; keep spec.md:1294-1314 as the reference model.

comparisons.note: Swift splits live references (classes) from values (structs) with one keyword choice, and checks exclusive access at run time where it cannot prove it: https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/memorysafety/.
Rust spreads the same job over references, Rc, RefCell, Arc, Mutex and Pin, a split often cited as its steepest learning cost: https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch15-00-smart-pointers.html.

recommendation.why: A gives users links soonest and makes each migration one `jet fix` run. Read-only links reuse today's view code, so step one costs no speed.
gains: Users get links soonest.
Each step's rewrite is applied by `jet fix`.
Step one reuses today's view code.

losses.loss: Users run `jet fix` once per step instead of once in total.
losses.mitigation: Each run is automatic, and the old spelling's error says exactly what to run.

whyNot.reason: B migrates once, but users wait longest for links.
C needs no migration but keeps five overlapping tools and reverses a ratified spelling.

recommendation.tradeoff: A few automatic rewrites in exchange for links now.

Repeat per step for ViewMut, Cell, Shared and Pin fields. Each step needs chain FIXED_POINT and goldens not worse.

decisions.title: Plain or thread-safe sharing counts for ordinary values
decisions.situation: Programs that never start a second task still pay a thread-safety cost every time two names share a list or string. Jet keeps a count of the sharers, called a reference count, and frees the memory when it reaches zero. Today every count update uses the slower thread-safe form, which is only needed when two threads touch it at once. The vote decides which values may use a plain, faster count.
decisions.gist: Should shared values use fast plain counts unless their type can reach another task?
decisions.lesson: A reference count records how many names share one block of memory. A thread-safe count is correct across threads, but each update costs more. A plain count is fast but safe on one thread only. This vote picks which count each value uses.
decisions.explainer: Under A the compiler gives plain counts to every type that never reaches another task, and thread-safe counts to the rest. Nothing switches at run time. A build note names each thread-safe type and the line that made it so. B decides per block at run time. C keeps thread-safe counts everywhere.
decisions.story: Mia writes a single-task text tool. Under A her shared strings use plain counts and run faster, with no change to her code. When she later adds a task, the build note tells her which type switched and why.
decisions.detail:
What exists today, read at dev 8d2082ea63. Every retain and release is LOCK XADD. See Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Refcount.jet:29-50, where rc_add uses os_fetch_add_i64, and the inlined x64 sequence in Compiler/JetIR/Source/X64Select.jet:855-887. Shared<T> also takes a mutex on each field access (Docs/spec/spec.md:1306-1309; Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Shared.jet:30-42).

No measurement was taken in the 2026-10-23 review; the cost claim is structural. [INFERENCE: an uncontended locked add on x64 typically costs several times a plain add.]

Settled law. D-MEMREF-TASK1=A already rules for links. If any link to a type can reach another task, links to that type use atomic counts. Otherwise they use the fast local form. jet inspect lists each switch with the task that caused it. #Local forbids crossing, and #Shared forces the thread-safe form.

D-CONC-CROSS1=A makes crossing safety one registered fact per type, with one prover. Option A reuses both rulings, so ordinary values and links follow one rule (I8). Related cards: #4620 (Rust-or-better) and #5041.

Beginner path. Nothing to write: a single-task program gets plain counts everywhere. Expert path. jet inspect shows which types switched and which task boundary caused it. #Local on a type guarantees it never crosses and stays fast. #Shared forces the safe form.

Edge cases. A type reached through another type that crosses is itself crossing, because the closure is transitive. Generic instances are decided per instance, so List<Int> can switch while List<Token> stays plain. Comptime code runs in a child on the same tier and is single-task unless it spawns.

Sandbox components never share blocks with the host, so they do not force a switch. Values captured by a spawned closure and values sent on a channel are both crossings.

Any atomic cost left under A? Only for types that can reach another task, and those already need it for correctness. A program with no tasks pays none. Any hidden switch? No. The choice is made at compile time per type and never changes at run time, and every build lists each thread-safe type with the send or spawn line that caused it.

Downsides engineered away. The surprise slowdown is made visible: adding a task that sends a type prints which type switched and why. It is also made controllable: `#Local` on the type turns the crossing into a compile error, and `#Shared` forces thread-safe counts on purpose. The only cost left is that a crossing type pays thread-safe counts for all its values, because a value's future thread is not always known at compile time.

Option B removes analysis but adds a header word and a branch to every update, a cost every program pays. Option C keeps the cost for all programs.

options.name: Plain counts unless the type can reach another task
options.detail: The compiler knows which types can reach another task. Types that never do use plain counts; the rest use thread-safe counts. The choice is made at compile time, and each build lists every thread-safe type with the line that caused it. `#Local` makes a crossing a compile error.
options.technical: Codegen selects rc_add or a plain add per IR type instance, from the crossing fact (D-CONC-CROSS1) closed over contained types. Retain, release and the unique test pick the same form. The build summary and jet inspect print each switched type with the send or spawn site. #Local and #Shared apply as in D-MEMREF-TASK1.

options.name: Biased counts decided at run time
options.detail: Each block remembers the thread that made it. That thread updates a plain count; other threads update a second, thread-safe count. No analysis is needed, but every block grows and every update checks the current thread.
options.technical: The header gains an owner-thread word and a shared count. Retain and release compare the thread id with the owner before choosing the path. Counts merge when the owner drops its last share, as in PEP 703.

options.name: Thread-safe counts everywhere
options.detail: Keep today's behaviour: every count update is thread-safe. It is simple and always correct, and single-task programs keep paying the cost.
options.technical: No change to Refcount.jet or X64Select.jet.

comparisons.note: Rust has Rc with a plain count and Arc with a thread-safe count, and the compiler refuses to send an Rc to another thread: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/rc/index.html.
comparisons.code:
let local = Rc::new(names);
let shared = Arc::new(names2);

comparisons.note: CPython's free-threaded build uses biased reference counting, with a fast path for the owning thread: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/.

# ob_ref_local: owner thread, plain
# ob_ref_shared: other threads, atomic

gains: Single-task programs pay no thread-safety cost.

whyNot.reason: B needs no analysis, but every block grows and every update checks the thread.

recommendation.tradeoff: Fast counts by default, with each thread-safe type visible and its cause named.

decisions.title: Where optional values, results and enum payloads live in memory
decisions.situation: Programs that return maybe-values or results run slower than they should, with no visible reason. Today every optional value, result and enum case that carries data gets its own block of heap memory, which costs an allocator request and a count update. Rust and Swift store these values directly inside the variable instead. The vote decides how Jet lays them out; source code does not change under any option.
decisions.gist: Should optional values, results and enum payloads be stored inline instead of in their own heap block?
decisions.lesson: A heap block costs a request to the allocator and a count update. Inline storage keeps a value directly in its variable or list slot, which is much faster. Your code reads the same either way; only speed and size change.
decisions.explainer: Under A every optional, result and payload sits inline, and only a field that contains its own type keeps a heap block. Copy and size costs are shown, never hidden: the size of each type is listed, and a lint flags an enum whose largest case is far bigger than the rest. B inlines small payloads only. C keeps a heap block per value.
decisions.story: Sam's search function returns `Int?` in a hot loop. Under A the loop runs without a single allocation and Sam changes nothing. When Sam adds a case carrying a large record, a lint shows the size and offers to box that one case.
decisions.detail:
What exists today, read at dev 8d2082ea63. Compiler/JetIR/Source/BuildTypes.jet:168-181 lays out .Option(inner) and .Result(ok, err) as an 8-byte box pointer. Option is null when absent with its payload at 0. Result has a selector word at 0 and its payload at 8. Payload enums are boxed the same way (BuildTypes.jet:276-285, per the 2026-10-23 memory review).

Each box is an allocator block with a 24-byte header (Compiler/JetRuntime/Source/Alloc.jet:114-126) and an atomic count (Refcount.jet:29-50). So Int? is 16 bytes of payload plus 24 of header, which rounds up to the 64-byte size class. Card #5469 holds a measurement on 3 million pops at O0. Card #4620 is the Rust-or-better goal this blocks.

Beginner path. Nothing to learn under any option: the same source runs faster under A or B. Expert path. Under A an expert reads each type's and each case's size from the ratified type-size display. They move a large, rare payload into a list field when its copies matter. Under B the expert must also learn where the 16-byte line falls.

Edge cases every option must handle. A self-containing enum, such as a tree whose case holds two trees, cannot be inline. A and B box exactly the self-containing fields, found by the compiler, like Swift's indirect but inferred. Containment through a struct is the same case. Generic instances get a layout per instance. Close types inside a payload keep their close order.

Foreign calls and #Layout(C) values never carried Jet optionals by pointer contract. [INFERENCE: confirm against the foreign-call checker before the build.] Comptime runs on the same native tier, so it changes in the same commit.

Any copy cost under A? A copy of an inline value copies its bytes, so a 200-byte case costs a 200-byte copy where a heap block cost a count update. The last use of a value still moves for free, and most optional values are a word or two. Any layout surprise? An enum is as big as its largest case. Both costs are made visible: the type-size display lists every type and case.

Downsides engineered away. The size lint fires when one case is more than four times the next and over 64 bytes, and its fix boxes just that case, an explicit opt-in. Self-containing fields are boxed automatically, because they cannot be inline at all, and the size display marks each one. Foreign and #Layout(C) types keep their declared layout. The only cost left is the byte copy of a large value the user chose to keep inline.

Option B removes large copies but keeps two layouts and a cliff where a payload grows past two words. Option C keeps an allocation on every optional value.

options.name: Inline everywhere; box only self-containing fields
options.detail: Optional values, results and payloads sit inside their variable or list slot. An optional list or text uses the empty pointer as its absent marker, so it costs no extra bytes. Only a field that contains its own type, such as a tree node's child, keeps a heap block. Sizes are listed, and a lint flags lopsided enums.
options.technical: Option<T> becomes {tag, T}, or a niche over a non-null pointer payload. Result and payload enums become {selector, union of payloads} with natural alignment. ir_copy_fixup, ir_close_parts and ir_drop_glue walk the inline payload by selector. Recursive fields are found on the type graph and boxed per field. A size lint fires when one case is over 4x the next and over 64 bytes, with a fix that boxes that case.

options.name: Inline small payloads, box large ones
options.detail: Payloads of two machine words or less sit inline; larger ones keep a heap block. Copies stay cheap for every type, but there are two layouts and a speed cliff where a payload crosses the line.
options.technical: Same inline layout as A for payloads of 16 bytes or less, plus the existing box path above that. Both glue paths stay live and are selected per type.

options.name: Keep one heap block per value
options.detail: Keep today's layout and only make the allocator's small-block path faster. Every optional value still costs an allocation and a count update.
options.technical: No IR layout change; work goes into the thread cache and header size (review items D2, D5).

comparisons.note: Rust stores Option inline and uses null as the absent marker for pointer payloads: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/option/index.html#representation.
Swift enums are inline; only cases marked indirect get a heap box: https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/enumerations/#Recursive-Enumerations.
comparisons.code: indirect enum Tree { case leaf(Int); case node(Tree, Tree) }

recommendation.why: Inline storage removes an allocation from every optional value with no source change. Size and copy costs become visible and fixable, which today's hidden allocations never were.
gains: No allocation for optional values or results.
Each type's size is listed; lopsided enums are flagged.
One layout rule, as in Rust and Swift.

losses.loss: Copying a value with a large inline payload copies its bytes.
losses.mitigation: A last use moves for free, and the size lint offers to box the large case.

whyNot.reason: B caps copy size but keeps two layouts and a speed cliff where payloads grow.
C avoids the rewrite but keeps an allocation on every optional value.

recommendation.tradeoff: Inline speed everywhere, with any large copy shown and boxable on request.
