decisions.title: `#Policy(gc)` opts in the types declared under it: their loops are collected wherever their values go
decisions.situation: Jet frees values by counting who holds them. A loop, such as two friends pointing at each other, never reaches zero, so today a write that closes a loop is refused (E0221). Graphs, scenes and family trees need such loops. The owner ruled that any collection must be opted into. `#Policy(gc)` already exists, but it opts in a block of code, and a graph made there can't leave it. The vote decides what the opt-in covers. We recommend the types declared under it.
decisions.gist: When a file opts in to collecting loops, what should the opt-in cover?
decisions.lesson: Jet frees a value when nothing holds it. Two values holding each other would never be freed, so Jet refuses that write. Put `#Policy(gc)` at the top of the file that declares `Person`, and loops of `Person` are allowed: a collector finds and frees them.
decisions.story: Lin's editor keeps a scene graph where nodes point at parents. She opts in a block, builds the graph, and returns it. The compiler refuses: the graph can't leave the block it was made in.
decisions.inWild:
// Swift: strong reference loops leak unless a link is weak.
class Person { weak var friend: Person? }
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0dm40k5. This is the opt-in question from the D-MEM-GCSCOPE1 package, asked alone. Owner rule on this card, 2026-10-24: no hidden collection; any collection must be opt-in. Owner ruling 2026-08-07: `#Policy(gc)` keeps its one-line shape. Builds on D-OPTGC1=A, D-SHARED-CYCLE1=C (E0221), D-MARK-SCOPE1=A and D-MEMREF-LIFE1=A.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/gc, on dev. cycle.jet: `a.friend = Val(b.copy())` then `b.friend = Val(a.copy())` is E0221 "This write can close a strong `Shared` cycle through `Person`", twice. cyclegc.jet: the same under a file-level `#Policy(gc)` gives the same two E0221s. loop.jet: a type with `Shared<Person>` fields builds and runs; only a closing write is refused. Examples/features/memory/gc_cyclic.jet runs and prints `Next(Next(End(1)))`.

Option programs, same folder. optc.jet, C's weak back-links, runs and prints Ada. optb.jet, B's `#Policy(gc) { … }` block around the closing writes, still gives E0221 twice: the ratified block opt-in does not lift E0221 today.

Reads with D-GC-WHEN1, which decides when collection runs. `-[!Mem.Gc]>` already bans collection in a function and its callees (D-DENY-COST1=A), and a graph reaching another task takes the thread-safe form (D-MEMREF-TASK1=A). Under D-MEMREF1=A the field reads `friend: @Person?`; the rule is the same.

options.name: The types declared under it
options.detail:
`#Policy(gc)` on a module, or `policy: { gc: true }` in a package, opts in every type declared there. E0221 skips writes through opted types, and a collector frees their loops.

Unopted types are unchanged: counted, freed at once, and refused on a closing write. The E0221 fix list gains "opt in this type", and `jet fix` writes the line.
options.technical: Moves D-OPTGC1=A's opt-in from code scopes to type declarations, on the same D-MARK-SCOPE1 ladder. Narrows D-MEMREF-LIFE1=A's "cycle collection only for types that can form cycles" to opted types, per the owner rule. Removes the unbuilt block plan (Sema/FunctionMemory.jet:476-881) and E2111.

options.name: The code under it
options.detail:
Values made inside an opted block, function or module are traced. A graph leaving that scope for ordinary code is refused.

A library can't ship a collected type; each user opts in where they build it.
options.technical: Today's ratified D-OPTGC1=A. Its block plan never reaches code generation (Docs/audits/2026-10-23-memory-model-review.md:55-58).

options.name: No collector
options.detail:
E0221 stays for every type. A back-link is `Shared.Weak<T>`, or the graph lives in a `Pool<T>` linked by `ID`.

`#Policy(gc)` is retired.
options.technical: Today's E0221 path; Examples/features/memory/shared_weak_cycle.jet shows it.

comparisons.note: Cycle collection tracks container types only. Source: https://docs.python.org/3/library/gc.html
No collector; weak and unowned links break loops. Source: https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/automaticreferencecounting/
ORC adds a cycle collector to reference counting; `{.acyclic.}` opts a type out. Source: https://nim-lang.org/docs/mm.html

recommendation.why: A puts the opt-in where the type is declared, as Python and Nim track by type. Graphs can then move freely, and every other type keeps exact freeing.
gains: Collected graphs behave like any value.
Libraries can ship collected types.

whyNot.reason: B traps a graph inside the scope that built it.
C makes every graph break its loops by hand.

recommendation.tradeoff: Opting in a type affects every user of that type.

decisions.title: Collection runs only where code already waits or allocates collected values: at task yields, at `gc.collect()`, and at opted allocation past a limit
decisions.situation: Once a type opts in to collection, something must find its unreachable loops and free them. A collector that runs at any moment makes any line a possible pause, which games and audio code can't afford. The owner ruled out hidden collection. The vote decides when collection may run. We recommend only at points that already wait or allocate collected values: a task yield, an explicit `gc.collect()`, or allocating an opted value once enough candidates pile up.
decisions.gist: When should Jet look for and free unreachable loops of collected values?
decisions.lesson: When a collected value is dropped, Jet only notes it as a candidate, which is quick. The real check runs at a few known points. A task waits, you call `gc.collect()`, or you make a collected value after many candidates. Code that does none of these never pauses.
decisions.story: Rui's audio callback drops a node from a collected scene graph. With a collector that runs anywhere, the callback stalls for two milliseconds and the speaker clicks.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0dm40k5. This is the timing question from the D-MEM-GCSCOPE1 package, asked alone. Owner rule on this card, 2026-10-24: no hidden collection; any collection must be opt-in. Owner ruling 2026-08-07: `#Policy(gc)` keeps its one-line shape. Builds on D-OPTGC1=A, D-SHARED-CYCLE1=C (E0221), D-MARK-SCOPE1=A and D-MEMREF-LIFE1=A.

Probes, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/gc, on dev. cycle.jet: `a.friend = Val(b.copy())` then `b.friend = Val(a.copy())` is E0221 "This write can close a strong `Shared` cycle through `Person`", twice. cyclegc.jet: the same under a file-level `#Policy(gc)` gives the same two E0221s. loop.jet: a type with `Shared<Person>` fields builds and runs; only a closing write is refused. Examples/features/memory/gc_cyclic.jet runs and prints `Next(Next(End(1)))`.

D-OPTGC1=A retired the old `core.gc` handle surface; `gc.collect()` here is a single function, not a handle type. It is new in every option that has it.

Reads with D-GC-OPTIN1, which decides which values are collected. The collection points here are exactly what `-[!Mem.Gc]>` bans under D-DENY-COST1=A: a ban on a function covers every point it can reach, and a violation names the call chain. Today `Mem.Gc` is not declared yet (nogc.jet: E0750 "`Mem.Gc` isn't a declared effect").

options.name: At waits and opted allocation
options.detail:
A drop of an opted value only adds it to a candidate list. Checks run at a task's yield points, at `gc.collect()`, or when an opted value is allocated and the list has passed its limit.

Each check takes one candidate group at a time, so a pause is bounded by the largest loop, not the heap. `jet gc report` shows where checks ran and how long they took.
options.technical: Same-thread trial deletion over the candidate list, in the D-DEP-GC1=A engine. Unopted types never enter the list. `gc.collect()` is a Core function with no code assigned yet; the limit is a package `policy:` key.

options.name: Only at `gc.collect()`
options.detail:
Collection is fully manual, like calling free for loops.

A program that never calls it grows until it runs out of memory.
options.technical: The same engine as A, with no automatic triggers.

options.name: A background collector
options.detail:
A concurrent collector traces opted types in the background.

Pauses are short but can land on any line, and opted counts become atomic, so they cost more.
options.technical: A concurrent mark phase with write barriers on opted types.

decisions.title: How a debugging build asks for the checked memory allocator
decisions.gist: Which signal tells jet to build a program with the checked allocator, now that jet itself refuses to start under JET_CHECKED_ALLOC=1?
decisions.lesson: JET_CHECKED_ALLOC=1 asks for a program whose every heap block is guarded and checked. jet reads it while building, but jet is itself a program built without that checking. So jet stops at start-up, and no checked program can be built today. Every unchecked program also scans its whole environment at start-up, only to refuse this variable.
decisions.story: Mia hunts a double free. She runs JET_CHECKED_ALLOC=1 jet build app.jet, and jet exits 70 before building anything. Under option A she runs jet build --checked-alloc app.jet, then ./app, and the bad free is reported with its call sites. Her everyday builds start faster, because no program checks its environment for the variable any more.
decisions.inWild:
Go: the race detector is chosen when building, with go build -race, and the built program checks itself. Source: https://go.dev/doc/articles/race_detector

AddressSanitizer: chosen at compile time with -fsanitize=address; ASAN_OPTIONS only tunes a program already built with it. Source: https://clang.llvm.org/docs/AddressSanitizer.html
decisions.detail:
Found 2026-11-01 by CardClose-1. Docs/spec/reference/environment.md says the variable is read when jet builds a program and again when the program starts. A program built without the checked heap but started with the variable set stops with exit 70. jet is such a program, so it stops first. No current rule lets only the toolchain carry a mark: double-underscore names are open only to Core and generated code, and the first-party reservation covers only import names. The variable is marked internal.

Redesign 2026-11-01 (owner: engineer the downsides away). The first version recommended two variables, one for the build and one for the run. That kept a cost on every program.

The start-up refusal hook (JetRuntime Alloc.jet jet_rt_alloc_check_refuse_init, 301 bytes in .init_array) walks the whole environment at every start. Measured by AsmPar-1 on hello: 2682 user instructions per run before the hook landed and 3235 after (+553, more with a larger environment), and the default hello binary grew 72 bytes. A build flag removes the run variable, so the hook, its refusal and its scan go away from every program, and jet never sees a variable at start-up.

Prior art: Go chooses the race detector with go build -race and the built program always checks itself. Clang chooses AddressSanitizer with -fsanitize=address; ASAN_OPTIONS only tunes a program already built with it. Neither turns checking on with a run-time variable in an unchecked program.

Switching is not a loss: checked and unchecked builds are cached under separate keys, so dropping or adding the flag reuses the other build at once, as Go does for -race.

Relation to ratified D-SIZE-PAYUSE1 A: its checker part ("the build environment holds JET_CHECKED_ALLOC=1", "every program keeps the class-limit load and the start test") is what A replaces. A keeps its intent, a checker linked only into programs that ask for it, but chooses it with the flag. Every program then drops the start test, and nothing runs unchecked by mistake, because no run-time variable exists to be ignored. The crash table and live inspection parts of D-SIZE-PAYUSE1 are unchanged.

Measured 2026-11-01 by AsmPar-1 on the wave-24 tree: with the start-up environment walk taken out, hello runs 1,273 user instructions in every environment, against 3,235 with the walk today. A deletes the hook outright, so hello costs no more than that. A lazy check that waits for the first allocation was also built, and is not offered: it lets user code run before the refusal, which the ratified rule forbids.

options.name: A build flag, like Go's -race

decisions.title: Service calls name the file and wait effects they reach
decisions.situation: The service runtime is moving from Rust into Jet. Its file and wait steps are effect-free today, so a tree writes its state store, rollout journal and delivery log with an empty effect row. A package that allows only reading files can therefore write them, and a function with an empty ceiling can start a tree. The vote decides whether service calls must name what they reach. We recommend they do.
decisions.gist: Should a service call that writes files say FS in its signature?
decisions.lesson: An effect row lists what a call may do, such as read files, write files or wait. The package grant and each function's ceiling are checked against those rows. A call with an empty row is trusted to do none of them. A row that hides a file write makes both checks pass when they should not.
decisions.story: Ana's billing package allows FS.Read so it can load a price file. She adds a service tree with an event log. Today the tree writes the log and its rollout journal anyway, and no check notices. Under A, `jet run` stops with E1803 and asks her to allow FS.Write.
decisions.detail:
Today. The port keeps the user surface unchanged, so its file and wait steps are effect-free core.service rows. Only `service.state_store()` asks for anything, and it asks for FS.Read. Start, stop, durable sends, snapshots, events, rollouts and delivery calls read and write files with an empty row.

What a tree touches. With a store at `orders.state`, a tree writes that file plus `orders.state.rollout`, `orders.state.workflows` and the delivery authority log. Every access also creates and removes a `.lock` file beside its target. While another process holds a lock, the call sleeps 1 ms at a time, for up to 30 s.

Probes. A package that allows [IO, Mem.Alloc, Time.Wait] and calls `service.state_store()` stops with E1803 for FS.Read. A package that allows [FS.Read, IO, Mem.Alloc] and appends to a file stops with E1803 for FS.Write. A function `boot() -[IO]>` that reaches that append stops with E0740 naming FS.Write. A package that allows only [IO, Mem.Alloc] ran `time.sleep(1ms)` with no grant.

What A does. The port's file steps flip from no effect to FS.Read or FS.Write, and the lock sleep to Time.Wait. Inference then carries those effects to every service call that reaches them. Calls that only touch memory keep an empty row: tree, worker, send, receive, show and observe. Each flip is one line in the effect table.

Who changes under A. All four durable service examples already allow FS, so none changes. Up to four test programs start a tree with no store and no FS grant, and each adds one allow line. Time.Wait needs no grant, so it only matters to function ceilings.

Beginner and expert paths under A. A beginner's lone file runs with `jet run --allow=FS run.jet`, and the E1803 fix line says how to keep that grant. An expert library writes `-[FS, Time.Wait]>` on its own service helpers. Helpers that only show or route, like `label`, keep `-[]>`.

Precedent. Core's file calls name their leaf even through a held handle. `Directory.remove` and `FileWriter.set_mode` both declare FS.Write. Under B the service store would be the one handle that does not.

Review. Author: Claude (LiveUI lane). No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft.

options.name: Each service call names the file and wait effects it reaches
options.detail:
A service call that can reach the state store says so: reads give FS.Read, writes and lock files give FS.Write, and lock waits give Time.Wait. Calls that only touch memory keep an empty row. The package grant and every function ceiling then see the real file writes.

A tree with no store still asks for FS to start, because start writes the rollout journal when a store is set.
options.technical: The port's core.service file rows (read, append, reserve, finish, rename, fsync, lstat, mkdirs) take FS.Read or FS.Write; the lock sleep row takes Time.Wait. Inference gives start, stop, send_durable, commit_snapshot, append_event, restore_snapshot, rollout and delivery calls FS plus Time.Wait. Status reads take the store lock, so they need FS.Write too. tree, worker, send, receive, show and observe stay `-[]>`.

options.name: The store asks for all of FS once; tree calls stay effect-free
options.detail:
`service.state_store()` asks for FS, reading and writing, when the program opens the store. Every tree call keeps an empty row, because holding the store value already proves the grant.

This is how Deno KV works: permission is checked when the store opens, not on each write.
options.technical: state_store's row widens from FS.Read to FS. The port's file rows stay effect-free. Package grants become honest, because no store can open without FS.Write. Function ceilings do not: a `-[]>` function handed a tree can still write its files.

options.name: Keep the port's effect-free rows
options.detail:
Only `service.state_store()` asks for FS.Read, as today. Every tree call keeps an empty row, including the ones that write files.

This is what the port ships now, so it costs no change.
options.technical: state_store stays `-[FS.Read]>`. Every core.service file and sleep row stays effect-free, as the Rust runtime rows were. A package that allows only FS.Read can write the state store, the rollout journal, the workflow store and the delivery log.

comparisons.note: Effects are inferred into every function type; a function that touches the file system carries `fsys` all the way up. Source: koka-lang.github.io/koka/doc/book.html, effect types.

comparisons.note: Permission is checked when a KV store opens; later writes ask nothing. Source: docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security and docs.deno.com/deploy/kv/manual.

await kv.set(["order", 1], "paid")

comparisons.note: No effect system: a gen_server or dets table writes files with nothing in its type. Source: erlang.org/doc/apps/stdlib/dets.html.

decisions.title: The state a durable delivery reads right after send_durable
decisions.situation: A durable send records the message, puts it in the worker's mailbox and returns a Delivery. The example golden says that Delivery reads Accepted. The runtime says Delivering, as the Rust runtime did. No spec line says which is right. The vote decides when a delivery becomes Delivering. We recommend the mailbox moment, as today.
decisions.gist: After send_durable returns, is the delivery Accepted or Delivering?
decisions.lesson: A durable delivery moves through states that are written to a log on disk. Accepted means the log has the message. Delivering means the worker has been handed it. Delivered means the worker committed it. A restarted program reads the log to know what to send again.
decisions.story: Ben sends an order with send_durable and prints its status to check it worked. Under B he sees Accepted until his worker calls receive. Under A he sees Delivering at once, because the order is already in the worker's mailbox.
decisions.detail:
Today. send_durable writes an acceptance record, puts the message in the worker's mailbox, then writes a Delivering record before it returns. The Rust runtime did the same: Services.rs 3215 calls mark_delivered, which appends Delivering (ServiceAuthority.rs 1862-1873). The base's Jet source keeps that order.

The golden. Examples/features/tooling/service_authority expects `first:accepted` and then `duplicate:delivering`. The duplicate send returns the same delivery, and nothing happens to it between the two prints. So the two lines cannot both hold under one rule. Line 1 was written by hand in 198561770c and never ran against this runtime.

What Accepted means under each. Under A, Accepted marks a message that is recorded but not yet in any mailbox: a retried delivery, or one recovered after a restart, waiting for the next receive to admit it. Under B, Accepted also covers a message already sitting in the mailbox.

What B costs. receive would write the Delivering record, so every durable receive adds one locked log append. send_durable would stop writing it. The receive path must also tell a first take from a re-take after a restart.

Who changes. Under B, lines 1 and 2 of the golden read accepted, and the runtime moves its marker. Under A, only line 1 of the golden changes, to delivering. No other golden or test prints this state right after a send.

Review. Author: Claude (LiveUI lane). No fresh adversarial pass has run on this draft.

options.name: Delivering starts when the message enters the worker's mailbox
options.detail: send_durable writes Delivering as soon as the message is in the worker's mailbox, before it returns. A status read right after the send says Delivering, and so does the duplicate's. This is what the runtime does today.
options.technical: No runtime change: send_durable and pending admission keep calling mark_delivered after the mailbox send. Golden line 1 becomes `first:delivering`; line 2 already says delivering.
options.code:
use core.service as service
use core.testing as testing

fn orders_worker() {}

fn label(delivery: ^Delivery) -> String {
    state :: delivery.status() ?? panic("status")
    if state == {
        .Accepted -> "accepted"
        .Delivering -> "delivering"
        else -> "other"
    }
}

fn run() {
    store :: Path.from(testing.temp_dir("orders")).join("orders.log").to_string()
    tree := service.tree("orders")
    &tree.set_delivery(service.delivery_durable()) ?? panic("delivery")
    &tree.set_state_event_log(service.state_store(store) ?? panic("store"), "orders", 1, "reversible") ?? panic("log")
    endpoint :: &tree.worker("orders", orders_worker, capacity: 2) ?? panic("worker")
    &tree.start() ?? panic("start")
    first :: &tree.send_durable(endpoint, "order", key: "order-1") ?? panic("first")
    print("first:{label(^first)}")
    duplicate :: &tree.send_durable(endpoint, "order", key: "order-1") ?? panic("duplicate")
    print("duplicate:{label(^duplicate)}")
    print("delivered:{&tree.receive(endpoint) ?? panic("receive")}")
}

// A: Delivering starts when the message enters the worker's mailbox
$ jet run run.jet
first:delivering
duplicate:delivering
delivered:order

options.name: Delivering starts when the worker takes the message
options.detail: send_durable leaves the delivery Accepted. The first receive that hands the message to the worker writes Delivering. A status read right after the send says Accepted, and so does the duplicate send's status.
options.technical: Move the mark_delivered append from send_durable and pending admission into receive. Every durable receive appends one E record under the store lock. Golden lines 1 and 2 become `first:accepted` and `duplicate:accepted`.

comparisons.note: A publisher confirm says the broker stored the message; delivery to a consumer and its ack are later, separate events. Source: rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms.
An activity task is Scheduled when recorded and Started only when a worker polls it, which is a separate history event. Source: docs.temporal.io/activities, activity execution states.
comparisons.code:
ActivityTaskScheduled  // recorded

decisions.title: How `jet fix` moves callers off an old function when the new one takes different arguments
decisions.situation: Libraries retire functions with a deprecation marker that names the replacement. Callers get a warning, and `jet fix` edits their code, but only by renaming the call. When the replacement takes different arguments, the rename breaks the caller, and the only safe path is a hand edit in every program. The owner decides how `jet fix` should handle that case. We recommend three steps in order: inline a wrapper, else use the author's pattern, else print the exact edit.
decisions.gist: When a library retires a function whose replacement takes different arguments, how should `jet fix` update the callers?
decisions.lesson: A library marks an old function as deprecated and names its replacement. Callers get a warning, and `jet fix` edits their code. Today that edit can only rename the call, so any change in arguments needs a hand edit in every program that uses the library.
decisions.story: Sam's charting package replaces `double(x)` with `scaled(x, 2)`. Two hundred programs call `double`. Each owner sees the warning and runs `jet fix`, which should leave every program building without a hand edit.
decisions.detail:
Source: card #6376, report Docs/research/language-release-notes-2026-10-30.md. Probe $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/MemDesign-4/probes/rel/r11_deprecated.jet on jet 03c64ad0c4: `jet fix` applied 2 fixes, and the fixed copy fails with E0766 because `double(4)` became `scaled(4)`. That misapplied rename is card #6405, a defect under any option.

Related law: D-STRUCT-LIFE1=A (#2052, `#Deprecated(since:, use:)`, rename-only fix), #6068 (every break ships a `jet fix` rewrite). Go 1.26 release notes, Tools section: go fix is the home of modernizers and a source-level inliner driven by `//go:fix inline`.

options.name: Inline, else a pattern, else an exact step
options.detail:
First, if the old function's body is one returned expression, `jet fix` puts that expression at each call with the caller's arguments. A plain rename is the simplest such body, so today's markers keep working.

Second, for any other body, the author may add a call pattern to the marker, and `jet fix` fills it in.

Otherwise `jet fix` leaves the call alone. The warning then prints the exact edit, such as which new argument `scaled` needs.
options.technical:
Step 1 needs no new marker word: `use:` plus a body of `return <expr>` whose names are all visible to callers. The rewrite works on the checked call and binds an argument to a local first when it is used other than exactly once, in order.

Step 2 is `rewrite: "scaled({a}, 2)"`, checked against the old signature when the library builds. A pattern on a wrapper body is refused with a registered error, so there is never a second copy.

Step 3: L2001 names the replacement's signature and each parameter without a default. `jet fix` re-checks every edited file and rolls back a failing edit.

options.name: Rename only
options.detail: The marker keeps `use:` for renames. `jet fix` applies it only when the replacement accepts the old call's arguments unchanged. Otherwise the warning says to edit the call by hand.
options.technical: No new marker form. The fix engine checks that the renamed call type-checks before applying it, and the L2001 text stops promising automatic migration when it would not.

options.name: Pattern only
options.detail: Every automatic migration is written as a text pattern in the marker, with holes named after the old parameters. `jet fix` fills the holes with each caller's arguments. Without a pattern, only plain renames are applied.
options.technical: Marker `#Deprecated(since: "1.2", rewrite: "scaled({a}, 2)")`. The pattern is parsed and checked against the old signature when the library builds. Argument binding follows A's evaluate-once rule. The checker does not compare the pattern with the body.

comparisons.note: `go fix` gained a source-level inliner; authors mark wrappers with `//go:fix inline` to migrate their own users.
comparisons.code:
//go:fix inline
func Double(a int) int { return Scaled(a, 2) }

comparisons.note: Breaking changes shipped with deprecated aliases and compiler fix-its, so code moved forward without hand edits.
comparisons.code: # old name kept as a deprecated alias; the compiler suggests the new spelling

comparisons.note: `#[deprecated(since, note)]` prints free text; stable Rust has no automatic rewrite for library deprecations.
comparisons.code:
#[deprecated(since = "1.2.0", note = "use scaled(x, 2)")]
pub fn double(x: i32) -> i32 { scaled(x, 2) }

recommendation.why: Most retirements are thin wrappers, so inlining the checked body handles them with nothing new to write. A pattern covers the rest, and an exact step covers what no tool can.
gains: Package upgrades need no hand edits whenever a wrapper or pattern exists.
`jet fix` never leaves a broken call behind.

whyNot.reason: It leaves every argument change as a hand edit in every program that uses the library.
It makes authors restate each wrapper as text, which can then disagree with the real body.

recommendation.tradeoff: A gives each case its best tool: the body when it is a wrapper, the author's pattern when given, and an exact instruction otherwise.

decisions.title: A module's effect cap is `#FX(...)` on its `module` line
decisions.situation: Jet limits what code may do at four levels: a block, a function, a package and a single run. A module has no limit of its own, so a team that wants its pricing code never to touch the network or files must repeat the promise on every function. Writing the same `#FX` marker on a module line is accepted today but silently does nothing. The vote decides where a module's cap is written. We recommend the `#FX` marker on the module line, the way a block already takes it.
decisions.gist: Where should a cap on what one module of code may do be written?
decisions.lesson: An effect is a kind of power, such as network or file access. Jet caps effects on a block with `#FX(...)` and on a function with its row. A package caps them with `authority:`, and a run with `--deny`. Modules are the missing step. A module cap covers every function inside, so the promise is written once and checked everywhere.
decisions.story: Ana's shop app keeps its price rules in `module pricing`. The team promises that pricing never reaches the network or the disk, so prices are reproducible in tests. Today that promise lives in a code-review checklist, and a helper that reads a file slipped in last month.
decisions.detail:
Provenance. Card c0rzkb53. Folded into the D-EFFECT-LIMITS1 package ballot, which the owner rejected; this is its module question alone. Ratified and not on this ballot: function rows in the arrow (D-SHAPE8=A), `#FX` on blocks (D-ABILITY-NAME2=A) and denials through calls (D-PROP1). Also settled: inferred rows (D-EFFECT-OMIT1=A) and package `authority:` (D-AUTH-AMBIENT3=A, D-AUTHORITY-DENYROW1=A).

What the probes found, in $JET_SCRATCH_ROOT/lanes/Main/q/bd/probe/fx. modcap.jet: `#FX(!Net, !FS)` above `module pricing { }` parses. modcap_breach.jet: the same cap over a function that reads a file checks clean, so the marker is accepted and ignored today.

fn_marker.jet: `#FX(!FS)` above a `fn` is an internal compiler error ("the function marker `#FX` is not supported by the self-hosted checker yet"). rungs_a/run.jet is option A's program; it checks clean today because the cap is ignored. These findings are notes for existing cards, not new cards.

Central review. A lead who wants one place still has it: package `authority.deny` applies to every module, and `jet explain effects --caps` lists each module cap with its file and line.

Reads with the related ballots. D-EFFTYPE-MODEL1 asks whether types and traits get their own cap; under A here, a type's promise comes from its module's cap. D-EFFTYPE-USES1 puts the same `#FX` above an `effect` declaration with the same "at most" meaning. D-MARK-SCOPE1 already lets `#Policy` sit on module lines; A here gives `#FX` the same place. D-EFFTYPE-TARGET1 adds the artifact limit below the package.

options.name: `#FX` on the module line
options.detail:
A module takes the `#FX(...)` marker on the line above its `module` declaration, exactly as a block takes it. The cap covers every function inside, including nested modules. An inner cap or function row may only tighten it.

The cap sits in the parent file, so code inside the module cannot loosen its own cap. `#Policy` already sits on module lines the same way. `jet explain effects` lists every cap in force, nearest first.
options.technical:
Ladder after A: `#FX` block, `-[ ]>` function, `#FX` module, package `authority:`, run `--allow/--deny`. The marker already parses on module declarations (probe/fx/modcap.jet) but sema ignores it: probe/fx/modcap_breach.jet reads a file under `#FX(!Net, !FS)` and checks clean.

A makes the module cap a ceiling plus denials, the function-row rule (Effects/Checks.jet:2207-2219). E0712 and E0749 gain the cap line as a secondary label. D-MARK-SCOPE1 matrix mode for `#FX` on modules: tighten (intersect). Grants stay site-bound: `#FX(grant: …)` is still block-only. Note: `#FX` above a `fn` today is an internal compiler error (probe/fx/fn_marker.jet), not a refusal; a function's limit is its row.

options.name: Caps in package `authority:`
options.detail:
The package file's `authority:` gains a `modules:` table naming each module and its cap. The project's rights and its module caps then sit in one file that one person can review, as Deno and LavaMoat keep policy in one place.

The cost is that each module name appears twice. A module renamed in code keeps no cap until package.jet is updated, so the checker must refuse unknown names.
options.technical: New `authority.modules: { path: { allow?, deny? } }` in package.jet, parsed beside allow, deny and grants (packages/typed_settings/package.jet shape). Unknown module paths are an error. D-TEAMPOLICY1's parsed-but-unenforced `policy.effects` is retired into it.

options.name: Rows on each function
options.detail:
Modules stay without a cap. A team that wants pricing free of network and files writes `-[!Net, !FS]>` on each function, as Koka and Flix put every effect on functions. Callers see the promise exactly where they look.

The promise is repeated on every function, and a helper added without a row is inferred instead of capped. The silent marker on module lines becomes an error.
options.technical: Today's rule kept. `#FX` on a module declaration becomes a refusal naming the per-function row as the fix, closing the silent no-op found in probe/fx/modcap_breach.jet.

comparisons.note: Lint levels on a `mod` line cover the whole module; forbid cannot be loosened inside. Source: Rust reference, lint attributes.
Permissions are listed in one config for the whole program, as option B lists caps. Source: https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/security/
Effects live only on function types; there is no module-level limit, as in option C. Source: https://koka-lang.github.io/koka/doc/book.html

recommendation.why: A adds the missing step with the marker blocks already use, written once where the module is declared. Code inside cannot loosen it, and beginners never see it.
gains: One promise covers every function in the module.
The marker that silently did nothing now works.

whyNot.reason: B writes each module name twice, and a rename silently drops the cap until package.jet is fixed.
C repeats the promise on every function, and a new helper slips past it.

recommendation.tradeoff: Caps live beside the modules they cover rather than in one file; `jet explain effects` gathers them.
